reference: Yes, both November ISM PMIs came in below expectations. Analysts and economists in aggregate were expecting a bounce higher in these purchasing manager surveys, but instead the results drifted down. The manufacturing PMI was in contraction territory (below 50%) at 48.1%, while the non-manufacturing PMI was in slow-expansion mode at 53.9%. These misses contributed to the unclear economic inflection point, and the NY Fed noted that "Negative surprises from the ISM manufacturing survey were only partially offset by positive surprises from employment data," with their Nowcast at just 0.6% GDP growth for Q4 versus the Atlanta Fed GDPNow estimate of 2.0%.
reference_contexts: U.S. Business Cycle Status As a recap, in my free newsletter from three weeks ago, I discussed that we were at an unclear U.S. economic inflection point, and then two weeks ago in the previous premium report, I gave some updated data and re-iterated this inflection point that we’re in. Unfortunately, we still have an unclear rate-of-change direction for this inflection point and are thus still basically within a “Schrodinger’s zone” of potential divergence in both directions, but we do have some more data points to work with. This past week, we had November ISM manufacturing and non-manufacturing purchasing manger’s indices (PMIs) come in below expectations. Analysts and economists in aggregate were expecting a bounce higher in these PMI surveys, but instead the results drifted down. The manufacturing PMI is in contraction (below 50%) with a reading of 48.1%. The non-manufacturing PMI was in slow-expansion mode at 53.9%. Chart Source: Trading Economics On the other hand, we also had a better-than-expected non-farm payroll report on Friday, with 266K net jobs added in November and a dip in the official unemployment rate from 3.6% to just 3.5%. This number included the end of the GM strike, but even considering that, it was stronger than expected. This strong jobs report was supported by two weeks in a row of relatively tame initial jobless claims reports as well. In my premium report from two weeks ago, I said we need to watch these initial jobless claims numbers. During the first two weeks of November, initial jobless claims were ticking up, indicating a potential bottom in employment, which would be very bearish. However, we’ve had two weeks in a row since then of declining initial jobless claims, which means we don’t really have a confirmed unemployment bottom yet, which is therefore neutral or bullish for now. The Atlanta Fed GDPNow estimate is for 2.0% GDP growth in Q4, and their estimate was below 0.5% just a few weeks ago in early/mid November. New data have significantly boosted their estimate from almost-recessionary levels to moderate levels. On the other hand, the NY Fed’s Nowcast estimate stands at 0.6% GDP growth for Q4, and 0.7% growth for Q1 of next year, which is very bearish. As they describe it, “Negative surprises from the ISM manufacturing survey were only partially offset by positive surprises from employment data.” So, even different Federal Reserve bank models have conflicting views based on current data. Here is an updated heatmap of various economic indicators for the U.S. economy for the past five years to break it down further, measured in year-over-year percent change terms: The chart starts from the bottom and goes up over five years (20 quarters, plus recent months where data exist), and each column represents one of the economic indicators. The interesting pattern in the chart is that the hardest-hit deep-red indicators during the 2016 slowdown (industrial production, capital goods orders, exports, imports, CPI, and overall GDP) have been holding up better during this 2019 slowdown (just orange or yellow at the moment), while the indicators that remained strong in 2016 (construction spending, payroll growth, and yield curve steepness) are the ones deeper in the red this time around in 2019. Basically, these sets of metrics have been taking turns for their periods of strength and weakness rather than all going up or down together. The stock market may have gotten a bit ahead of itself with bullishness throughout November, but overall there is no obvious deterioration in economic strength during this past month. On the other hand, there is no confirmed bounce towards a new cycle of growth just yet either. My strategy continues to be to maintain some defensive elements in my portfolio, along with ETFs for diversification, while hunting for attractively-priced high-quality stocks domestically and abroad.

There are currently three licensee operators of those 24 locations. The biggest licensee by far is based in Kuwait and has 16 locations throughout multiple Middle East countries and rights/options to expand into eastern Europe. I was in Egypt during much of October visiting family, and malls and restaurants there (often developed operators from Gulf states like Kuwait) are absolutely booming, and many of them have American restaurant brands like Chili’s. reference: Fox Restaurant Concepts ("FRC") is a small company founded by Sam Fox in 1998 that serves as an incubator/developer for new restaurant concepts. Sam Fox built a highly successful record of developing restaurant ideas and selling some of the mature ones off to other funds or businesses. Cheesecake Factory Inc first invested in 2016 into two of Fox's mature concepts, North Italia and Flower Child. After that multi-year period of successful co-investment, the company was in talks to purchase just those mature chains from Fox, but decided to go a step further and in July 2019 announced an agreement to acquire all of Fox Restaurant Concepts. They now own North Italia, Flower Child, a variety of smaller concepts, and the incubator structure itself. Sam Fox continues to lead FRC as an independent subsidiary, operating as a restaurant concept incubator, with North Italia operations moving from FRC's Arizona HQ to Cheesecake Factory's California HQ so the chain can be scaled up. On the debt question: the company historically maintained little or no long term debt, giving exceptional balance sheet strength for a small company, but in the most recent quarter they borrowed approximately $300 million to finance the FRC acquisition, which they plan to gradually pay down. Even with the added leverage, their debt/income ratio is only about 2-3x, compared to over 8x for Bloomin Brands. Worth noting for your research: FRC also has an unusually high Glassdoor rating of 4.1, versus 3.7 for The Cheesecake Factory itself.

Growth Plans and FRC Acquisition There was a small company called Fox Restaurant Concepts (“FRC” for short), founded by Sam Fox in 1998, that serves as an incubator/developer for new restaurant concepts. Sam Fox has developed a highly successful record of building out restaurant ideas and selling some of the mature ones to other funds or businesses. In 2016, Cheesecake Factory Inc invested into two of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, North Italia and Flower Child. Recently, after this multi-year period of successful co-investment, the company was in talks to purchase those mature restaurant chains from Fox. However, they decided to go a step further, and in July 2019, they announced an agreement to acquire all of Fox Restaurant Concepts. They now own North Italia, Flower Child, and a variety of smaller concepts, as well as the incubator structure itself. Sam Fox will continue to lead FRC as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, operating as a restaurant concept incubator. North Italia operations will move from FRC’s HQ in Arizona to the Cheesecake Factory’s HQ in California, so that the company can begin scaling that chain up alongside The Cheesecake Factory. The rest of the smaller concepts will continue to be led by FRC in Arizona, with the option to scale the mature ones up over time as they become mature and proven enough. North Italia currently has 21 locations, and Cheesecake Factory Inc expects that they can scale the chain to about 200 in the United States. They have a streamlined Italian upscale casual menu with an extensive wine and cocktail selection, and alcohol sales account for over 30% of total sales (compared to only 12% for The Cheesecake Factory restaurants). Private dining is a more significant portion of their sales than most restaurant chains. These locations are very profitable, with a 35% cash-on-cash return according to the company. The company expects to increase the location count of The Cheesecake Factory by about 3% per year, while North Italia and various FRC locations are expected to increase by 20% per year or more. The company’s namesake brand is the mature cash-generator, while these other concepts are the growth drivers. I think this acquisition has great synergy. FRC and their North Italia brand bring diversification and significant growth potential. Cheesecake Factory Inc brings plenty of capital for more rapid expansion of Fox’s mature restaurant concepts, and provides logistics and other operational infrastructure to scale them up as well. user_input: For The Cheesecake Factory, how severe is the margin pressure risk?
reference: Margin pressure is classified as a major risk. While the international licensed locations offer high margins, the company-operated locations, which represent the bulk of revenue, have been under margin pressure because labor costs have been increasing while the company has been slow to raise menu prices. Operating margins peaked at 8.8% in 2016 but are currently as low as 5.9%. The growth of North Italia, whose significant alcohol mix supports 35% cash-on-cash return potential per location, may help offset these margin pressures as that chain becomes a larger portion of the overall company.
reference_contexts: Risks Industry Competition- Moderate Risk The primary risk for any restaurant stock is that it ceases to have the most relevant food and environment for changing consumer preferences. The restaurant industry is one of the most challenging, and it requires good management to keep a tight ship and to continually update the menu and environment in order to maintain strong customer traffic. The company updates their menu twice per year, including pricing changes, and in response to criticism about their large portion sizes, The Cheesecake Factory has introduced what they refer to as a SkinnyLicious menu subset that focuses on lower-calorie portions. With Cheesecake Factory Inc’s strong management team, and with the added diversification of North Italia and other brands within Fox Restaurant Concepts, I believe that the company is well-protected from some of the more negative scenarios that restaurants can face. However, it’s always a risk worth monitoring. Margin Pressure- Major Risk Cheesecake Factory’s international licensed locations offer high margins, but their company-operated locations, which represent the bulk of their revenue, have been under margin pressure. Labor costs have been increasing but the company has been slow to raise menu prices. Operating margins reached a peak of 8.8% in 2016 but are currently as low as 5.9%. The growth of North Italia, with its significant alcohol mix leading to 35% cash-on-cash return potential per location, may help to offset these margin pressures as that chain becomes a larger portion of the overall company. Executive Retention- Moderate Risk As previously described, Cheesecake Factory Inc has been well-managed by its co-founder, David Overton, since 1992. He is currently 73, which means he could potentially have a decade or more leading the company ahead of him, or could retire at any time. The company has a strong executive team with long tenures at the company, but losing a co-founder as its long-time CEO would bring about transition risk. Specifically, there’s always a risk with new non-founder management that the company could lose its long-term focus and become more “corporate” with an increased focus on quarterly results and executive compensation, rather than focusing on the long-term process of building a successful company as they have been doing. On the flip side, fresh management at the top might help the company boost margins. For example, they might decide to streamline The Cheesecake Factory’s massive menu, which it seems to me as a customer/investor is something that is at least worth exploring. In addition, Cheesecake Factory Inc recently acquired Fox Restaurant Concepts, which is reliant on Sam Fox’s expertise. Fox is now leading this segment as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, and he has a proven track record of successful restaurant concepts. If he were to leave the company, it would bring about significant transition risk for this smaller but promising segment of the overall company. Economic Cycle- Moderate Risk Restaurant sales are moderately affected by the economic cycle. People eat out less, and may choose less expensive options, during recessionary periods. The U.S. restaurant industry is healthy and growing, with about $55 billion in revenue per month: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Industry-wide revenue grows by about 5% per year on average, but during the severe recession of 2008/2009, the year-over-year industry growth briefly dropped to about -2%: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed This doesn’t seem like much, but it can have a substantial impact on operating margins, which are only 5-8% for a company like Cheesecake Factory Inc. Their earnings per share dropped by over 20% during the 2008/2009 recession. For the full year 2018, the company’s earnings per share were already down 14% from their 2016 highs, and is what led to a significant part of the stock’s recent decline. This is a risk worth factoring into growth rates, and is one reason why I instantly knocked down the company’s 8% target revenue growth to a baseline estimate of 6%. Growing by 8% represents an ideal potential year, where the industry is great and the company executes its new growth strategy well. Any long-term growth period, however, needs to assume that a recession occurs somewhere in there, severely throwing off expected growth numbers for a year or two. Stock Market Selloff- Moderate Risk Regardless of economic and earnings performance, Cheesecake’s stock could easily be subject to a sell-off should the S&P 500 face a severe correction. This particular stock was less volatile than the S&P 500 during the 2001 recession, but far more volatile than the S&P 500 during the 2008/2009 recession, with an 80% draw down from its high point. As of today, the stock is already in a 35% draw down from its 2017 all-time high of over $64/share. Chart Source: Y Charts It’s not hard to model a pretty severe scenario. Earnings drop by 20-25%, the valuation on those earnings falls by 20-25%, and you temporarily have share prices cut in half from their previous highs. This is the kind of stock that I approach as though I want to own the company for its future cash flows and mostly ignore fluctuating stock prices. However, those fluctuating stock prices can give us attractive entry prices to increase our position, and if the stock price ever gets way ahead of fundamentals, we can trim the position. Tax Changes- Moderate Risk U.S. corporations are enjoying the lowest tax rates they’ve had in modern history. Due to the U.S. corporate tax cuts that were passed in 2017 and came into effect in 2018, Cheesecake Factory has sharply reduced tax rates. These tax cuts were not paid for by reduced government spending; they were merely additive to the U.S. deficit, which now stands at 5% of GDP and growing. It’s quite possible that future administrations will reverse these corporate tax cuts, which would negatively impact the net income of most U.S. companies including Cheesecake Factory Inc. user_input: so i been reading yer letter and them charts all say St. Louis Fed on them, can u explain me what the St. Louis Fed data actually showing about them housing starts number and also the job openings thing, cuz i cant tell if economy is slowing or not for my 18-24 month positioning?
reference: The St. Louis Fed charts in the letter point to an inconclusive-but-slowing pattern for U.S. economic output, even while stocks push to new highs. On housing starts, the St. Louis Fed chart showed a blockbuster December number with a massive spike well above estimates, helped by the drop in thirty-year fixed mortgage rates from cycle highs of about 5% in late 2018 down to between 3.50% and 3.75% in recent months, which improves affordability and appears to be supporting housing demand. However, the non-seasonally-adjusted St. Louis Fed chart was far less spectacular: December is normally the weakest month for starts due to cold weather and the holidays, but this December was among the warmest and least-snowy on record, so starts still declined, just less than usual, which made the seasonally-adjusted figure look remarkably high. On job openings, the St. Louis Fed data show total U.S. job openings fell from over 7.3 million to 6.8 million, well below expectations, putting the metric in its deepest year-over-year percent decline of this business cycle. That matters because the year-over-year percent change in job openings tracks closely with the year-over-year percent change in real GDP, and since job openings is monthly while real GDP is quarterly and lagged, it gives an information lead on where GDP may be headed. Some analysts still call 6.8 million solid because in absolute terms it is high and above the number of officially unemployed, but there is a skill/education/salary mismatch, and most indicators look great in absolute terms at this point in the cycle; the year-over-year change view is more sensitive and informative. Additionally, the St. Louis Fed chart on jobless claims showed the moving average of initial claims improved to resume a flattish trend rather than worsening, while continuing claims worsened. The unemployment rate and its related indicators are the key things to watch in 2020 to determine whether the business cycle has another spurt of growth left or is likely to enter a significant downturn.
reference_contexts: U.S. Business Cycle Status The U.S. economy continues to show an inconclusive-but-slowing pattern for economic output, even as the stock market pushes to new highs. Housing Starts: Solid, but Over-Reported The most surprising number from this past week, reported on Friday, was that housing starts came in with a blockbuster number. They had a massive spike up, which was way above estimates and received quite a bit of attention: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed The reduction in interest rates over the past year has been helpful for the housing market. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates had increased to cycle highs of about 5% in late 2018, but have since fallen back down to between 3.50% and 3.75% within the past several months, which makes a big difference for home affordability. This seems to be helping housing demand. However, digging into it a bit more, December’s big gain was mainly due to seasonal adjustments. The non-seasonally-adjusted figure was far less spectacular: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed December is usually the lowest month for housing starts, because it’s cold in many parts of the country and because it’s the holiday season. However, this December was among the warmest and least-snowy Decembers on record for most of the United States, meaning it was a much “less-bad” home-building month than a typical December. So, housing starts declined, but did not decline as much as they usually do in December, and thus the seasonally-adjusted figure was remarkably high. Job Openings: Not So Good It was also reported on Friday that the total amount of U.S. job openings fell from over 7.3 million to 6.8 million, which was well below expectations. The job openings metric is now in its deepest year-over-year percent decline of this business cycle. The year-over-year percentage change in job openings tracks very closely to year-over-year percentage change in real GDP. Real GDP is reported quarterly with a considerable lag (we’re still waiting on the Q4 2019 figure, for example, which will come out at the end of January and then will be subject to revisions for a while), while job openings is a monthly metric, and therefore it gives an information lead on what the GDP report might look like or where it’s potentially headed. Job openings is only one economic variable and thus what it says is not perfect, but what it does say isn’t good: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Some analysts are still referring to this as a solid number because they are looking at in absolute terms rather than year-over-year change terms, and the latter is more sensitive and informative of the two ways of organizing it. In absolute terms, the 6.8 million number of job openings remains high, and remains above the number of people who are officially unemployed. However, there is a skill/education/salary mismatch between job openings and people looking for work. Most economic indicators look great in absolute terms at this point in the economic cycle (earnings, employment, spending, etc). The moments that matter are when they start to fall from those great levels, which is why viewing the numbers in year-over-year percent change terms is usually more informative. Jobless Claims: Some Stabilization Lastly, the moving average of initial jobless claims improved/reduced last week to resume a flattish trend rather than pushing forward with a worsening/upward trend, while the moving average of continuing jobless claims worsened: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed The unemployment rate, along with its various indicators like jobless claims and job openings, are the key areas to watch throughout 2020 because this is what will be the deciding factor for whether the U.S. business cycle has another spurt of growth left in it, or if it is likely to enter a significant downturn.

user_input: As someone who allocates across precious metals and uses relative valuation to time entries, I would like to understand how the author's long-standing bullish stance on gold compares to their view on platinum, particularly regarding the historical price relationship between the two metals and what makes platinum attractive now.
reference: The author has been significantly bullish on gold and silver, along with their various miners and financiers, since October 2018 (and to a more limited extent prior to that) as allocations within a diversified portfolio, and is bullish on them for fundamental reasons. Both gold and silver "bottomed" right around the start of 2016 and have been in a choppy uptrend since. Platinum, by contrast, also reached a low point in that same 2016 time-frame but then made even lower lows in late 2018, putting it on its own bearish trend; the author had no position in platinum because there was no visible bullish catalyst for a trend reversal, despite a very long-term bullish outlook. Historically, platinum traded at a higher price than gold, but within roughly the past decade it has traded at a discount to gold, which made it attractive from a valuation perspective even while its price chart remained ugly. Currently platinum sits at about $1,000+ versus gold at $1,550+. With palladium trading at well over twice the price of both platinum and gold, and rhodium also very expensive, platinum is arguably the true value play among the precious metals. Its historically cheap price relative to gold should also make platinum increasingly attractive for jewelry as a more cost-effective option, even though it has generally been considered the more premium material. The author recently added platinum bars to their bullion collection and considers the long-term risk/reward of platinum and the PPLT ETF attractive as a "buy" for a small allocation within a diversified, regularly rebalanced portfolio, with ongoing dollar-cost averaging.
reference_contexts: ETF Spotlight: PPLT I recently became a bit more bullish on platinum, so I want to take a moment to highlight it. Long-time readers know that I’ve been significantly bullish on gold and silver and their various miners and financiers since October 2018 (and to a more limited extent prior to that) as allocations within a diversified portfolio, but I haven’t written much about platinum. Gold and silver both “bottomed” right around the start of 2016 and have been in a choppy uptrend since. More importantly, I am bullish on them for fundamental reasons, and have an article dedicated to precious metals here. Platinum also reached a low point back in the same 2016 time-frame, but reached even lower lows in late 2018, so it has been on its own bearish trend. While I’ve been bullish on platinum with a very long-term outlook, the problem was that I did not see a bullish catalyst for a trend reversal yet, so I was less interested in it than I was with gold and silver, and thus had no position in it. Platinum has historically traded at a higher price than gold, but roughly within the past decade, it has traded at a discount to gold. So it has been attractive from a valuation perspective for some time, but has had a very ugly price chart for a while. Here’s a 10-year chart: Platinum has had a perfect storm of bearishness until recently. The metal is heavily used for catalytic converters in vehicles to reduce harmful emissions. Electric vehicles do not need catalytic converters, so that is a long-term demand destruction risk for platinum usage. Car sales in general have been in a significant downtrend over the past year; that industry is one of the weakest parts of the global economy. In addition, another platinum-group metal, palladium, has been substituted for platinum in the past several years for a lot of catalytic converter usage. Historically, palladium was cheaper than platinum, but now palladium trades for well over twice the price of both platinum and gold, which is historically extremely unusual. This hasn’t had much financial media attention, but within the past two weeks alone, the prices of both palladium and its rarer counterpart rhodium (both platinum-group metals) went absolutely vertical: Chart Source: Kitco Unlike gold and silver that are mined all over the world, a very small number of emerging market countries produce almost all platinum-group metals, including platinum, palladium, and rhodium. So, supply/demand balances are quite strict. New emissions standards in China and elsewhere are likely a factor in the increased demand and prices since the beginning of 2020. Palladium and platinum are able to be substituted for each other for catalytic converters in many cases, with some engineering work involved. Palladium has historically been the cheaper metal, but in this current cycle where most designs are made for it, palladium demand has been strong, driving the price up. As long as palladium prices remain elevated, it makes the engineering case for switching to platinum more attractive. These things tend to go in cycles. In addition, while platinum remains historically cheap compared to gold (about $1,000+ vs $1,550+ at the moment), platinum’s usage in jewelry should become increasingly attractive as a more cost-effective option, even though ironically it has generally been considered the more premium material. For most of history, platinum has been the more expensive metal compared to gold. With palladium and rhodium at very high prices, and gold priced well above platinum, platinum is arguably the true value play among the precious metals. In the past couple weeks, it has shown small signs of life, indicating that the past year may have been the actual bottom for the metal, and that the expensive prices for rhodium and platinum are spilling over into platinum. Last week, I added some platinum bars to my bullion collection for the first time. I may also add a small allocation to the Aberdeen Standard Physical Platinum Shares ETF (PPLT) to some of my portfolios for a more liquid and cost-effective source of exposure. Although it’s not certain, there are signs that platinum, and subsequently the PPLT ETF, may have formed a bottoming process. When it comes to metals, especially physical bullion, I am extraordinarily patient. Frankly, I don’t know how platinum will do this year or next, for example. However, I now consider the long-term risk/reward ratio of platinum and the PPLT ETF to be attractive as part of a diversified and regularly rebalanced portfolio, and thus consider it to be a “buy” for a small allocation, with ongoing dollar-cost averaging.

reference: Since inception, EPD has absolutely crushed the S&P 500 in terms of total returns, and it currently pays a distribution yield of over 6% per year with two decades of consecutive annual distribution increases, which makes it an attractive higher-yielding investment. Within the past five years, however, EPD has significantly under-performed the S&P 500. This mirrors the broader U.S. energy sector, which dramatically outperformed the S&P 500 during the 2000-2009 decade only to dramatically underperform it during the 2010-2019 decade, especially in the second half of that latter decade. The key point is that the fundamentals of EPD's business have done very well this whole time since inception; it is merely the price that has done poorly in recent years. In other words, it is a high-quality business at a historically low valuation. With the recent major run-up in the S&P 500 and the comparative flat performance from EPD, the expected value of long-term forward returns for EPD has improved relative to the S&P 500, making it more seriously interesting.
reference_contexts: Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) Deep Dive Analysis Enterprise Products Partners LP (ticker: EPD) is one of the largest midstream operators in North America. They own a huge set of infrastructure for transportation, processing, storing, and exporting natural gas, crude oil, natural gas liquids (NGL), and petrochemicals. Chart Source: EPD December 2019 Investor Presentation at Wells Fargo Since inception, EPD has absolutely crushed the S&P 500 in terms of total returns: Plus, it currently pays a distribution yield of over 6% per year with two decades of consecutive annual distribution increases, which makes it an attractive higher-yielding investment. However, within the past five years, EPD has significantly under-performed the S&P 500: In the previous report about oil company Lukoil, I showed how the U.S. energy sector dramatically outperformed the S&P 500 during the 2000-2009 decade only to dramatically underperform it during the 2010-2019 decade, especially during the second half of that latter decade. EPD is in a similar situation that I believe could begin to turn favorable. The key factor for EPD is that the fundamentals of the business have done very well this whole time since inception; it’s merely the price that has done poorly in recent years. In other words, it’s a high-quality business at a historically low valuation. I’ve been bullish on EPD in recent years as an income investment after its big price decline, and wrote about it from time to time, but haven’t invested in it myself yet. The reason is that it requires filing an additional tax form, and the relative attractiveness of the business compared to the broader market hasn’t been compelling enough yet for a younger and more aggressive total-return investor such as myself (compared to someone who specifically wants the reliable distribution income from it, such as a retiree, for whom it would be great). I’ve been buying ENB, KMI, and OKE for my midstream exposure, which has been enough for me. However, with the recent major run-up in the S&P 500 and the comparative flat performance from EPD, my expected value of long-term forward returns for EPD has improved relative to the S&P 500. So, now I’m getting seriously more interested in it. Management and Performance The important aspect of EPD, unlike the previous recommendation of Lukoil, is that EPD primarily makes money from energy volumes, not energy prices. Their job is to transport, process, store, and/or export it, regardless of how cheap or expensive it is. So, as oil prices and natural gas prices have gone up and down, EPD has continued to increase its distributable cash flow per share and its distributions (dividends) per share. EPD also happens to be heavily focused on natural gas, natural gas liquids, and petrochemicals, with only about a quarter of its business exposed to crude oil volumes. Over the past two decades, there has been a major build-out of North American energy infrastructure, which is starting to flatten out. Therefore, it does make sense for midstream companies to trade at lower valuations than they use to, and to focus on total returns rather than aggressive growth. However, EPD is arguably the highest-quality business in the sector, and they’ve been grouped in valuation-wise with many of the more poorly-managed and highly-leveraged midstream businesses. This gives discerning investors a good opportunity, in my opinion. The oil price crash of 2015 due to oversupply of new shale oil was the big bearish moment for energy stocks and midstream companies, from which the U.S. energy industry still has not fully recovered. Many midstream businesses were over-leveraged, and had to cut their dividends, sell assets, and destroy unitholder capital. However, EPD was one of the few midstream businesses that emerged almost unscathed in terms of its fundamentals. Although its overvalued unit price came back down to reality (which is outside of management’s control), the business continued to raise dividends and grow distributable cash flow. Chart Source: EPD December 2019 Investor Presentation at Wells Fargo This was because, even during the boom times of high energy prices and strong growth, EPD management never over-leveraged the business, and never tried to maximize returns at the cost of financial safety. In both good times and bad for the energy sector, EPD management continued to prudently operate the business with proper risk management and a focus on sustainable growth with 12% or better returns on invested capital while maintaining a fortress balance sheet. During bull markets (whether in stocks, or energy, or junk bonds, or cryptocurrencies, or whatever market you’re looking at), the most leveraged and risk-taking members look like they’re the smartest ones for a while, with the best growth. Then when the bear market comes and the leveraged ones go down in flames, the prudent ones turn out to be the real winners. It’s the classic “tortoise vs hare” analogy, in other words. That was what EPD did compared to many of its midstream competitors, and is a good way of thinking about investing in general. In addition, EPD has been near the forefront of good management practices in the midstream sector. They eliminated their 50% incentive distribution rights (IDRs) in 2002, which made the partnership more financially sustainable for limited partners. More recently, they have shifted towards a mostly self-funding model, which means they have intentionally slowed-down their distribution growth to let distributable cash flow per share outpace cash distributions per share, so that the distribution payout ratio would decrease. That’s the gap between the blue and gray areas in the chart above. EPD is one-third owned by management, including the Duncan family, which partially explains why it has been so well-managed. The late Dan Duncan was the co-founder and chairman of EPD, and now his descendants have his big multi-billion-dollar stake in the business, and continue to oversee it with a long-term view rather than quarter-by-quarter short-sightedness. EPD currently has a BBB+ credit rating, which places it as being tied in first place, along with ENB and MMP, as having the highest credit rating in the midstream industry.

Considering that EPD only pays out about 2/3rds of its distributable cash flow as distributions, leaving the other 1/3rd for growth reinvestment or potentially for forward unit buybacks, this should be a fair baseline. Even in a more bearish scenario, where distribution increases slow down to 2-3%, it still has a solid chance of outperforming the S&P 500 for the long run from current levels, particularly within a diversified portfolio, and especially for investors that need investment income. MLPs vs Corporations, and a Potential Catalyst EPD is a master limited partnership (MLP) rather than a standard corporation, so the tax situation is a bit more complex. Instead of being broken into shares, it is broken into units, and investors are called unitholders rather than shareholders. Historically, the MLP is a tax-advantaged structure compared to corporations. However, investors will receive an extra tax form during tax season, and will need to file that as part of their tax return. Tax professionals and programs like Turbo Tax can generally do these forms without a problem, but it does represent an extra thing to deal with. Investors also need to be careful about putting a large allocation of an MLP into a retirement account, because if it creates more than $1,000 in unrelated business taxable income (UBTI), investors may have to pay a tax bill on their retirement account for that holding. This makes some investors not want to own MLPs, and most funds don’t include MLPs. So, a company like EPD can be under-owned, which can push down its valuation. As corporate tax rates have decreased over decades and as growth has slowed in the midstream sector, the comparative advantages to being an MLP compared to a corporation have diminished. Many other midstream businesses, such as KMI and the various subsidiaries of ENB have consolidated into corporate structures. EPD, however, remains an MLP. EPD has reported that they have carefully considered the possibility of a transition to a corporation, but have not seen a strong reason to do so yet. If it were to occur, it could be a catalyst for a moderate valuation increase as more investors and funds buy into it, but there have also been instances of big tax bills associated with MLP-to-corporation conversions. However, because EPD is so heavily family-owned, they likely wouldn’t make any move that would be tax-disadvantaged for unitholders as some MLPs have in the past. Whether they ultimately convert or not will surely be a well-reasoned decision, and performed in the most tax-efficient way. If converted, it could result in a moderate valuation increase, serving as a potential catalyst for improved stock performance. reference_contexts: their own stock, meaning they regularly issue new shares and use that capital to invest in new projects and make acquisitions. Traditionally high-yield industries like real estate investment trusts (REITs), master limited partnerships (MLPs), yieldcos, and business development companies (BDCs) usually fall under this category. They’re paying out most of their cash flow as dividends/distributions, so in order to raise new capital and expand, they need to issue new shares. All else being equal, they do very well when their shares are expensive. Here’s the problem. Companies that are heavily reliant on selling shares to fund growth can quickly collapse if their share price gets too low, because they can no longer profitably sell their shares to fund projects. There’s a red line somewhere for each of these net sellers of stock at which they can not grow per-share value by selling new shares to raise capital. For example, if their share prices sink and their dividend yield is 12%, they can’t issue new shares to fund projects that give them only 10% returns. They then have to rely on issuing debt or cutting the dividend to raise liquidity. Most dividend investors are aware of what happened to Kinder Morgan (KMI) and a bunch of other MLPs a few years ago during the oil price crash. Kinder Morgan was considered the blue chip version of a master limited partnership; the long-standing gold standard of its industry. They built extensive pipelines throughout the United States, and funded that growth by issuing new units and by using high levels of debt leverage. For a very long time, this was a market-beating strategy with an amazing combo of yield and growth. But when oil prices crashed in 2015, the industry ran into a serious problem and MLP valuations fell dramatically. For a normal corporation, this would not have been as big of a deal. But because Kinder Morgan was reliant on continually issuing new shares to fund growth, and its share prices were suddenly cut in half, it quickly fell into a liquidity trap by losing its usual source of new capital. And because they were already highly leveraged, they couldn’t take on too much new debt. As a result, they had to cut the dividend and sell some of their assets at bad prices to raise liquidity and remain solvent, and years later they are still recovering. EPD avoided that problem by not having excessive leverage; they were able to operate normally and let their unit price recover before issuing more units for further growth projects. They used a mild increase in debt to get through that harder period, which they have since reduced. Now, many midstream companies including KMI and EPD have shifted towards a self-funding model. (Of course, the way EPD did it by choice rather than necessity was the smarter move.) This means that they have purposely slowed down their distribution growth (or cut them in the case of KMI and many others) to create a larger source of inside capital. In other words, if a company earns $1.00 in distributable cash flow per share and pays $0.95 in distributions, then it only has 5% of its cashflow left over to fund growth projects. So, it needs to dilute its unit base, sell units, and raise cash, if it wants to grow. This works very well in a strong growth environment, but causes problems during recessions when unit prices are low. If they decide to become self-funding, and distributable cash flow increases at, say, 6% per year, they can keep their distribution growing at, say, 3% per year. And then companies all have different levels of balance sheet strength to get through hard times. This low oil price environment is bad for all oil producers, but is a deathblow to that second type of group that has high ongoing production costs, because after the oil companies’ hedges wear off, it’s unprofitable to produce every new marginal barrel. They are the ones that will have a tough time surviving, and many will go bankrupt if this continues for a while. The first type of oil producer, the kind that already made a big upfront investment and now has low-cost operational production, can weather the storm better and come out the other side. For both groups, a strong balance sheet and the amount of hedging they had in place both help their survival odds.

user_input: In the March 2020 macro deep dive, how is Mexico characterized relative to other emerging markets in terms of financial stability?
reference: Mexico is grouped among the more troubled emerging markets. The report notes that financial conditions vary significantly by nation within emerging markets: some, such as Taiwan and Thailand, are described as financially stable, while others, including Argentina, Indonesia, and Mexico, are characterized as more troubled. This distinction is made in the context of a global financial system that is about to be tested in both anticipated and unanticipated ways, amid record-high debt levels, flat corporate profit growth in 2019, and economic indicators pointing flat or down even before the coronavirus and the quarantine response accelerated the downturn.
reference_contexts: Market Crash Deep Dive Analysis Published March 15, 2020 This past week has been one of the most historic weeks in global stock market history, on par in terms of volatility with 2008, 1987, or 1929. Rather than do a deep dive on an individual stock as usual, this report’s deep dive will be on the whole macro situation along with several stock examples, due to the unprecedented market situation. Nobody has the full picture including me, and in this environment anything can happen, but a lot of the things we’ve been tracking for a couple years now, in my free newsletters and articles, and more recently in this premium research service, are coming home to roost and these are key turning points to see how they turn out. The main surprise is that it’s all happening faster than expected, accelerated by the coronavirus and more specifically the quarantine response to it. There’s often a curve ball or black swan somewhere, and this time it was a virus. Many pundits on CNBC and other media outlets seem to think that the economy was doing just fine before this hit, but that was not the case. Corporate profit growth was 0% in 2019, and excluding buybacks and tax cuts has been flat for several years before the involvement of trade wars or viruses. Most year-over-year economic indicators were pointing flat or down. Debt levels are near record highs, and the bottom half of the U.S. population is deeply financially insecure, more than they have been historically. The U.S. government deficit as a percentage of GDP has been rising dramatically since 2016; it’s supposed to shrink during a strong economy. Europe and Japan are better or worse in some ways, with even higher total debt levels but more financially secure people in the lower income levels. Germany has had a government budget surplus from which it can now draw from. With emerging markets, it varies significantly depending on the specific nation. Some are financially stable, like Taiwan or Thailand, while others like Argentina, Indonesia, and Mexico are more troubled. This situation will put the global financial system to the test in ways we saw coming, and in ways we won’t. For example, Thailand is in financially good shape with large financial reserves, but is heavily reliant on $60+ billion/year in tourism revenue, which is drying up from this virus more than it would in a normal recession. Many U.S. restaurants are in decent shape financially, but can they handle months with limited customers, in a far deeper restaurant sales decline than a normal recession? We’ll see. The Systemic Debt Issue The United States reached a peak total debt (public + private) at 380% of GDP in 2009. That was our all-time record high. More specifically, the U.S. entered that recession with a total debt/GDP ratio of a bit under 350%, and it grew to 380% during the process. After a period of modest deleveraging, mainly in the housing sector, we’re currently back down to just under 350% debt to GDP. So, we’re entering this likely recession with a similar level of debt as 2007. Specifically, we have way higher government debt, as well as higher consumer credit and corporate debt, but lower mortgage debt compared to that time, as a percentage of GDP. The third highest debt level ever reached was back in the Great Depression that started in 1929. In the early 1930’s at its peak, we reached 300% debt to GDP. It’s too far back to be on the St. Louis Fed chart above, but there are other data sources that recorded it. In fourth place was the 2001 recession, which was entered with about 275% debt to GDP. Debt magnifies everything, and is a big variable for what makes some recessions worse than others. The Great Depression of 1929 and the Great Recession of 2008 were so severe in part because debt levels were so historically high. Those two periods are “special” in terms of how rapidly the monetary base was expanded to deal with them compared to every other recession. This is a chart of the U.S. monetary base in log form, so every move up is exponential and this makes it easier to see the differences between normal exponential growth and accelerated exponential growth. Those periods from 1930-1950 and 2008-present represent multi-fold increases in the monetary base in a short period of time, while every other recession on the chart looks normal. The zero bound on interest rates was hit in these two major periods, so they just printed money for stimulus instead, roughly speaking. A few years after the initial 1929 crash, the U.S. devalued the dollar and began printing money from 1932 and onward to fund various programs. Then it slowed down, and in 1937 they encountered another recession, which was still within the larger context of the Great Depression period. So they turned on the printing presses again, and kept them on all through WW2. We’re most likely about to mirror that period in the 2020’s in terms of monetary policy (hopefully without the war part). The Great Recession triggered several rounds of exponential monetary base expansion from 2008 to 2014, and then they stopped until 2019. During this next period, we’re about to have another big increase in the monetary base, similar to what happened in 1937. We already started in September 2019 when the repo spike happened and the Fed started monetizing Treasury bills, and it’s likely about to get amplified.

Growth vs Value Updates As I discussed (and quantified) in a 2021 article, high-valuation growth equities are generally more sensitive to interest rates than value-oriented equities. Throughout 2022, as the Federal Reserve aggressively raised interest rates, unprofitable hypergrowth equities were basically killed, and profitable growth equities took a major valuation haircut. As a result, growth equities underperformed value equities in aggregate. During 2023, especially after the March banking crisis, the market has increasingly priced in a top in interest rates, and along with the AI craze, has bid up growth equities relative to value equities. This chart shows the ratio of value equities to growth equities. When it’s rising it means value is outperforming in aggregate, and when it’s falling it means growth is outperforming in aggregate: Value outperformed in the strong growth era of the 1980s. Growth outperformed in the tech boom of the 1990s. Value outperformed during the commodity bull market and the rise of BRICS in the 2000s. Growth outperformed in the 2010s decade of relative economic stagnation, and accelerated during the pandemic. Value began outperforming from the depths of the pandemic during the recovery, although 2023 is challenging that. If we take Alphabet (GOOGL) as an example (one of the growth stocks I have in the Newsletter portfolio), it has returned to its average decade valuation (the blue line): Arguably, it should be at a lower valuation, because interest rates are higher than average. If we look at the spread between Alphabet’s earnings yield and the 10-year Treasury rate or 3-month Treasury rate, it doesn’t look great: During the 2000s decade, Alphabet had tremendous growth rate, and so a wide valuation spread vs interest rates made sense. Now as a $1.7 trillion company, its growth is slowing and maturing, and so the fact that its earnings yield is less than the 10-year Treasury rate and significantly less than the 3-month Treasury rate, is potentially more of a concern. However, Alphabet is by no means one of the worst offenders. Separately, on the Strategy earnings call, Michael Saylor described the company adopting a similar cycle-positioning discipline through a specific metric: Strategy added bitcoin metrics to its website including the 200-week moving average, the premium to the 200-week moving average, and the percentage of time bitcoin trades above that level. Going forward, he said they will be "staring at metrics like the premium to the 200-week moving average": if bitcoin is sitting at, say, a 100% premium to the 200-week moving average, the likelihood of it trading the opposite way rises, so they would lean counter-cyclically toward dollars; at discounts or very small premiums they would be more bullish on BTC. He cautioned it is not as simple as just one metric — there is community debate about the best way to calculate whether bitcoin is at a cycle top or bottom — but those signals will help drive allocation of cash flow, alongside credit coverage considerations (e.g., 24 vs. 36 months of dividend coverage). Phong Le added that at STRC's one-year mark they learned the hard way not to pour everything issued into bitcoin, and that reducing the dividend rate when bitcoin is strong and at a strong premium to the 200-week moving average makes sense. Notably, the company has rebuilt its USD reserve from 6 months to 25 months of dividend/interest coverage and initiated STRC repurchases at stressed levels rather than ratcheting the dividend higher, which is consistent with this more counter-cyclical, cycle-aware posture.

They calculate that ATI reduced 10-year yields by roughly a quarter of a percent over the past year, providing stimulus similar to a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, meaning the combined stance of monetary and issuance policy is roughly neutral. This helps explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises. Separately, after the weak manufacturing PMI and the payrolls report that showed fewer jobs than expected and unemployment jumping from 4.1% to 4.3%, Treasury yields and the dollar index dropped sharply, and futures markets began pricing in a high likelihood of a 0.50% "double cut" at the Fed's September meeting. On the bitcoin side, at the Bitcoin Conference 2024, Trump, Robert Kennedy Jr, and Senator Cynthia Lummis all called for a U.S. strategic bitcoin reserve similar to its gold reserves, but at very different scales: Trump's was the smallest, merely vowing to stop selling the 200,000+ coins the U.S. already holds; Kennedy's was the most aggressive, calling for keeping existing coins and acquiring 550 coins per day until reaching at least 4 million coins (roughly 20% of supply), plus effectively ending taxes on bitcoin; and Lummis' proposal called for a 1 million coin reserve and was the most specific, backed by an actual Senate bill detailing secure geographically-distributed custody facilities, a minimum 20-year holding period, state access via segregated accounts, quarterly cryptographic proof-of-reserves, and protections for individual property rights.

Macro View Liquidity Indicators Domestic liquidity indicators continue to run almost perfectly sideways, in large part because the Treasury and Fed have been in lockstep regarding this: Notably, Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini recently published a paper about “Activist Treasury Issuance” which is their term that refers to the Treasury Department taking unusual actions to offset the Fed’s tightness. Both Miran and Roubini are economics PhDs and worked in various capacities with the Treasury Department in the past. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. I’d argue that it’s a symptom of the ongoing fiscal dominance that the United States finds itself in. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. If ATI is unwound via terming out $1 trillion of excess Treasury Bills, we expect it to temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, before settling into a permanent 30-bp increase, with corresponding price changes in risk assets. A 50-bp increase in the 10-year yield will have similar economic effects as a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate. If ATI is not unwound but becomes a permanently employed policy tool, we are likely to see higher equilibrium inflation and interest rates priced in over time due to political business cycles becoming reality. Regular readers of my work will be quite familiar with this concept. I start most of my reports by discussing liquidity conditions, including what the Treasury has been doing with its excess T-bill issuance. And at the start of this year, I dedicated my January 2024 newsletter to this phenomenon of the Treasury offsetting the Fed. Here was a key snippet: Ever since the fourth quarter of 2022, and extending all throughout 2023, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury have been operating opposite policies from each other. And the Treasury has had to pull two different levers to keep up with the Fed. -From September 2022 through May 2023, the Treasury drained their own cash reserves back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. -From June 2023 to the present, the Treasury rapidly increased their T-bill issuance as a percentage of their debt issuance and thus drained reverse repos back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. This following chart shows the Fed vs Treasury liquidity actions in year-over-year change terms. For this chart, higher means more liquidity, and lower means less liquidity. The Fed in blue has been doing its part to reduce liquidity in the financial system since early 2022. The Treasury in red (reflecting both their own cash balances and their ability to affect the reverse repo facility based on their ability to issue T-bills) has been doing its part to increase liquidity in the financial system since late 2022. The net result is that domestic liquidity was decreasing until Q4 2022 but then began to flatten out and turn slightly upward when the Treasury began its inverse operation: -January 2024 Newsletter, “Fiscal and Monetary Divergence While I’m more focused on the liquidity impacts, Miran and Roubini’s paper attempts to quantify the effect by comparing it to interest rate changes. They argue that the Treasury’s excessive T-bill issuance has been the equivalent of the Fed cutting interest rates by 1%. And they argue that if this were to be unwound, it would temporarily be similar to a 2% rate hike by the Fed. I don’t have any particular view regarding if their interest rate comparison is accurate or not, but in my view it’s less about rates per se, and more about liquidity and smooth financial plumbing, of which rates are only a part. Meanwhile, global liquidity is rangebound, but I continue to have a view that it’ll likely grind higher over the next 18 months. If we get some of the capital rotations discussed later in this report, then that could be a catalyst for such a move higher, which can feed on itself. I don’t have any firm conviction for the next quarter. U.S. Economic Weakening In the latter half of this past week, two very weak economic reports were released. The first

The manufacturing part of the economy has been weak for over a year and a half, had been kind of stabilizing, but recently has deteriorated again: The second weak report was that payrolls came in sharply below consensus. Fewer jobs were created last month than expected, and the official unemployment rate jumped from 4.1% to 4.3%. And the problem is that the payrolls have thus far been the good number. A couple months ago I highlighted the widening gap between payroll numbers (surveys of businesses) vs surveys of households regarding employment: There is currently conflicting data between the household survey and the payroll survey for overall U.S. employment trends, which is a data quality issue that complicates analysis. The payroll survey continues to show strong numbers, while the household survey has been notably weaker, with a widening gap. The payroll survey counts people with multiple jobs, whereas the household survey does not, and there are a variety of other differences as well, which post-pandemic remote work and gig work might be amplifying to some degree. -June 9th premium report Dario Perkins recently provided a chart of that divergence on social media. Both of these lines are supposed to measure changes in employment levels for the country: Household employment data had already been stagnant, and now the better-performing payroll data came in surprisingly weak for the past month. And a lot of this is vulnerable to future data revisions from the reporting agencies; recessions are generally declared in hindsight with some subset of the data revised down later. Currently, the unemployment rate is low in absolute terms, but with the sharp move up from 3.4% to 4.3%, it has moved sufficiently enough to be associated with recession concerns. Given some of the structural tightness in the labor market and large structural fiscal deficits which are stimulatory for certain industries (i.e. fiscal dominance), my base case would be to expect a milder peak in the unemployment rate than the average recession, akin to the early 1970s or the early 2000s. In other words, I’m in a camp that expects a mild recession, at least by some metrics. Recessions in emerging markets tend to have different characteristics than recessions in developed markets (e.g. more stagflationary, more mixed signals or divergent industries that are booming or suffering, more capital outflows). But a recession in a developed market that is in a state of fiscal dominance tends to have certain “emerging market lite” characteristics. As soon as the payrolls report came out, Treasury yields and the dollar index dropped sharply. The futures market is now pricing in a high likelihood of a 0.50% interest rate cut (a “double cut”) at the Fed’s September meeting. Stocks performed very poorly on the day as well. U.S. Business Cycle Summary Here is an updated heatmap of various economic indicators for the U.S. economy over the past five years, measured in year-over-year percent change terms. This lets us see a broad spectrum of the economy rather than to over-emphasize any particularly strong or weak data point. The economy was decelerating from a high growth rate since the third quarter of 2021, entered stall speed for a while, began to show signs of stabilization, but recently weakened again. Retail spending, construction spending, capital spending, exports, and imports are shown in nominal dollar numbers, and so when they are below the inflation rate (as most of them are now except for construction spending and to some extent retail spending), it means their growth rate is negative in real terms. Construction spending has been getting a big fiscal boost from the Inflation Reduction Act. The chart starts from the bottom and goes up over five years, and each column represents one of the economic indicators. For most of the chart, I use a green/yellow/red color spectrum. Green indicates solid growth, yellow indicates medium, and orange/red indicate slow growth or contraction, relative to the rest of the 5-year period for that indicator. In other words, green is good and red is bad. For inflation CPI, there is a separate blue/white/red color scale, because high or low inflation in a vacuum is not necessarily “good” or “bad” in the same way as the rest of the heat map. Red indicates higher price inflation, white indicates medium, and blue is lower price inflation, relative to the 5-year period. Economic slowdowns tend to be dis-inflationary while economic booms tend to be pro-inflationary, but there are also some business cycles that slow down with high inflation, and thus become “stagflationary”. So, inflation gets its own color scheme. It continues to be chop along in a range that it’s been in since March of this year, and has fallen toward the lower end of that range. Bitcoin Conference 2024 For the past few months, I have been reporting on how the broad crypto industry, including some elements of the bitcoin industry, have raised a lot of money to support pro-bitcoin/crypto congressmen and senators (for both parties), including supporting Donald Trump for the presidency. Within that context, and given that Bitcoin Magazine’s annual conference is the largest bitcoin conference in the world (and by extension, one of the most widely-attended tech/finance conferences in the world), it was very political this year. In addition to many technical and business speakers, this year they had Donald Trump as their headline speaker, in addition to Robert Kennedy Jr and a large number of sitting senators and representatives. Donald Trump, Robert Kennedy Jr, and Senator Cynthia Lummis all called for the United States to build a strategic bitcoin reserve, similar to its gold reserves. -Surprisingly to some, given his normal persona, Trump’s proposal was the smallest of the three, as he merely vowed to stop selling the 200,000+ coins that the United States already has, in addition to repeating some of his prior promises to support the industry. His keynote speech was instead more similar to one of his rallies, and he demonstrated less familiarity with the subject and with his audience than many other politicians there, but he hit on a number of key points and has the biggest public reach of any speaker there. He framed himself as a pro-energy, pro-AI, pro-bitcoin candidate and said the bitcoin industry looks like the steel industry from a century ago. -Kennedy’s proposal was the most aggressive, calling for the United States to keep its existing coins and acquire 550 coins per day until it reaches at least 4 million (roughly 20% of coins), which would be very hard to do as the price appreciates from that amount of persistent buying. He also called for effectively ending taxes on bitcoin, which makes it functionally similar to a second legal tender. Over the past year, he and his campaign have done a lot of outreach to people who work in the field. I don’t reach out to politicians since that’s not my focus, but due to outreach from a mutual contact on behalf of Kennedy’s team, I did a private group call with Kennedy and some of his team to answer bitcoin-related questions a while ago. -Lummis’ proposal called for establishing a reserve of 1 million coins, and provided the most specifics since she actually submitted a bill in the Senate to do this (which likely won’t pass as-is, but rather sets a precedent). Her bill included specific details regarding the U.S. federal government creating geographically-distributed state-of-the-art secure facilities to hold the keys, establishing a minimum 20-year holding period by the government, enabling individual states to make use of the facilities with segregated accounts, mandating cryptographic proof-of-reserves which allows the reserves to be well-evidenced to the public each quarter in ways that gold cannot be, and clarifying that nothing in the act can infringe on individual property rights (which is relevant considering that the U.S. gold reserve was partially built by forcing citizens to hand over their gold to the government). Lummis and her team regularly meet with a number of people who work in the field and are rather well-versed on the subject. An area I think that went under the radar at the conference were the Democratic politicians. They were in the minority compared to Republicans, but their presence made it effectively bipartisan. Ro Khanna for example gave a fireside chat on the main stage and said, “Bitcoin is about freedom. Bitcoin is about human rights.” And during the conference, Ro Khanna and 13 other sitting Democratic congress people wrote a letter to the Democratic National Committee saying that the party needs to pivot to embrace the industry better. They called for selecting a vice president candidate and SEC chair that are sophisticated with regard to the industry, called for including pro-digital asset support in their party platform, and called for engaging with industry experts. During the past several years, much of the Democratic party’s anti-bitcoin/crypto stance has come from certain politicians like Elizabeth Warren, Brad Sherman, and some others. Warren has been influential on the Biden/Harris administration, which has largely been in her camp on the issue. However, an increasing number of Democratic politicians have broken from that outlook, including Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi who have recently voted in favor of bipartisan bills that benefit the industry, which President Biden vetoed. Politico reported on this growing schism within the party, and the question remains whether Harris will do a soft reset toward a more neutral approach than her camp has had recently, or if she will remain with the Warren camp of the party on this topic. The reason I bring this up is that for years, one of the identified risk factors for bitcoin was government attacks on it and its holders, in a variety of ways. However, government is not a monolith, and recently many politicians have increasingly concluded that money and votes come from supporting the industry, and there isn’t really much money or votes to be gained from specifically opposing it. In my view, financial privacy in general will be the main battleground that many governments will continue to have a problem with, rather than owning bitcoin per se. Who Owns Bitcoin? user_input: how does fiscal dominance vs monetary dominance explain the weak private sector but resilient economy, and why does it support the structural shift from US Treasuries to gold?
reference: Under fiscal dominance, the economy behaves differently than under monetary dominance, which is the framework most analysts are trained on. The baseline of the economy runs hotter, and those on the receiving end of government deficits do fine while those who are not tend to suffer. That is why the private sector looks weak in isolation — housing and commercial real estate have stalled, ISM manufacturing is weak, and bank lending is tepid — yet the overall economy holds up: the 6-7% of GDP fiscal deficits (roughly $2 trillion) act as continuous background stimulus flowing to retirees via Social Security, to the healthcare sector via Medicare and Medicaid, to Defense, and via interest expense to individuals and financial institutions, all of which gets respent into the broader economy. The roughly $300+ billion in new annualized tariff revenue offsets only about 15% of that, so the stimulative effect persists. Because of this, the author focuses on the labor market as the key variable alongside deficits (the "Thanos" combination that overrides other weak indicators), noting a recent warning sign as initial jobless claims spiked to a 3+ year high, though still a yellow rather than red light at levels below the ~300,000 threshold. This same persistent U.S. fiscal dominance underpins the case for gold: combined with the end of a four-decade structurally declining interest rate cycle and a global shift in sovereign interest from US Treasuries to gold at the margins in an increasingly multi-polar world, fiscal dominance fuels the attractiveness of hard assets. The dollar is no longer expanding as a share of global reserves while gold is no longer falling, likely marking the bottom of a post-WWII trend. Accordingly, gold's breakout above the psychologically important $3,500/oz level has sustained, adding another $160-$170/oz, and despite reservations about a structurally overbought monthly RSI and general frothiness, the author remains structurally long, viewing gold as an attractive long-term holding in a diversified portfolio amid a gradual "monetary reset" of the global financial system.

A Tale of Two Sectors September 14, 2025 The macro section of this report discusses the US business cycle (including an indicator flashing a warning sign) and declining liquidity conditions. The digital asset section discusses bitcoin price action and treasury company mNAV compression. The investment analysis section takes a look at apparel makers vs the financial sector to analyze the difference in performance. Macro View US Business Cycle Traditional measures of the economy continue to look mixed. The Atlanta Fed’s estimator tool continues to suggest healthy GDP growth here in Q3: And yet the aggregate assessment of leading indicators continues to flash a mild recession, which it has been doing for the better part of three years now without any NBER-defined recession having occurred. This index includes weekly manufacturing hours, weekly jobless claims, various indices of new orders, building permits, a leading credit index, interest rate spreads, consumer expectations of business conditions, and stock prices. The point I’ve been emphasizing for a while is that amid fiscal dominance, the economy functions differently than under monetary dominance, which is what everyone is trained to analyze. The baseline runs hotter, and those who are on the receiving side of deficits tend to be fine, while those who are not tend to suffer unless they’re able to position for it. The private sector in isolation is indeed pretty weak by many metrics. The housing sector and commercial real estate sector have both pretty much stalled, ISM manufacturing is weak, bank lending is tepid, etc. However, the 6-7% of GDP fiscal deficits (~$2 trillion nominally) serve as a continuous background stimulus. This flows to retirees via Social Security who spend it into the consumer economy, flows to the health care sector via Medicare and Medicaid (including healthcare employees who spend it into the non-healthcare economy), flows to Defense (including soldiers and defense employees who spend it into the non-defense economy), and interest expense (which flows to individuals and financial institutions, some of which gets spent into the non-financial economy). The $300+ billion in new annualized tariff revenue reduces that slightly (which is why I monitor it pretty closely), but only by around 15%, which is why the overall effect remains. Due to that fiscal dominance environment, I’ve been more focused on the labor market. If the labor market remains in decent shape along with the deficits, then it tends to override the other weak variables. It’s like Thanos and his Infinity Stones (deficits and labor market) beating the Avengers (basically every other indicator). And for a while, the labor market has been fine. Well, these past two weeks, the labor market flashed a warning. Initial jobless claims (which are one of the fastest pulse checks we have available) suddenly spiked to a 3+ year high: Now, that’s still a reasonably low number. Roughly 300,000 is the level that would flash more of a red light, whereas this is just a yellow light. Thanos took a punch, maybe lost a stone, but otherwise is still winning for now. But it’s worth watching more closely.

Final Thoughts: Gold’s Sustained Breakout (so far) In my prior report, I flagged the fact that gold was nudging up to a new high, potentially breaking out of the consolidation it has been in since April. I went back and forth with the pro and con arguments for the sustainability of the breakout. Pros: It was touching new highs, poking above the psychologically important $3,500/oz level, and the multi-decade structural changes are in its favor. Cons: The breakout was still within the margin of error of the high end of its consolidation range, and the price was still structurally overbought in terms of the monthly relative strength indicator and similar measures of sentiment. Ultimately I sided with the pro argument, saying that due to the structural changes happening with developed market fiscal environments and a globally shifting central bank policy of leaning a bit more into gold, that’s the side I want to err on despite the frothiness: The good news lately is that gold is back to the top end of that consolidation range, and has touched above the psychologically important $3,500/oz range. user_input: how tariff being tax on consumers and business also hit banks like US Bancorp and Truist in trade war?
reference: The tariffs act like a tax hike because the US imports roughly $4 trillion of goods and services a year, so a broad sustained 10% tariff would on its surface be about a $400 billion tax mostly falling on American consumers and businesses (though actual revenue would be lower since import volumes shrink, and some of the burden spreads to Chinese shipment volumes). Banks such as US Bancorp and Truist Financial have virtually no direct exposure to the trade war, but their clients do, so they could face loan losses on business loans, and if the tariffs trigger a broad economic slowdown or recession, they would likely see an uptick in both business and consumer loan losses. That is why their stock prices faced turmoil again in the 2025 trade war after being fine through the 2023 unrealized-loss crisis. Even so, these super-regionals (5th and 8th biggest US banks) are seen as attractive because the sell-off already priced in worse-than-base-case scenarios, the Fed has room to cut rates which would lower deposit costs and support net interest margins, high fiscal deficits remain stimulative, and tariffs themselves would likely be reversed or offset in a recession, especially heading into the 2026 mid-term year.
