Macro View US Economic Update Since gross domestic product or “GDP” is such a complicated measure, it is reported with three different estimates after a fiscal quarter ends. As such, sometimes the second or third estimate will revise the numbers higher or lower than the first estimate. The first estimate is in for Q1 2025, and it showed the first negative quarter since Q1 2022: A trade deficit weighs negatively on real GDP, and the record trade deficit that occurred in Q1 2025 was the primary variable for the contraction in real GDP. This was temporary, as many businesses front-ran tariffs and pulled as much imports as possible into the quarter. This was partially offset by a dramatic rise in inventories that those imports went into, which are positive for the GDP calculation. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow subcomponent tool showed the negative impact from tariff front-running in light blue and the positive impact from inventory increases in purple: The Atlanta Fed does have a positive outlook for Q2 2025, but all of the economic data remains uncertain and could change quickly: Meanwhile, the US manufacturing sector continues to be in mild contraction, in what has thus far been the longest ever period without a sustained growth in the ISM manufacturing purchasing manager’s index. This has remained bearish for longer than my base case, with two failed breakouts to the upside: Domestic Liquidity Domestic liquidity conditions continue to be flat, as they have been for three years since mid-2022: This flat liquidity situation will likely to persist into Q4 2025. They’ve already slowed their rate of quantitative tightening twice, which extends the time they can continue to do it. By 2026, the Fed will likely shift toward persistent balance sheet expansion, albeit at a mild pace. At that point, they’ll most likely be accumulating Treasuries but will continue to let mortgage-backed securities mature off their balance sheet. The Treasury General Account has $583 billion in liquidity. It got a boost from tax season as it normally does, but is now likely to roll over again. Here’s an updated version of the chart showing that the losses have lessened a bit since then. These unrealized losses are still sitting on bank balance sheets: The context that many people did not realize as they spread charts like this around social media, is that banks went into that period with $2.35 trillion in aggregate equity capital. That $650 billion hit temporarily wiped out less than 30% of their capital, and for the vast majority of them, it would take away little or no capital permanently because they would hold until maturity and recoup those losses. That decelerating economy and tightening liquidity is exactly why bitcoin price action was cautioned as unclear over the immediate term, since bitcoin is historically weak in such environments. In practice this played out through the Terra/Luna death spiral forcing bitcoin liquidation into a weak market in May (capitulation to just under $30k), then contagion at Three Arrows Capital and lender liquidations in June pushing price below $20k (briefly around $17.5k), plus miners selling coins to cover expenses. Despite the troubling macro backdrop keeping the next six months uncertain, bitcoin is now seen as being in a deep value zone, trading below its on-chain cost basis for the fifth time in its history, with an appealing risk/reward on a 3-5 year view.

Macro View The US economy continues to weaken. Leading indicators are pointing to levels that are historically associated with recessions or near-recessions: Chart Source: Advisor Perspectives Atlanta Fed’s aggregate indicator is pointing towards a negative real GDP print in Q2, which we just finished up but was not reported yet since it takes time to compile the data. Chart Source: Atlanta Fed We already had a negative real GDP print in Q1, so if this model ends up being roughly correct, it will mark two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth. The one pillar of the economy that continues to hold up decently is the labor market. However, this does tend to be a lagging indicator; we’re often firmly in a recession by the time it has noticeably rolled over, especially after revisions to the data are done later. Here’s the total nonfarm payroll numbers, represented as % off high: If I zoom in on the 1970s, which was the last time that we had inflation levels this high, we can see that payrolls often didn’t start falling until well into a recession: Here’s the employment to population ratio of 25-54 year olds in the past four decades or so: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Additionally, we need to look at real wages. CrossBorder Capital does great research on cycles and liquidity in particular, and has been showing near-record low levels of global liquidity lately. The dollar index, which is very heavily weighted towards the euro and the yen, has broken out to multi-decade highs: However, the sheer scale of that recent rally has more to do with euro and yen weakness than it has to do with dollar strength. For example, the US dollar vs the Canadian dollar has been strengthening a bit from a low base, but with nothing particularly remarkable going on: The US dollar vs the Brazilian real, the Chinese yuan, or the Australian dollar, is showing a bout of strength in 2022 but nothing really notable there either. There are also of course some specific emerging or frontier market countries having currency problems, such as Sri Lanka, Argentina, Turkey, and so forth. To a lot of people, this probably sounds like a good thing for the United States. Our dollar is strengthening, which is great for us, right? Well, not really, as I’ve covered before. When the dollar strengthens notably, the foreign sector tends to get pretty squeezed, because they buy dollar-based commodities and in many cases have dollar-denominated debts. However, they also have tens of trillions of dollars worth of US financial assets, which they accumulated over decades from structural trade surpluses against the US. The US has a deeply negative net international investment position, which we dug into from decades of structural trade deficits with the rest of the world. When the dollar strengthens markedly, the foreign sector in aggregate tends to stop buying and even start trimming their dollar assets, which can render US financial markets illiquid. This chart shows the portion of US Treasuries that the foreign sector holds in custody at the US Federal Reserve. However, all of this destruction in asset prices and economic deceleration will likely start weighing on tax revenue, and by Q4 of this year or during the first half of next year, Treasury issuance will likely pick up. This will be when the Treasury is more vulnerable to liquidity problems and lack of foreign buyers, if these types of conditions are still present by that point. user_input: How does the Miran-Roubini concept of Activist Treasury Issuance (ATI) relate to expectations for Federal Reserve interest rate cuts after the weak payrolls and manufacturing PMI data, and how do the strategic bitcoin reserve proposals from Trump, Kennedy, and Lummis differ in scale and specificity?
reference: Miran and Roubini's paper defines Activist Treasury Issuance (ATI) as the Treasury shortening the average duration of its debt issuance through excess T-bill issuance, thereby manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors and working through the same channels as the Fed's quantitative easing. They calculate ATI has reduced 10-year yields by roughly a quarter of a percent over the past year, providing stimulus similar to a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, effectively interdicting the Fed's attempt to restrain the economy and helping explain inflation persistence; if unwound by terming out $1 trillion of excess T-bills, they expect a temporary 50 bp rise in 10-year yields (akin to a two-point Fed hike) settling into a permanent 30 bp increase. This offsetting dynamic is why domestic liquidity indicators have run almost perfectly sideways, with the Fed reducing liquidity since early 2022 while the Treasury added liquidity from late 2022 onward. Against that backdrop, the recent data turned notably weak: manufacturing PMI came in well below consensus and payrolls came in sharply below expectations, with the unemployment rate jumping from 4.1% to 4.3% (up from a 3.4% low). Treasury yields and the dollar index dropped sharply, and futures markets began pricing a high likelihood of a 0.50% "double cut" at the Fed's September meeting, with the author expecting a mild recession given structural labor tightness and fiscal dominance. On the digital asset side, at the Bitcoin Conference 2024, Trump, Robert Kennedy Jr, and Senator Cynthia Lummis all called for a U.S. strategic bitcoin reserve similar to its gold reserves, but with differing ambition: Trump's was the smallest, merely vowing to stop selling the 200,000+ coins the U.S. already holds while framing himself as pro-energy, pro-AI, and pro-bitcoin; Kennedy's was the most aggressive, calling for keeping existing coins and acquiring 550 coins per day until reaching at least 4 million coins (roughly 20% of supply), plus effectively ending taxes on bitcoin; and Lummis' was the most specific, proposing a 1 million coin reserve via an actual Senate bill detailing geographically distributed secure key-holding facilities, a minimum 20-year government holding period, state access with segregated accounts, quarterly cryptographic proof-of-reserves, and protections for individual property rights.

Macro View Liquidity Indicators Domestic liquidity indicators continue to run almost perfectly sideways, in large part because the Treasury and Fed have been in lockstep regarding this: Notably, Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini recently published a paper about “Activist Treasury Issuance” which is their term that refers to the Treasury Department taking unusual actions to offset the Fed’s tightness. Both Miran and Roubini are economics PhDs and worked in various capacities with the Treasury Department in the past. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. I’d argue that it’s a symptom of the ongoing fiscal dominance that the United States finds itself in. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. If ATI is unwound via terming out $1 trillion of excess Treasury Bills, we expect it to temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, before settling into a permanent 30-bp increase, with corresponding price changes in risk assets. A 50-bp increase in the 10-year yield will have similar economic effects as a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate. If ATI is not unwound but becomes a permanently employed policy tool, we are likely to see higher equilibrium inflation and interest rates priced in over time due to political business cycles becoming reality. Regular readers of my work will be quite familiar with this concept. I start most of my reports by discussing liquidity conditions, including what the Treasury has been doing with its excess T-bill issuance. And at the start of this year, I dedicated my January 2024 newsletter to this phenomenon of the Treasury offsetting the Fed. Here was a key snippet: Ever since the fourth quarter of 2022, and extending all throughout 2023, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury have been operating opposite policies from each other. And the Treasury has had to pull two different levers to keep up with the Fed. -From September 2022 through May 2023, the Treasury drained their own cash reserves back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. -From June 2023 to the present, the Treasury rapidly increased their T-bill issuance as a percentage of their debt issuance and thus drained reverse repos back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. This following chart shows the Fed vs Treasury liquidity actions in year-over-year change terms. For this chart, higher means more liquidity, and lower means less liquidity. The Fed in blue has been doing its part to reduce liquidity in the financial system since early 2022. The Treasury in red (reflecting both their own cash balances and their ability to affect the reverse repo facility based on their ability to issue T-bills) has been doing its part to increase liquidity in the financial system since late 2022. The net result is that domestic liquidity was decreasing until Q4 2022 but then began to flatten out and turn slightly upward when the Treasury began its inverse operation: -January 2024 Newsletter, “Fiscal and Monetary Divergence While I’m more focused on the liquidity impacts, Miran and Roubini’s paper attempts to quantify the effect by comparing it to interest rate changes. They argue that the Treasury’s excessive T-bill issuance has been the equivalent of the Fed cutting interest rates by 1%. And they argue that if this were to be unwound, it would temporarily be similar to a 2% rate hike by the Fed. I don’t have any particular view regarding if their interest rate comparison is accurate or not, but in my view it’s less about rates per se, and more about liquidity and smooth financial plumbing, of which rates are only a part. Meanwhile, global liquidity is rangebound, but I continue to have a view that it’ll likely grind higher over the next 18 months. If we get some of the capital rotations discussed later in this report, then that could be a catalyst for such a move higher, which can feed on itself. I don’t have any firm conviction for the next quarter. U.S. Economic Weakening In the latter half of this past week, two very weak economic reports were released. The first

<2-hop>

weak report was that the manufacturing PMI came in well below consensus expectations. The manufacturing part of the economy has been weak for over a year and a half, had been kind of stabilizing, but recently has deteriorated again: The second weak report was that payrolls came in sharply below consensus. Fewer jobs were created last month than expected, and the official unemployment rate jumped from 4.1% to 4.3%. And the problem is that the payrolls have thus far been the good number. A couple months ago I highlighted the widening gap between payroll numbers (surveys of businesses) vs surveys of households regarding employment: There is currently conflicting data between the household survey and the payroll survey for overall U.S. employment trends, which is a data quality issue that complicates analysis. The payroll survey continues to show strong numbers, while the household survey has been notably weaker, with a widening gap. The payroll survey counts people with multiple jobs, whereas the household survey does not, and there are a variety of other differences as well, which post-pandemic remote work and gig work might be amplifying to some degree. -June 9th premium report Dario Perkins recently provided a chart of that divergence on social media. Both of these lines are supposed to measure changes in employment levels for the country: Household employment data had already been stagnant, and now the better-performing payroll data came in surprisingly weak for the past month. And a lot of this is vulnerable to future data revisions from the reporting agencies; recessions are generally declared in hindsight with some subset of the data revised down later. Currently, the unemployment rate is low in absolute terms, but with the sharp move up from 3.4% to 4.3%, it has moved sufficiently enough to be associated with recession concerns. Given some of the structural tightness in the labor market and large structural fiscal deficits which are stimulatory for certain industries (i.e. fiscal dominance), my base case would be to expect a milder peak in the unemployment rate than the average recession, akin to the early 1970s or the early 2000s. In other words, I’m in a camp that expects a mild recession, at least by some metrics. Recessions in emerging markets tend to have different characteristics than recessions in developed markets (e.g. more stagflationary, more mixed signals or divergent industries that are booming or suffering, more capital outflows). But a recession in a developed market that is in a state of fiscal dominance tends to have certain “emerging market lite” characteristics. As soon as the payrolls report came out, Treasury yields and the dollar index dropped sharply. The futures market is now pricing in a high likelihood of a 0.50% interest rate cut (a “double cut”) at the Fed’s September meeting. Stocks performed very poorly on the day as well. U.S. Business Cycle Summary Here is an updated heatmap of various economic indicators for the U.S. economy over the past five years, measured in year-over-year percent change terms. This lets us see a broad spectrum of the economy rather than to over-emphasize any particularly strong or weak data point. The economy was decelerating from a high growth rate since the third quarter of 2021, entered stall speed for a while, began to show signs of stabilization, but recently weakened again. Retail spending, construction spending, capital spending, exports, and imports are shown in nominal dollar numbers, and so when they are below the inflation rate (as most of them are now except for construction spending and to some extent retail spending), it means their growth rate is negative in real terms. Construction spending has been getting a big fiscal boost from the Inflation Reduction Act. The chart starts from the bottom and goes up over five years, and each column represents one of the economic indicators. For most of the chart, I use a green/yellow/red color spectrum. Green indicates solid growth, yellow indicates medium, and orange/red indicate slow growth or contraction, relative to the rest of the 5-year period for that indicator. In other words, green is good and red is bad. For inflation CPI, there is a separate blue/white/red color scale, because high or low inflation in a vacuum is not necessarily “good” or “bad” in the same way as the rest of the heat map. Red indicates higher price inflation, white indicates medium, and blue is lower price inflation, relative to the 5-year period. Economic slowdowns tend to be dis-inflationary while economic booms tend to be pro-inflationary, but there are also some business cycles that slow down with high inflation, and thus become “stagflationary”. So, inflation gets its own color scheme. Digital Assets Note Bitcoin Price Action Along with stocks and most volatile assets, bitcoin has not fared well amid the recent spike in volatility across asset markets. It continues to be chop along in a range that it’s been in since March of this year, and has fallen toward the lower end of that range. Bitcoin Conference 2024 For the past few months, I have been reporting on how the broad crypto industry, including some elements of the bitcoin industry, have raised a lot of money to support pro-bitcoin/crypto congressmen and senators (for both parties), including supporting Donald Trump for the presidency. Within that context, and given that Bitcoin Magazine’s annual conference is the largest bitcoin conference in the world (and by extension, one of the most widely-attended tech/finance conferences in the world), it was very political this year. In addition to many technical and business speakers, this year they had Donald Trump as their headline speaker, in addition to Robert Kennedy Jr and a large number of sitting senators and representatives. Donald Trump, Robert Kennedy Jr, and Senator Cynthia Lummis all called for the United States to build a strategic bitcoin reserve, similar to its gold reserves. -Surprisingly to some, given his normal persona, Trump’s proposal was the smallest of the three, as he merely vowed to stop selling the 200,000+ coins that the United States already has, in addition to repeating some of his prior promises to support the industry. His keynote speech was instead more similar to one of his rallies, and he demonstrated less familiarity with the subject and with his audience than many other politicians there, but he hit on a number of key points and has the biggest public reach of any speaker there. He framed himself as a pro-energy, pro-AI, pro-bitcoin candidate and said the bitcoin industry looks like the steel industry from a century ago. -Kennedy’s proposal was the most aggressive, calling for the United States to keep its existing coins and acquire 550 coins per day until it reaches at least 4 million (roughly 20% of coins), which would be very hard to do as the price appreciates from that amount of persistent buying. He also called for effectively ending taxes on bitcoin, which makes it functionally similar to a second legal tender. Over the past year, he and his campaign have done a lot of outreach to people who work in the field. I don’t reach out to politicians since that’s not my focus, but due to outreach from a mutual contact on behalf of Kennedy’s team, I did a private group call with Kennedy and some of his team to answer bitcoin-related questions a while ago. -Lummis’ proposal called for establishing a reserve of 1 million coins, and provided the most specifics since she actually submitted a bill in the Senate to do this (which likely won’t pass as-is, but rather sets a precedent). Her bill included specific details regarding the U.S. federal government creating geographically-distributed state-of-the-art secure facilities to hold the keys, establishing a minimum 20-year holding period by the government, enabling individual states to make use of the facilities with segregated accounts, mandating cryptographic proof-of-reserves which allows the reserves to be well-evidenced to the public each quarter in ways that gold cannot be, and clarifying that nothing in the act can infringe on individual property rights (which is relevant considering that the U.S. gold reserve was partially built by forcing citizens to hand over their gold to the government). Lummis and her team regularly meet with a number of people who work in the field and are rather well-versed on the subject. An area I think that went under the radar at the conference were the Democratic politicians. They were in the minority compared to Republicans, but their presence made it effectively bipartisan. Ro Khanna for example gave a fireside chat on the main stage and said, “Bitcoin is about freedom. Bitcoin is about human rights.” And during the conference, Ro Khanna and 13 other sitting Democratic congress people wrote a letter to the Democratic National Committee saying that the party needs to pivot to embrace the industry better. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. reference: The base case was that year-over-year headline inflation would reach a local top by late Q1 or early Q2 2022, in the 7-9% range, because of base effects: monthly inflation had been steady for about a year, so high prints were lapping similarly high year-ago prints, meaning monthly inflation would have to break out higher to push the yearly figure up. The caveat was a right-tail risk that an energy price spike could cause an overshoot. That risk got activated in the unusual macroeconomic environment where demand-side inflation was subsiding in the US as fiscal stimulus was removed, but supply-side inflation stayed a significant problem, exacerbated by the war in Ukraine and China\u2019s unusually strict lockdowns. The Russian war on Ukraine and the Shanghai and other Chinese city lockdowns (with record numbers of cargo ships waiting outside ports and roughly 40% of the Chinese population under strict lockdown) were a one-two punch to the supply side, spiking energy and food prices in March and pushing headline CPI to 8.5%, while core inflation excluding food and energy did indeed start to look toppy as originally expected. Macro View This continues to be an unusual macroeconomic environment. Demand-side inflation is beginning to subside in the US and elsewhere, with the removal of fiscal stimulus. However, supply-side inflation continues to be a significant problem, exacerbated by the war in Ukraine and China’s unusually strict lockdowns. Chinese Lockdowns China went through several weeks of doubling down on its zero-COVID policy, which has been quite a headscratcher for many analysts, myself included. The Omicron variant is extremely contagious but relatively mild, and yet they seem to be treating it like a zombie apocalypse disease from a horror movie. Large portions of Shanghai and dozens of other cities have been locked down over the past three weeks even more thoroughly than they locked down in spring of 2020. For example, overall subway traffic in Shanghai slowed to basically zero during these weeks, whereas there was still some minimal activity in spring 2020. Most notably, the number of cargo ships waiting outside of ports in Shanghai spiked to a record high, far surpassing the disruption that occurred two years ago in spring 2020. This has been confirmed with satellite ship tracking: Chart Source: Rodrigo Zeidan Documenting things in China is always difficult. The Chinese government is restrictive with data and speech, but then on the other hand, some western sources outside of the China sometimes try to sensationalize things to a greater degree than what is happening, and come off as xenophobic or unreliable. Filtering through sources to find what’s really happening is tricky. However, the available data clearly show that what’s happening is massive, and it’s confirmed in various ways by on-the-ground reporting. Approximately 40% of the Chinese population is estimated to be in strict lockdowns, with Shanghai being among the strictest. Jared Nelson, an American data compliance officer living in Shanghai has documented this situation in depth. People in his community were unable to leave apartments. Some volunteers for each building were allowed to exit and get supplies for the building but they had to wear a full-body hazmat-style suit to do so. Yaxue Cao pointed towards 100+ videos and images of rather extreme lockdown behavior throughout Shanghai. The government workers are often appearing as large groups of people all dressed in hazmat-style suits enforcing compliance on groups of people that are getting frustrated with their limited mobility and lack of resources. Patrick Madrid shared a video from a Chinese friend that showed tons of people screaming from their high-rise apartment windows. Similar videos have been shot and shared elsewhere in Shanghai. The issue is that food production, food delivery, medicine delivery systems are all strained. Many people have had trouble getting basic supplies while forced to remain in their apartments. Anthony Fu shared that he has been pretty lucky due to having some food stockpiles during his lockdown, but that the situation is harsh for his neighborhood. People have trouble getting food, and they get turned away from hospitals for many serious conditions. Qin Chen, who is locked down, shared a timeline of the lockdowns throughout Shanghai. Major media have reported on this as well. CNN reports of the difficulties getting food in the locked-down city of 25 million people, since the delivery system is not designed to handle 100% of food going through it. Reuters reports of the rising stress and difficulties that many residents are sharing on social media. The South China Morning Post had a very critical piece against the lockdowns, reporting that residents are frustrated with clunky lockdowns, lack of food and medicine, forced culling of their pets suspected to have the virus by health workers in hazmat suits, etc. In addition to having negative implications for Chinese asset prices and domestic politics, this breakdown in logistics and economic output has negative implications for global supply chains and global economic growth in the quarters ahead. Shanghai and other Chinese cities are massive manufacturing and logistics hubs, and all of that is now more disrupted in 2022 than in 2020. Inflation I’ve had an inflationary view for the past few years, which has played out even faster than I thought. This is due to both monetary inflation on the demand side and real resources constraints on the supply side. However, over the past several months I’ve been tracking a possible local top in year-over-year headline inflation occurring by the end of Q1 of this year. I described this back in December: From base effects in the CPI calculation, there’s a decent chance that we’ll see a local top in official CPI sometime in Q1 2022 within the 7-9% year-over-year range. As we look later into 2022 beyond that point, the future is less clear and depends on certain variables. -December 12, 2021 Two months ago, I re-iterated that year-over-year headline inflation would likely top by the end of Q1 or the early part of Q2. The caveat, however, was that if something caused energy prices to spike; in that scenario inflation could overshoot my base case. Here was my description, since it’s still mostly relevant: The producer price index is showing signs of having reached a local top in year-over-year terms. I think we’ll probably see the same for headline CPI by late Q1 or early Q2. The reason has to do with base effects. Monthly inflation has been rather steady for about a year now, so now high inflation prints are about to start lapping year-ago similarly-high inflation prints, and thus the year-over-year figures are likely to stop going up. Monthly inflation would need to break out to a higher level in order to get yearly inflation up at this point. However, if inflation remains relatively high (4-8%), even if it stops going higher on a year-over-year basis, that’s still a significant problem. Investor views about what inflation is going to do next tend to be very polarized. There is one camp that argues that all of this inflation is transitory, just caused by supply chain disruptions, and that it’ll go back to normal soon.

<2-hop>

There is another camp that thinks this is all just starting and that we’re entering a period of secular inflation. My view falls near the middle but towards the secular inflation view. For the past couple years I’ve been in the “inflation camp” overall, which has been correct so far. Basically, I think there is a good chance that year-over-year inflation will reach a local top in a couple months, and that we’ll have a period of flat or lower year-over-year inflation prints for a period of time, while still being above-target. And I think this is within the context of an overall inflationary decade; the 2020s decade will likely have higher average inflation than the 2010s decade due to tighter commodity supply and tighter labor markets. In other words, I think inflation will be a persistent problem, but not necessarily in a straight line that just keeps going up. The right-tail risk to that view is that if oil prices spike higher this summer due to lack of supply and solid emerging market demand, it can result in inflation (or more precisely, stagflation) that is even higher than my base case. There is a reasonable probability of that happening, and I’ve written a number of times about energy shortages, which is part of why I remain in the inflationary camp overall. I do think we’ll probably have oil price spikes to new highs this decade; I just don’t know if they will spike this summer or not. I continue to have a structurally bullish view on oil and gas equities in general, and am willing to hold them through periods of volatility. -February 20th, 2022 Well, the Russian war on Ukraine certainly added some fuel to the inflationary fire by disrupting more of the supply side. The unusually-strict Chinese lockdowns are a second important factor contributing to that. So that’s a one-two punch to the supply side, pointing towards more inflation and/or shortages. These events weren’t part of my base case, so they activated the right-tail risk of even higher inflation prints in March than originally expected. Energy and food prices spiked in March due to war-related supply chain disruptions, above and beyond what was already happening from monetary inflation. It partly depends on geopolitics at this point, including Russian energy trade, Chinese lockdowns, Europe/US recession risks, and so forth. Basically, Americans are no longer receiving stimulus checks, economic growth is slowing, and oil prices are currently off of their March highs. But the Chinese logistics situation is the worst ever, and there are plenty of headlines we could wake up to that would add more fuel to the supply-side inflationary fire. Monthly retail sales are on the right axis in blue, and the percent change in retail sales from last year is on the left axis in red: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Back in 2009, retail sales dropped during the recession, and there was no massive fiscal stimulatory response. The retail sales trend simply continued on from that lower base, and so it took a few years to surpass the pre-recession high. In 2020, retail sales dropped briefly, but then as lockdowns ended and stimulus went out to people, retail sales exploded higher. The amount of broad money in the system increased by almost 40% in two years. Here in 2022, the rate of change is getting back to normal levels, as direct fiscal stimulus is no longer occurring. But with more money permanently in the system, most prices are permanently higher. Here’s a way to think about the current price inflation. Back in 2020 and 2021, we had demand-side monetary inflation from massive stimulus, as well as supply-side limitations, which resulted in both price inflation and shortages/delays, but more-so towards price inflation. In 2022, the demand-side monetary inflation is heading back to normal, but the supply-side limitations are still bad and arguably getting worse. When the demand side is strong and the supply side is limited, we get inflation and shortages/delays. If the demand side is weak and the supply side is limited, it’ll have a tendency to lean more towards shortages/delays, since the public can’t pay higher prices for many things outside of the essentials, since they simply don’t have the money. Eventually that results in recessionary conditions, and probably more stimulus, but that’s a big valley to go over. user_input: how does fiscal stimulus withdrawal and monetary tightening interact with a strong dollar environment to reduce foreign demand for Treasuries, and what does that mean for global liquidity and bitcoin correlation
reference: The analysis links these dynamics in sequence. First, with fiscal stimulus being withdrawn and monetary policy tightening, the demand side of the economy became weak, which showed up in poor risk asset performance and contributed to imbalances in the global financial system centered on inflation and currency. Those imbalances (the BOJ pegging 10-year JGBs at 0.25% via unlimited money creation, Europe's self-imposed energy crisis, and China's yuan devaluation) drove foreign currencies lower and pushed the dollar to a new cycle high, stronger than expected. A strong dollar is problematic because the foreign official sector stops buying U.S. Treasuries - they held fewer Treasuries than a year earlier despite record U.S. monthly trade deficits sending them investable dollars. The inverse correlation between dollar strength and foreign demand for Treasuries remains strong, because foreign countries trim Treasuries to buy back and defend their own currencies; they only tend to accumulate Treasuries when the dollar weakens. This matters because falling stock prices reduce federal tax receipts (stock prices are tightly correlated with and lead tax receipts), which widens deficits and requires more Treasury issuance precisely when foreign buyers are absent. The resolution, per the analysis, is that the Fed would be forced to step in and buy Treasuries (a severe degradation of central bank independence during high inflation, similar to the 1940s), or use other levers like the supplementary leverage ratio to get banks to buy more. Ultimately, running loose fiscal policy and tight monetary policy simultaneously is like pressing the gas and brake at once, and monetary policy is expected to blink first and return to structural monetary base expansion, which would take steam out of the dollar index. For bitcoin, the author is bullish on an 18-month view while having no firm view on the next 3-6 months, expecting bitcoin to continue exhibiting a significant degree of correlation with global liquidity indicators - and since liquidity is expected to be higher 18 months out (once the Fed and/or Treasury pivot to maintain Treasury market functioning), that supports the constructive longer-term stance, alongside preferences for short- and intermediate-term Treasuries, inflation-protected Treasuries, gold, and appropriately valued equities over long-duration bonds.

Macro View With a withdrawal of fiscal stimulus and a tightening of monetary policy, the demand side of the economy has been rather weak. This is increasingly being reflected in the performance of risk assets. Meanwhile, there are a lot of imbalances in the global financial system, mainly revolving around inflation and currency. Currency Problems The Bank of Japan is doing firm yield curve control to peg their 10-year government bonds at 0.25% or lower. The mechanism for this is that they have an unlimited bid to create new bank reserves and buy bonds at the price that they set. They can override all market participants thanks to the monopoly ability to create new base money. However, if the BOJ holds bond yields below a market-clearing rate, it means that market participants will sell the assets and this will be expressed through currency markets. And so, the yen has sharply devalued vs the dollar: Chart Source: Trading Economics There is no ability for the bond market to “break the Bank of Japan” or anything like that directly; the BOJ has complete control over bond yields denominated in their own currency due to unlimited balance sheet capacity. However, if the yen weakens enough, it might convince BOJ policymakers to change their approach and adjust the yield cap. The BOJ could have chosen a higher yield cap, like 0.50% or 0.75% or 1.00%, which would have made it less costly on the currency to defend. With their debt as high as it is, they have no choice other than to keep yields low, but I would argue that they chose too low of a yield cap. So, this is basically an unforced error, unless significant currency devaluation was indeed their intention. Meanwhile, the euro is suffering due to a mostly self-imposed energy crisis. Over the past decade they shut down nuclear plants and decided not to diversify their natural gas import mix very much. Natural gas prices in Europe spiked to being 15x higher than in the US during late 2021, prior to any war. Then, Russia’s war on Ukraine in 2022 along with the associated breakdown in geopolitical relations led to further uncertainty regarding Europe’s ability to get natural gas at anything resembling reasonable prices. Chart Source: Trading Economics Russia has been demanding over the past month that European companies pay for gas in rubles, by opening Russian bank accounts. The European companies can still fund the accounts with euros, but the point is that the funds are held in a Russian bank and converted to rubles, rather than Russia having bank accounts in Europe that can be frozen by European policymakers. At first, many European nations refused, but with Russia now cutting off gas supplies to some countries, Bloomberg and other outlets have been reporting in recent days that a number of large European energy providers are indeed opening up Russian bank accounts out of necessity. To fix this energy situation in the long run, Europe has to build a lot of LNG capacity (which takes years), as well as pipelines from North Africa and such. And Europe would have significant problems if the European Central Bank were to stop buying government bonds for a long period of time; heavily indebted southern European countries like Italy are reliant on the ongoing monetization of their government debt. This puts the ECB in a tough spot when it comes to dealing with inflation. Additionally, Chinese policymakers performed a yuan devaluation in mid-April, after a period of significant yuan strength. Ongoing lockdowns continue to stagnate their economy, but their policymakers have spoken a number of times about stimulus they will do this year. One move was that they performed a mild but sharp devaluation on their exchange peg: This currency devaluation (particularly what’s going on in Europe and Japan) is cumulatively resulting in a stronger dollar than I anticipated. I was correct about inflation and energy shortages materializing, but the degree to which foreign sector policymakers impacted their energy security and currency in some of these countries is hurting their exchange rates more than I was expecting as my base case. I thought we’d get a lower high in DXY rather than a new cycle high: What’s happening with the dollar, however, is not good for the US either. It’s indicative of the global financial system not working smoothly. With so much dollar strength, the foreign official sector is not buying US Treasuries; they hold fewer Treasuries than this time last year despite the fact that the US is running record monthly trade deficits and thus is sending them a ton of investable dollars: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed This widening of the US trade deficit was a significant contributor to the recent negative real GDP growth print that recently came out for Q1 2022. Plus, when S&P companies report their quarterly numbers, the overseas revenue will translate into fewer dollars due to the relative strength of the dollar. Companies will have a large number of “unfavorable exchange rate” comparisons. If the dollar gets too strong, it can also put pressure on emerging markets (due to them having so much dollar-denominated debt, mostly owed to lenders in Europe and China and Japan and elsewhere), which can soften global growth and consequently can soften US export volumes. Due to this dynamic, strong dollar periods (blue/red line below) are highly correlated with stagnating US corporate profits (green line below): Chart Source: St. Louis Fed As a few analysts, especially Luke Gromen, have pointed out that US stock prices are tightly correlated with US Federal tax receipts, and lead them. Any lull in stock price growth results in a reverse wealth effect, with less consumer spending, less GDP activity, and less realized capital gains taxes. Here’s the year-over-year percentage change in the Wilshire 5000, along with the year-over-year percentage change in tax receipts: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Lower tax receipts results in larger deficits, which requires more Treasury debt issuance, which is a problem in

a strong dollar environment because the foreign sector doesn’t usually buy a lot of Treasuries in strong dollar environments. The Fed can of course step in to buy Treasury securities if necessary, and I think they’ll be forced to at some point, but to do so during a high inflation environment would represent a severe degradation in central bank independence, similar to the 1940s. Alternatively, the Fed could use other levers like changes in the supplementary leverage ratio to get banks to buy more Treasuries as well. Bond Problems This has been the absolute worst start to a year for Treasury bonds in decades. The 10-year yield started the year a bit over 1.5% and by mid-April reached nearly 3%, which means bond prices went down considerably. It’s worse for the ultra long duration ones: The performance is even worse in inflation-adjusted terms. Usually bonds serve as a ballast to stocks, but that doesn’t work out in a stagflationary environment. Something like a stock/commodity/gold/cash portfolio historically works better during stagflation. This year-to-date period has been one of the worst 4 months on record for a 60/40 stock/bond portfolio. We have to go back to 2008 to find a similar period. The fact that bonds are selling off with stocks will further impact tax receipts over time. I have maintained zero long-duration bonds in my portfolios due to this risk. I’ve been a bond bear mainly due to inflation, let alone what can happen with prices if yields do rise in response to that inflation. However, the 10-year yield piercing above 2.5% has been higher than my base case, even as an inflation bull and a bond bear. Due to how financialized the United States is, a drawdown in the stock market generally leads to less consumer spending (due to a reverse wealth effect), and consequently lower GDP growth and lower tax revenue. If bonds aren’t serving as a ballast for that, then the drawdown can be more impactful. The same is true for many other countries, but it is more often about their housing market rather than their stock market. As someone who has completely avoided long duration Treasury bonds for years, I’m actually somewhat sympathetic to them at this time on the long side. The degree to which they have crashed is unusual, and with decelerating economic growth, there is a decent case to go long for a decline in yields (and thus a bounce in prices) here. However, if we do see a reversal on bond yields, I think being long gold is another way to play it, which is in line with my existing positioning. Before I’d consider buying long-duration bonds, I’d want to see more of a reversal in the price trend. Treasury-Eurodollar Spreads The spread in rates between 3-month T-bills and 3-month global interbank loans, has been increasing. This represents increased market perceptions of bank credit risk: Basically, across multiple indicators including this one, there are increasing signs of stress in domestic and global markets. The China Situation Lockdowns have seemingly reached their peak in Shanghai, and are easing a bit, but are now moving to Beijing. A number of virus cases were found in Beijing, which doesn’t work well with China’s zero-COVID policy. Various anti-COVID measures are now on the upswing in Beijing. Chinese policymakers, however, threw the market some meat on Friday by suggesting that they would end the regulatory storm against Chinese tech companies. They have been signaling this for a couple months now, but this is another instance. They’re also pointing towards fiscal and monetary easing. The KWEB Chinese Internet ETF was up 7% on Friday when most assets were down significantly. Do we have a higher low in place? Is this a good time to buy, with blood in the streets? Probably yes, but only time will tell. I’ve been too early on these Chinese stock turnarounds before. The capital outflows from China have been massive recently. That clearly has policymakers’ attention. With China’s credit impulse turning up, regulatory pressures easing, and stimulus coming into the market, it wouldn’t be surprising if the bottom in Chinese stocks is already in. Lockdowns, however, continue to provide a lot of uncertainty for their performance. Theoretically, the internet-focused low-debt companies should have decent performance in this type of environment, but only at the approval of the Politburo. US Business Cycle Analysis Here is my updated heatmap of various economic indicators for the US economy over the past five years, measured in year-over-year percent change terms. Rather than describing the economy in narratives or qualitative terms, or cherry pick data to fit a particularly bullish or bearish view, it quantifies a broad section of data. The economic growth rate in year-over-year terms peaked in Q2 2021, while Q3 and Q4 had decelerating (but still positive) growth, along with persistently hot inflation. The first half of 2022 appears to be continuing the trend of decelerating growth and with still-hot inflation. The chart starts from the bottom and goes up over five years, and each column represents one of the economic indicators. For most of the chart, I use a green/yellow/red color spectrum. Green indicates solid growth, yellow indicates medium, and orange/red indicate slow growth or contraction, relative to the rest of the 5-year period for that indicator. In other words, green is good and red is bad. For inflation CPI, there is a separate blue/white/red color scale, because high or low inflation in a vacuum is not necessarily “good” or “bad” in the same way as the rest of the heat map. Red indicates higher price inflation, white indicates medium, and blue is lower price inflation, relative to the 5-year period. Economic slowdowns tend to be dis-inflationary while economic booms tend to be pro-inflationary, but there are also some business cycles that slow down with high inflation, and thus become “stagflationary”. So, inflation gets its own color scheme. Heat Map Indicators Referenced: Real Gross Domestic Product Industrial Production Advance Retail Sales, Excluding Food Services Total

More conceptually, running loose fiscal policy and tight monetary policy at the same time is like the driver of a car pushing down the gas pedal and using the break at the same time, causing some burnout on the tires. Between the two opposing forces, I expect monetary policy to eventually blink and become more accommodative (in terms of balance sheet capacity more-so than rates per se), and so the fiscal side will win and the car will go forward. There are already tensions with the dollar index at current levels. But the current set of forces supports a strong dollar for the rest of 2024 or until such time that this sort of intervention occurs. Meanwhile, Japan’s yen-to-dollar exchange rate broke out to fresh multi-decade highs (meaning a weaker yen): Japan currently has 0.1% short term interest rates despite experiencing above-target inflation, at a time when most other developed countries have 4-5% interest rates or higher. This makes holding yen unattractive, and thus hurts the exchange rate. The Bank of Japan has thus far chosen not to meaningfully tighten monetary policy in the face of this, although they previously intervened when the exchange rate moved faster than they prefer. That’s the problem with being in fiscal dominance, which applies even more to Japan than the United States. Japan has such large government debts (over 250% public debt to GDP) that if they raise interest rates meaningfully in line with the rest of the developed world, it would blow out their public interest expense to huge levels, which in large part flows to the private sector and is nominally stimulatory and would require support from the central bank. If Japan wants to defend its exchange rate at some point again, they could sell some U.S. Treasuries and buy back some yen. They have a strong current account surplus and accumulated positive net international investment position, and are the biggest foreign holder of U.S. Treasuries in the world. Thus far, the yen has weakened because they have allowed it to weaken. They have plenty of ammo to deploy if the devaluation gets too disorderly for their preferences, even if interest rates are not necessarily the ideal tool for them to use. In the meantime, a weaker yen is good for Japanese exporters and for inbound tourism. It’s bad for Japanese savers, importers, and those who want to travel abroad. Sometimes subsidies are used to minimize the most obvious effects for consumers and businesses, such as with energy prices. More broadly, whenever the dollar index gets too strong, foreign holdings of Treasuries tend to decrease across the board, because those foreign countries trim some of their Treasuries to buy back and defend their own currencies around the margins, or at least stop buying additional Treasuries. Foreign countries only tend to accumulate Treasuries when the dollar weakens. The inverse correlation between dollar strength and foreign demand for Treasuries remains strong: In summary, when the dollar starts to get too strong as has it been recently, it starts pressuring U.S. exports, and starts contributing to higher U.S. yields and sloppy U.S. Treasury auctions as foreign countries take defensive action. If it gets disorderly enough, either the Treasury or Fed eventually steps in to provide liquidity and smooth out market functioning. They’ve done this multiple times since 2019. I don’t think we’re quite there yet, but as we reach the later stages of the Fed’s balance sheet contraction amid ongoing large deficit spending, we should expect some Treasury market disorder, growing frictions in liquidity measures, and then eventually a pivot from the Fed and/or Treasury to maintain adequate functioning and liquidity in the Treasury securities market. That’s why I currently find the next 3-6 months to be challenging to forecast, but have more confidence over an 18 month forecast. I expect liquidity to be higher 18 months from now, but the timing to get there for the rest of 2024 is harder to predict. Overall, I continue to find long-duration Treasuries uncompelling on a risk-reward basis. I prefer short-term or intermediate-term Treasuries, inflation-protected Treasuries, gold, bitcoin, and appropriately valued equities. user_input: In the February 4, 2024 report, how do the macroeconomic liquidity conditions described in the macro section relate to the digital asset section's discussion of bitcoin price consolidation and spot bitcoin ETF fund flows?
reference: The February 4, 2024 report explicitly frames itself as covering liquidity conditions and the rate-of-change of economic indicators in its macro section, while its digital asset section addresses bitcoin price action and the unique intersection between macro and the bitcoin industry. In the macro section, the author argues that in the current era of fiscal dominance (beginning around 2019), liquidity has become an even stronger driver of asset prices than it has been historically. Domestic liquidity has been flat-to-up since bottoming in late 2022/early 2023, because the Federal Reserve's tight monetary policy has been offset by the Treasury running large deficits, shortening average debt duration, and pulling capital out of reverse repos back into the financial system. The first three quarters of 2022 were brutal for liquidity with both the Fed and Treasury pointing downward, but the five quarters from late 2022 through 2023 were decent, U.S. broad money supply turned from contracting to flat and then upward by spring 2023, and global broad money supply in dollars has consolidated sideways while remaining well off its late-2022 lows. The author expects flat-to-upward liquidity in 2024 and rising liquidity over the next few years. Against that backdrop of mixed, mildly positive but consolidating liquidity, bitcoin itself has been consolidating between $40k and $45k for two months. Rather than the widely expected massive rally on spot ETF inflows or a big "sell the news" collapse after the ETFs launched, the market delivered sideways, choppy, and boring price action, which was the least expected outcome. On fund flows, thousands of bitcoin flowed out of the higher-fee Grayscale GBTC ETF into the lower-fee competing ETFs within the first few weeks, but that outflow trend is starting to slow and net inflows appear to be gradually taking over. Longer term, the author views the spot ETFs as constructive for price and considers it sensible for an asset of bitcoin's size and liquidity to have spot ETFs, which aligns with his broader expectation of improving liquidity conditions supporting asset prices over the next few years.

Macro View Liquidity Indicators In the current era of fiscal dominance (which I would generally categorize as beginning in 2019), liquidity has been a driving force for many asset prices even more-so than it has been historically. Domestic liquidity has been flat-to-up since bottoming in late 2022 and early 2023. The Federal Reserve continues to run tight monetary policy, but the Treasury has offset that since late 2022 by running large deficits and shortening its average debt duration and helping to bring capital from reverse repos back into the financial system. As a result, the first three quarters of 2022 were particularly bad for liquidity, but the five quarters from late 2022 through 2023 have been decent for liquidity. This following chart shows the rate-of-change of domestic liquidity, where higher means better liquidity and down means worse liquidity. Sometimes the Fed and Treasury are moving in a similar direction, but more often than not they are moving in opposite directions and it comes down to a difference in magnitudes between them. The most recent major trend changes (Fed in early 2022 and Treasury in late 2022) are highlighted in green: That period during the first three quarters of 2022 was particularly brutal as both the Fed and Treasury were pointing downward for liquidity. Ever since the Treasury flipped the other way, it has been a more mixed situation with a mild upward bias. Meanwhile, the U.S. broad money supply was decreasing until spring 2023, but then began turning flat and more recently, upward: Looking globally, the dollar index matters quite a bit, and it has been moderately strengthening here in 2024. To summarize the past couple of years, it was rising in 2021 and 2022 until Q4 of 2022 coinciding with the bottom in liquidity, fell sharply in Q4 of 2022 as the Treasury’s operations became more positive for liquidity, and then has been flat throughout 2023 and into 2024. The global broad money supply denominated in dollars is a broad and straightforward global liquidity measure, and it has been consolidating sideways for two years generally but is well off its late-2022 lows. The base effects from exactly 12 months ago have reset the year-over-year percentage change (orange line) to zero, even as the absolute figure (blue line) remains roughly sideways: Overall, I expect flat-to-upward liquidity in 2024, and rising liquidity over the next few years, but I continue to monitor it every two weeks both quantitatively and policy-wise to look for potential changes to that outlook. U.S. Economy Over the past two years, the U.S. economy has been in sharp divergence mode. Some cyclical sectors have been sharply decelerating and then ultimately contracting, like manufacturing. Commercial real estate was severely damaged by the combination of work-from-home trends and higher interest rates. But industries directly or indirectly on the receiving side of the large fiscal deficits have been doing relatively good. A big challenge over the past several months has been to determine whether the cyclical aspects of the economy are still decelerating or if they are finding a floor and starting to stabilize. There are great analysts on both sides of that debate. Liquidity and PMIs are starting to stabilize and turn upward, while some other areas continue to point downward. Although I was in the recession camp during 2022, by early 2023 I’ve instead been straddling that debate somewhat by saying that there are no immediate signs of recession due to improving liquidity conditions, and to the extent that one materializes, I expect it to be a mild recession or “emerging market-like” recession due to the huge fiscal deficits that continue to stimulate parts of the economy. This coincided with the period where the Treasury began offsetting the Fed’s liquidity drain, and we entered a more neutral or positive liquidity regime. Overall, the trends in my view are pointing towards economic re-acceleration as a base case, but some of the downward areas can turn bad in a nonlinear way. Therefore, I don’t rule out the possibility of recession either, and still view us to be in this indeterminate state. PMIs and some of their leading sub-components are pointing upward from a low level: The Atlanta Fed’s current data points toward no recession here in Q1, although much of these inputs can be subject to revisions in hindsight: The cyclical side of the labor market (e.g. temporary workers and overtime hours) still looks weak. A drop of this magnitude is normally associated with a recession and there’s no significant sign of stabilization yet: Temporary workers were basically flat in January and technically ever-so-slightly up, which gave them the first uptick in two years. There were some months that were flat with a tiny downtick, so it’s all within the margin of error. Overall, the majority of indicators I track suggest some degree of upward re-acceleration, but it’s still fragile and subject to change, and not confirmed by all indicators. If it were to be confirmed by all indicators, it would likely already be in the middle of the uptrend by that point. Global Economy The copper-to-gold ratio is something I check regularly as a sort of “tiebreaker” on global economic trends. It correlates significantly with global PMIs, and so far has not shown a firm sign of bottoming yet: The domestic economies of China and Europe continue to be weak. This is partially due to the difference in fiscal policy between the United States and the rest of the world. The large fiscal deficits are stimulatory, and while they can cause considerable problems later, as long as there is considerable foreign demand for U.S. assets to keep the exchange rate of the currency strong, it allows the United States to outperform its developed country peers and expand its marketshare of global GDP.

user_input: How did the MSCI index de-listing discussion around crypto asset treasury companies affect bitcoin demand compared to the earlier GBTC premium collapse, and how do these demand drivers relate to bitcoin's market capitalization milestones?
reference: Both episodes involve the removal of a major structural source of bitcoin demand. Earlier in the cycle, when bitcoin reached as high as $58,000 with a market capitalization of just over $1 trillion before correcting roughly 25% to around $43,000 intraday, one of the two fundamental headwinds cited was that the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust (GBTC) had lost its premium to net asset value and was in fact trading at a slight discount. GBTC had been the biggest buyer of bitcoin in 2020, both for long exposure and for a market-neutral arbitrage trade in which accredited investors and institutions bought at NAV with a six-month lock-up, shorted bitcoin elsewhere, and later sold at a premium. That process permanently converted liquid bitcoin into illiquid cold-storage bitcoin, so once the premium vanished, that source of demand ended. Later, a comparable dynamic emerged with crypto asset treasury companies: on November 20th JP Morgan publicized an MSCI announcement (originally made October 10th) that MSCI might de-list Strategy (MSTR) and other crypto asset treasury companies from its indices, a decision to be confirmed in January. Notably, October 10th coincided with a crypto flash-crash involving $19 billion of leveraged liquidations, suggesting institutions may have been de-risking in response to the MSCI news alongside the Trump trade-war escalation. Bitcoin can survive such de-listings because MSTR holds only about 3.2% of all bitcoin and all treasury companies combined hold a relatively low share. However, treasury companies, along with ETFs, were the major source of demand over the past year, and index exclusion would reduce demand for their shares and thus their ability to acquire bitcoin through share dilution. In both cases, prices corrected sharply: from the roughly $1 trillion market cap peak near $58,000 in the earlier instance, and from about $110,000 at the start of November to below $90,000 in the later one, with metrics showing the most oversold conditions in years.

ETF Spotlight: PPLT I recently became a bit more bullish on platinum, so I want to take a moment to highlight it. Long-time readers know that I’ve been significantly bullish on gold and silver and their various miners and financiers since October 2018 (and to a more limited extent prior to that) as allocations within a diversified portfolio, but I haven’t written much about platinum. Gold and silver both “bottomed” right around the start of 2016 and have been in a choppy uptrend since. More importantly, I am bullish on them for fundamental reasons, and have an article dedicated to precious metals here. Platinum also reached a low point back in the same 2016 time-frame, but reached even lower lows in late 2018, so it has been on its own bearish trend. While I’ve been bullish on platinum with a very long-term outlook, the problem was that I did not see a bullish catalyst for a trend reversal yet, so I was less interested in it than I was with gold and silver, and thus had no position in it. Platinum has historically traded at a higher price than gold, but roughly within the past decade, it has traded at a discount to gold. So it has been attractive from a valuation perspective for some time, but has had a very ugly price chart for a while. Here’s a 10-year chart: Platinum has had a perfect storm of bearishness until recently. The metal is heavily used for catalytic converters in vehicles to reduce harmful emissions. Electric vehicles do not need catalytic converters, so that is a long-term demand destruction risk for platinum usage. Car sales in general have been in a significant downtrend over the past year; that industry is one of the weakest parts of the global economy. In addition, another platinum-group metal, palladium, has been substituted for platinum in the past several years for a lot of catalytic converter usage. Historically, palladium was cheaper than platinum, but now palladium trades for well over twice the price of both platinum and gold, which is historically extremely unusual. This hasn’t had much financial media attention, but within the past two weeks alone, the prices of both palladium and its rarer counterpart rhodium (both platinum-group metals) went absolutely vertical: Chart Source: Kitco Unlike gold and silver that are mined all over the world, a very small number of emerging market countries produce almost all platinum-group metals, including platinum, palladium, and rhodium. So, supply/demand balances are quite strict. New emissions standards in China and elsewhere are likely a factor in the increased demand and prices since the beginning of 2020. Palladium and platinum are able to be substituted for each other for catalytic converters in many cases, with some engineering work involved. Palladium has historically been the cheaper metal, but in this current cycle where most designs are made for it, palladium demand has been strong, driving the price up. As long as palladium prices remain elevated, it makes the engineering case for switching to platinum more attractive. These things tend to go in cycles. In addition, while platinum remains historically cheap compared to gold (about $1,000+ vs $1,550+ at the moment), platinum’s usage in jewelry should become increasingly attractive as a more cost-effective option, even though ironically it has generally been considered the more premium material. For most of history, platinum has been the more expensive metal compared to gold. With palladium and rhodium at very high prices, and gold priced well above platinum, platinum is arguably the true value play among the precious metals. In the past couple weeks, it has shown small signs of life, indicating that the past year may have been the actual bottom for the metal, and that the expensive prices for rhodium and platinum are spilling over into platinum. Last week, I added some platinum bars to my bullion collection for the first time. I may also add a small allocation to the Aberdeen Standard Physical Platinum Shares ETF (PPLT) to some of my portfolios for a more liquid and cost-effective source of exposure. Although it’s not certain, there are signs that platinum, and subsequently the PPLT ETF, may have formed a bottoming process. When it comes to metals, especially physical bullion, I am extraordinarily patient. Frankly, I don’t know how platinum will do this year or next, for example. However, I now consider the long-term risk/reward ratio of platinum and the PPLT ETF to be attractive as part of a diversified and regularly rebalanced portfolio, and thus consider it to be a “buy” for a small allocation, with ongoing dollar-cost averaging.

Sberbank has a massive market share of the Russian banking industry, ranging from 30-50% or more of market share in various areas: Chart Source: Sberbank June 2020 Investor Presentation The degree to which Sberbank has dominant market share in Russia cannot be overstated. For American readers, it’s like J.P. Morgan Chase and Wells Fargo and a bunch of fintech firms combined into one bank, for that country. Sberbank’s economic moat in Russia is exceptionally wide. Sberbank has 96.3 million active retail clients, 2.6 million active corporate clients, 14.2 thousand branches, and 279 thousand employees. They have more employees than J.P. Morgan Chase, (JPM), the largest bank in the United States, even though Sberbank’s market capitalization is less than 1/4th of JPM’s value, with Sberbank’s market cap at $64 billion and JPM’s at $282 billion. This is significantly due to lower valuation and currency value for Sberbank. Sberbank also invests in, acquires, and/or partners with a variety of fintech firms in Russia, and some global partnerships as well. This prevents those firms from taking Sberbank market share, and diversifies and extends Sberbank’s reach. These investments range from health records to restaurant delivery apps to ride-sharing apps to mobile payment processors to various types of insurance, and so forth. In other words, rather than being a stodgy old bank in a declining industry, Sberbank has above-average adoption of digital technologies and new markets compared to most global peer banks around the world. user_input: Given the persistent market regime uncertainty described in the discussion of the Fed's balance sheet and the "three pillar portfolio," how does the author's view that gold should "climb a wall of worry" over the longer term fit within that framework?
reference: The author argues that markets have exited one uncertain regime and entered another with different characteristics, in which the Fed balance sheet is likely to trend sideways, liquidity is only mildly positive, and policymakers face a difficult choice between continuing to tighten (damaging small and medium banks and the shadow banking system) or pausing and letting inflation run hot. Because of this ongoing uncertainty and volatility, the author favors a "three pillar portfolio" for the decade: high-quality profitable, dividend-paying equities at reasonable valuations with some emerging market exposure; commodity and hard money exposure including energy and commodity producers, royalty companies, futures, precious metals, and/or bitcoin; and cash or cash-equivalents such as T-bills and money markets to reduce volatility. Gold sits squarely in the second pillar. The author remains long-term bullish on gold but has been wary of it being overbought, and with a renewed surge in the dollar and long-end rates creating headwinds, he would actually prefer to see gold chop around and consolidate to release overbought momentum and sentiment, so that it can continue to climb a "wall of worry" over the longer term. In other words, the pullback does not change the long-term thesis; it makes gold's role as an inflation-and-uncertainty hedge within the second pillar more sustainable amid the unresolved liquidity and policy regime.

The Fed balance sheet is likely to trend sideways-ish for months, unless or until some big catalyst forces it higher. They don’t want to flood the system with liquidity but they want to keep the wheels from falling off. The price action of gold (up), bitcoin (up), the Nasdaq 100 (up), and the dollar index (down) have been pretty clear that this banking event and the response by the Fed represents a gain in liquidity. Some analysts are quick to point out that the Fed’s recent uptick in balance sheet size is not QE and that’s correct, but that doesn’t change the fact that it’s positive for liquidity compared to the prior week and the prior year-long downward trend. I think some people are overestimating how much liquidity the Fed is likely to provide within a 3-month period, while other people are dismissing it as a bank-specific problem and therefore not something that has consequences for the Fed’s tightening attempts. My view currently lands in the middle; all else equal it’s mildly positive for liquidity. The Fed’s pulldown in total liquidity is probably over, but that doesn’t mean liquidity is going to go straight up, either. Going back to my “century chart” that I’ve posted a number of times (with some new annotations this time), the Fed has been fighting 1940s-style fiscal-driven inflation (when debts are high and most of the monetary expansion is coming from fiscal deficits) with hawkish 1970s-style monetary policy (which works when debts are low and most of the monetary expansion is coming from bank lending). Raising rates that quickly and sucking liquidity out that quickly, when debts are still that high, leads to financial chaos. user_input: How did the reverse repo facility drawdown offset the Fed's balance sheet reduction (quantitative tightening) in 2023 versus late 2024, and what did those liquidity conditions mean for bitcoin price action heading into January 2025?
reference: In late 2023, the Treasury increased its share of short-duration T-bill issuance, which met the excess T-bill demand parked in the Fed's reverse repo facility and pulled that money out of the facility and back into the financial system. The reverse repo facility fell below $1 trillion for the first time since 2021, and at that pace the drawdown almost exactly offset the Fed's ongoing quantitative tightening, producing an essentially flat or neutral domestic liquidity environment. By January 2025, the cumulative picture was that the Fed had removed a little over $3 trillion in liquidity since beginning balance sheet reduction in mid-2022, while over $2 trillion that had been stored in the reverse repo facility began flowing back into banks starting mid-2023, leaving a net reduction of about $1 trillion from over-filled levels. Commercial bank cash levels consequently fell from a peak of a little over $4 trillion in late 2021 to a little over $3 trillion, only about $100-$200 billion above the level associated with the March 2023 regional bank crisis, with SOFR spiking above the interest on reserve balances at the ends of Q3 and Q4 as a sign of tight balance sheet space. Reverse repo usage itself had shrunk to as little as $98 billion on December 20th before a quarter-end spike to $473 billion and a fall back to $237 billion, and was expected to keep inching down, suggesting the Fed would likely end its balance sheet reduction around mid-2025 though not imminently. Combined with a strengthening dollar index since the election, these strained global liquidity conditions coincided with corrections in the S&P 500, gold, and bitcoin. Bitcoin had run from about $69k at the start of November to roughly $99k by November 22nd, spiked above $100k and touched as high as $108k in mid-December, then corrected back to around its November 22nd level, consolidating for about a month and a half. The author viewed this as a healthy mid-cycle consolidation rather than a multi-year top, noting that while market capitalization went sideways at about $1.95 trillion, the on-chain realized value (cost basis) rose from $718 billion to $815 billion, a 13% increase that effectively ratchets up the floor price, with on-chain indicators resembling March 2024, which preceded a seven-month consolidation.

If we look at bank cash levels as a percentage of assets or as a percentage of deposits, the numbers aren’t quite as low as March 2023 but are getting there. And they’re still above 2019 levels: Meanwhile, there have been some noises happening in the liquidity-related financial plumbing, similar to what was occurring in 2019 prior to the repo spike. During the end of each fiscal quarter, especially the end of the fourth quarter, there is a lot of “window dressing” that occurs where financial institutions want to lock in good numbers for the reporting period. Entities with very liquid balance sheets can provide liquidity to other entities, but the available system-wide liquidity is getting tight lately.
