Liquidity Indicators: Focusing on the Treasury Domestic liquidity in the United States continues to be almost perfectly flat, and is likely what policymakers are managing for. The Treasury Department surprised market participants with their quarterly refunding announcement by substantially raising the percentage of upcoming debt issuance that will be done with T-bills. In a sign of fiscal dominance, this is probably the first time where a Treasury refunding announcement was more important for markets than a Fed FOMC policy update. This is all kind of wonky but can be simplified as follows. A healthy sovereign bond market has plenty of liquidity (i.e. good trading volumes where even a large entity can buy or sell a ton of bonds without moving the price noticeably), and no problem issuing a sizable percentage of long duration bonds. However, the U.S. sovereign bond market is not very healthy due to such large ongoing deficits combined with the Fed’s ongoing balance sheet reduction. So, yields keep rising and are very volatile, bond liquidity is low, and small banks are being squeezed in the process. So, the Treasury decided to increase its issuance of short-duration T-bills for its upcoming deficit issuance beyond its normal T-bill ratio. This improves liquidity conditions, but around the margins is the kind of thing that emerging markets do when facing debt and currency problems. The big pool of remaining liquidity available to buy Treasuries is the money that is still stuck in the reverse repo facility. All of this reverse repo money basically represents excess T-bill demand, and the Fed maintains the reserve repo facility so that the market doesn’t drive T-bill yields below the lower floor of their interest rate target. In contrast, there isn’t much demand for longer-duration bonds. And so as the Treasury issues more and more T-bills, it helps meet that excess T-bill demand that exists, and money starts to come out of the reverse repo facility and into holding T-bills. The Treasury then spends this money back into the economy and financial system. The reverse repo facility is now under $1 trillion for the first time since 2021: The ongoing drawdown of the reverse repo facility is putting liquidity back into the system, and how fast it is drained partially depends on how many T-bills the Treasury issues as a ratio of their total debt issuance. By increasing T-bill issuance, they continue to draw money out of the reverse repo facility. And at the current pace, it almost exactly offsets the Fed’s ongoing quantitative tightening (balance sheet reduction), to create a neutral domestic liquidity environment. Once it runs out, liquidity problems could become pretty severe and require a change of course by the Fed. Why is this important? The reason is because the U.S. is facing a slow-moving fiscal crisis for the first time in decades. We’re running 7%-of-GDP deficits despite unemployment rates being very low, and since we are no longer in an environment of structurally falling interest rates, interest expense is starting to become a problem for the first time in decades. And that chart somewhat understates the issue. At $34 trillion in debt, and if interest rates just stay where they are, then as more and more public debt matures and gets refinanced at these higher rates, it will approach $1.7 trillion in annual interest expense, or 6% of GDP (a record high). A recession that forces the Fed to cut interest rates would alleviate some of the interest expense, but usually in recessions fiscal deficits rise sharply because tax revenue drops. user_input: How does Activist Treasury Issuance (ATI) relate to fiscal dominance and structural deficits, and why does a strong dollar environment make such Treasury bill issuance necessary?
reference: Activist Treasury Issuance (ATI), a term coined by Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini, describes the Treasury Department shortening the average duration of its debt issuance through excess T-bill issuance, thereby offsetting the Fed's monetary tightening and dynamically managing financial conditions in a way similar to quantitative easing. They calculate that ATI reduced 10-year yields by roughly a quarter of a percent over the past year, providing stimulus comparable to a one-point Fed Funds rate cut, and that unwinding it (terming out $1 trillion of excess bills) would temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, akin to a two-point rate hike. Doing this in benign economic conditions rather than a crisis is viewed as a symptom of ongoing fiscal dominance in the United States, in which large structural fiscal deficits are stimulatory for certain industries and tend to give a developed-market recession "emerging market lite" characteristics, likely producing a milder peak in unemployment than an average recession. The necessity for short-duration issuance arises because a strong dollar environment discourages the foreign sector from buying many Treasuries, so with neither the central bank nor primary foreign investors absorbing the issuance, the Treasury leans on more "money-like" T-bills that investors can hold much like cash. The Fed could step in to buy Treasuries, but doing so amid high inflation would represent a severe degradation of central bank independence, similar to the 1940s; alternatively it could adjust levers such as the supplementary leverage ratio to induce banks to buy more Treasuries.

Macro View Liquidity Indicators Domestic liquidity indicators continue to run almost perfectly sideways, in large part because the Treasury and Fed have been in lockstep regarding this: Notably, Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini recently published a paper about “Activist Treasury Issuance” which is their term that refers to the Treasury Department taking unusual actions to offset the Fed’s tightness. Both Miran and Roubini are economics PhDs and worked in various capacities with the Treasury Department in the past. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. I’d argue that it’s a symptom of the ongoing fiscal dominance that the United States finds itself in. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. If ATI is unwound via terming out $1 trillion of excess Treasury Bills, we expect it to temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, before settling into a permanent 30-bp increase, with corresponding price changes in risk assets. A 50-bp increase in the 10-year yield will have similar economic effects as a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate. If ATI is not unwound but becomes a permanently employed policy tool, we are likely to see higher equilibrium inflation and interest rates priced in over time due to political business cycles becoming reality. Regular readers of my work will be quite familiar with this concept. I start most of my reports by discussing liquidity conditions, including what the Treasury has been doing with its excess T-bill issuance. And at the start of this year, I dedicated my January 2024 newsletter to this phenomenon of the Treasury offsetting the Fed. Here was a key snippet: Ever since the fourth quarter of 2022, and extending all throughout 2023, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury have been operating opposite policies from each other. And the Treasury has had to pull two different levers to keep up with the Fed. -From September 2022 through May 2023, the Treasury drained their own cash reserves back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. -From June 2023 to the present, the Treasury rapidly increased their T-bill issuance as a percentage of their debt issuance and thus drained reverse repos back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. This following chart shows the Fed vs Treasury liquidity actions in year-over-year change terms. For this chart, higher means more liquidity, and lower means less liquidity. The Fed in blue has been doing its part to reduce liquidity in the financial system since early 2022. The Treasury in red (reflecting both their own cash balances and their ability to affect the reverse repo facility based on their ability to issue T-bills) has been doing its part to increase liquidity in the financial system since late 2022. The net result is that domestic liquidity was decreasing until Q4 2022 but then began to flatten out and turn slightly upward when the Treasury began its inverse operation: -January 2024 Newsletter, “Fiscal and Monetary Divergence While I’m more focused on the liquidity impacts, Miran and Roubini’s paper attempts to quantify the effect by comparing it to interest rate changes. They argue that the Treasury’s excessive T-bill issuance has been the equivalent of the Fed cutting interest rates by 1%. And they argue that if this were to be unwound, it would temporarily be similar to a 2% rate hike by the Fed. I don’t have any particular view regarding if their interest rate comparison is accurate or not, but in my view it’s less about rates per se, and more about liquidity and smooth financial plumbing, of which rates are only a part. The payroll survey continues to show strong numbers, while the household survey has been notably weaker, with a widening gap. But a recession in a developed market that is in a state of fiscal dominance tends to have certain “emerging market lite” characteristics. This lets us see a broad spectrum of the economy rather than to over-emphasize any particularly strong or weak data point. If bonds aren’t serving as a ballast for that, then the drawdown can be more impactful. user_input: Why are financials outperforming consumer discretionary apparel stocks like Lululemon and Nike year-to-date in 2025, and how do tariffs, the fiscal-dominance business cycle backdrop, and insurance/banking resilience explain the sector divergence?
reference: Over the long run the consumer discretionary sector has outperformed financials by more than 3x, but year-to-date in 2025 financials are winning by nearly 2x. The main reason for this divergence is exposure to tariffs and to the fiscal versus monetary policy mix. Banks and insurers are impacted by interest rates and other aspects of the economy, but they are not in the direct crosshairs of tariffs, so they have continued to do well; the report highlighted banks in a prior issue and cites Travelers (TRV) as an insurance example that is just chugging along right at its average valuation. Consumer discretionary companies, by contrast, sit near the epicenter of tariffs. Lululemon is the clearest case: its stock round-tripped its entire post-pandemic gain even though earnings remain elevated, because of severe valuation compression. It slashed FY25 profit and sales guidance on tariff headwinds and soft U.S. sales, with tariffs expected to shave 300 basis points off gross margins, largely from the end of the de minimis exemption since two-thirds of its e-commerce orders ship from Canada, and because the great majority of its sales are U.S.-based it has less geographic diversification to cushion the blow. It also faces a second problem of stale lounge and social wear offerings failing to resonate with Millennial and Gen Z buyers amid intense competition. Nike shows a similar multi-year collapse in growth and price after trading at 48x earnings in 2021, and still carries a P/E roughly 3x Lululemon's despite weaker growth. This sector split sits atop a mixed macro backdrop: the Atlanta Fed's estimator suggests healthy Q3 GDP growth while aggregate leading indicators have flashed mild recession for nearly three years, and under fiscal dominance the 6-7% of GDP deficits (about $2 trillion, only ~15% offset by $300+ billion in new tariff revenue) act as continuous background stimulus even as housing, commercial real estate, ISM manufacturing and bank lending stay weak. The key variable has been the labor market, which recently flashed a yellow warning as initial jobless claims spiked to a 3+ year high, though still well below the roughly 300,000 level that would signal a red light.

Macro View US Business Cycle Traditional measures of the economy continue to look mixed. The Atlanta Fed’s estimator tool continues to suggest healthy GDP growth here in Q3: And yet the aggregate assessment of leading indicators continues to flash a mild recession, which it has been doing for the better part of three years now without any NBER-defined recession having occurred. This index includes weekly manufacturing hours, weekly jobless claims, various indices of new orders, building permits, a leading credit index, interest rate spreads, consumer expectations of business conditions, and stock prices. The point I’ve been emphasizing for a while is that amid fiscal dominance, the economy functions differently than under monetary dominance, which is what everyone is trained to analyze. The baseline runs hotter, and those who are on the receiving side of deficits tend to be fine, while those who are not tend to suffer unless they’re able to position for it. The private sector in isolation is indeed pretty weak by many metrics. The housing sector and commercial real estate sector have both pretty much stalled, ISM manufacturing is weak, bank lending is tepid, etc. However, the 6-7% of GDP fiscal deficits (~$2 trillion nominally) serve as a continuous background stimulus. This flows to retirees via Social Security who spend it into the consumer economy, flows to the health care sector via Medicare and Medicaid (including healthcare employees who spend it into the non-healthcare economy), flows to Defense (including soldiers and defense employees who spend it into the non-defense economy), and interest expense (which flows to individuals and financial institutions, some of which gets spent into the non-financial economy). The $300+ billion in new annualized tariff revenue reduces that slightly (which is why I monitor it pretty closely), but only by around 15%, which is why the overall effect remains. Due to that fiscal dominance environment, I’ve been more focused on the labor market. If the labor market remains in decent shape along with the deficits, then it tends to override the other weak variables. It’s like Thanos and his Infinity Stones (deficits and labor market) beating the Avengers (basically every other indicator). And for a while, the labor market has been fine. Well, these past two weeks, the labor market flashed a warning. Initial jobless claims (which are one of the fastest pulse checks we have available) suddenly spiked to a 3+ year high: Now, that’s still a reasonably low number. Roughly 300,000 is the level that would flash more of a red light, whereas this is just a yellow light. Thanos took a punch, maybe lost a stone, but otherwise is still winning for now. But it’s worth watching more closely.

Throughout 2022, as the Federal Reserve aggressively raised interest rates, unprofitable hypergrowth equities were basically killed, and profitable growth equities took a major valuation haircut. As a result, growth equities underperformed value equities in aggregate. During 2023, especially after the March banking crisis, the market has increasingly priced in a top in interest rates, and along with the AI craze, has bid up growth equities relative to value equities. This chart shows the ratio of value equities to growth equities. When it’s rising it means value is outperforming in aggregate, and when it’s falling it means growth is outperforming in aggregate: Value outperformed in the strong growth era of the 1980s. Growth outperformed in the tech boom of the 1990s. Value outperformed during the commodity bull market and the rise of BRICS in the 2000s. Growth outperformed in the 2010s decade of relative economic stagnation, and accelerated during the pandemic. Value began outperforming from the depths of the pandemic during the recovery, although 2023 is challenging that. If we take Alphabet (GOOGL) as an example (one of the growth stocks I have in the Newsletter portfolio), it has returned to its average decade valuation (the blue line): Arguably, it should be at a lower valuation, because interest rates are higher than average. For growth equities, what I look for is a dominant market position and a major entrenched economic moat along with a good balance sheet, like Visa. AI Cybersecurity Risks Ramping Up There is a growing divide between closed-weight and open-weight AI models. Closed-weight models such as Claude and ChatGPT are typically developed by the leading labs, are the most advanced, and the user has no control over them. To use them, the user connects with the provider’s server. The provider can restrict access, block certain queries, and see all the personal or business secrets that the user hands over as part of their AI usage. Open-weight models (which are almost all Chinese now) are several months behind the leading labs’ closed weight models in terms of capability at any given time, but much like open-source software, they come with a lot of advantages. The user can download them and run them on their own machine (or many other third parties can run it for users on their servers as a service), which means privacy for the user and lack of control by the producer. They can additionally be evaluated and fine-tuned by the user. As a result, open-weight models have been sharply gaining market share here in 2026. Advocates for closed-weight models often argue that it’s dangerous for open-weight models to exist. They view AI as extremely powerful and thus it must be controlled. And of course, the leading labs are worth about a trillion dollars in market cap and don’t enjoy having countless open-weight competitors. Advocates for open-weight models generally argue that it’s inevitable (there’s no way to take down code globally), and it broadens access to AI rather than forming regulatory moats around a small group of AI corporations to protect them from competition. Here’s the topical problem: Both closed-weight and open-weight models, when they produce software, can create cybersecurity problems that closed-weight models often refuse to fix, because fixing a cybersecurity issue is very similar in practice to creating a cybersecurity issue (i.e. “white hat” hacking vs “black hat” hacking). There’s no way around this. When humans or bots write a lot of code, it comes with imperfections. And now, people are ironically turning to Chinese open-weight models to fix the bugs in their software, including ones created by American closed-weight models, since the American closed-weight models won’t fix them and the Chinese open-weight models will. The leading AI models are particularly good at exploiting bugs and creating cybersecurity problems, and the main way to defend against that is to have leading AI models stress-test your own software and fix the problems before the software is put into active use, and to regularly check them once they’re in use. I wrote about this back in 2023 when AI could barely write any usable code yet, and three short years later it’s starting to get there: Right now, at any given time, tons of hackers are trying to breach various software systems that we rely on, and some small percentage of them succeed, which results in a lot of data breaches and other issues. Now, imagine that a group of hackers or a government agency makes an AI that is optimized for hacking. In other words, some AI programs are optimized for beating humans in chess, and some AI programs can be optimized for hacking into systems better than humans can. Early chess AI learned from games between grandmaster human players, and then could beat those grandmasters every time. Recent chess AI instead learned from playing itself over and over, and then could beat those other AIs at chess. Now, suppose that a similar approach is used for hacking. In fact I would be surprised if multiple groups were not already working on this. So, first AI learns how to hack from absorbing existing techniques, and then graduates to learning how to hack from just iterating over and over at superhuman speed and rewriting its code to get better and better. Eventually it becomes orders of magnitude better at hacking than any human, and can breach any system that humans have designed. This could be open-sourced and broadly available. So what’s the defense against that? For systems that are connected to the internet and have a lot of complexity (and thus can’t realistically be made “unhackable” as some offline or basic systems can), the answer is more AI. Similar to how the only rivals to chess programs at chess are other chess programs, we’ll probably reach a point where the only defenses against AIs optimized for hacking are AIs optimized to update and defend software systems against being hacked. Imagine a world where superhuman hackers are always and everywhere trying to breach everything, and superhuman defenders are always and everywhere trying to prevent those breaches from happening. And both the attackers and defenders are constantly iterating and updating themselves as they learn from each other, while no human really knows what’s going on because the code is more complex than they can understand and is updated more quickly than they can keep up with. In that scenario, digital gods will be constantly battling each other in cyberspace in ways we can’t even comprehend, and yet the systems we all rely on are what’s at stake in that battle. -August 2023 Newsletter: Six AI Themes to Consider Calle, a physics PhD and open-source software developer, highlighted this problem recently in mid-July when he pointed out how he has to use Chinese AI to make his software secure: This got picked up by David Sacks, the President’s leading tech advisor: Shortly thereafter, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, joined Twitter/X and made his first post about the importance of open-weight models: The next week, someone exploited a deficient random number generator in Coldcard bitcoin wallets and stole 1,300+ total coins from hundreds of users. user_input: Considering how Lightning Labs Taro protocol lets assets be issed on the bitcoin blockchain and deposited into Lightning channels, and how bitcoin's base layer has a strict block space limmit of four megabytes every ten minutes, how do these two peices fit together to explain why stablecoin and small payments are pushed onto the Lightning Network rather than the base layer, and what real-world integrations and funding rasies suggest that Lightning is hitting a critical mass?
reference: The two points connect through Bitcoin's layered scaling design. The base layer deliberately keeps a small block space limit of four megabytes every ten minutes so bandwidth and storage requirements stay low enough for ordinary users to run nodes, preserving decentralization and permissionlessness. Because that limited space makes per-transaction base layer fees too high for small amounts, the solution is to scale through layers: large, high-density value (for example storing 10 bitcoin as long-term savings) stays on the base layer, while small amounts meant as a medium of exchange (for example 0.01 bitcoin) are pushed to layers like the Liquid network, Cash App, a noncustodial Lightning channel, or a Chaumian ecash custodian wallet, which offer higher throughput, speed, privacy and/or programmability in exchange for less security. Lightning Labs' Taro protocol builds on this by allowing assets to be issued on the bitcoin blockchain, leveraging taproot for privacy and scalability, and letting those assets be deposited into Lightning channels and transferred over the existing Lightning Network. Taro channels can hold both BTC and multiple Taro assets without additional overhead, it is light client friendly with low verification costs, supports atomic swaps between Taro assets and BTC, unique and non-unique assets, multi-signature and co-signatory arrangements, and flexible settlement times ranging from immediate to hourly or daily. Running stablecoins directly over Lightning makes stablecoin payments nearly instant and nearly free, and lets users avoid the capital gains tax problem of paying with bitcoins. Evidence of critical mass includes Jack Mallers of Strike announcing partnerships with NCR Corporation, Blackhawk Network, and Shopify so users can spend via Lightning at places like McDonald's and Walmart, BitPay integrating with Lightning, and a CNBC piece showing a real Lightning transfer from the U.S. to Poland with a cash withdrawal at a Wroclaw bitcoin ATM in under three minutes. Capital is also flowing in: OpenNode raised $20 million, Voltage $6 million, IBEX Mercado $4 million, and others such as Impervious also raised funds, alongside the launch of ego death capital by Jeff Booth, Nico Lechuga, and Andi Pitt. The author compares Lightning today to the Bitcoin network back in 2014, tiny and off most people's radar but hitting a critical mass of liquidity and usability.

And it’s open source and therefore widely available in a permissionless context. When you pay a bitcoin miner to put something into a new block on the Bitcoin blockchain, this information gets stored on tens of thousands of nodes around the world that sync with each other constantly. And it’s accessible to anyone in the world with an internet connection. Depending on precisely how/where you put that information into the blockchain, it might be prunable by nodes (i.e. some of them can decide not to store it and still remain synced to the network) or it might not be (i.e. nodes are basically stuck with it whether they want it or not). Unprunable information will generally be more complicated and costly to insert into the blockchain than prunable information. For the Bitcoin network, there is a block space limit of four megabytes every ten minutes. If the block space limit is designed to be too big, then the bandwidth and storage requirements to run a node would become too high, and thus only institutional entities could run a node, and the network would become less decentralized and permissionless. If the block space limit is made too small, then the number of people who would be able to pay for and get a transaction into the blockchain on a regular basis may be insufficient relative to demand, resulting in those people looking elsewhere for a solution. The main way to address those two design criteria is to have a moderately small block size and then scale through layers; layers can and have been built that have higher throughput, speed, privacy, and/or programmability than the base layer, in exchange for less security on those layers. To varying degrees, those layers inherent some of the properties of the base layer, but not all of those properties. This keeps the base layer for high-density valuable transactions, and pushes smaller transactions to the upper levels. For example, if you want to store 10 bitcoin as long-term savings, it’s best to do it on the base layer. But if you want to set aside 0.01 bitcoin to use as a medium of exchange, then storing that on the Liquid network, on Cash App, on a noncustodial Lightning channel, or on a Chaumian ecash custodian wallet for fast and private transactions is good for that purpose, since base layer fees will be too high on a per-transaction basis. The primary design goal of this distributed database by its creator Satoshi Nakamoto was for it to be used as money. The largest monies in the world (the dollar, the euro, the yuan, and all fiat currencies) run on centralized permissioned ledgers. Bitcoin is a decentralized permissionless ledger with a high degree of immutability, and so naturally a good killer app for that is to use it as decentralized money. It’s not the only use case, but it’s the obvious use case, and I would argue it’s by far the largest use case with the largest total addressable market. Although Bitcoin as a database was primarily optimized by Nakamoto to be used as money rather than non-monetary information storage, it’s likely impossible to design a blockchain in such a way that it can \only\ be used as money. And even Nakamoto himself put non-monetary information into the first block of the Bitcoin network when he timestamped an article headline about bank bailouts (“The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks”). There are almost always clever ways to store non-monetary information on a blockchain, no matter how restrictive the code is. A given blockchain can be designed with more or less flexibility on purpose, so that it’s harder and more expensive or easier and less expensive to stick that non-monetary information in it. Bitcoin in its current form is designed mainly for money but with some allowance for non-monetary information. If anything, it’s good to have some efficient prunable space where non-monetary information can go, to encourage it to go there if it’s going to exist. That way, nodes that don’t want it can prune it out, and nodes that do want it can keep it. The Bitcoin network currently does that with defined OP\_RETURN space, and people use that and also find more expensive ways to stick unprunable non-monetary information elsewhere in the blockchain as well. Decentralized money and savings is potentially a $100+ trillion global total addressable market. The demand for it is enormous, if a good enough solution proves itself, which the Bitcoin network has gradually been doing for 15 years now. Decentralized non-monetary information storage for utility or speculation is a much smaller market, probably a few trillion dollars or less. That’s why over time I expect monetary uses to price out the majority of non-monetary use cases and remain the largest use for the blockchain. Some bitcoin users want to strengthen the various filters against non-monetary information, to try to keep more of the blockchain reserved for monetary transfers. However, that’s extremely hard to do if there is real demand by paying users for those non-monetary use cases. A subset of bitcoin critics often say that bitcoin has no intrinsic value (meaning to say that it has no non-monetary use case), in contrast to gold which can be used for various ornamental and industrial purposes in addition to its role as money. However, the reality is the Bitcoin network as the world’s most immutable and decentralized database does have non-monetary uses cases, and bitcoin is the network’s unit of account. And ironically, some bitcoin proponents are unhappy with the fact that the Bitcoin network has non-monetary use cases, since those non-monetary use cases compete with fees for their monetary use case. user_input: Why is the US Treasury market getting illiquid when the dollar strengthens, and how do the Fed's new standing repo facilities relate to Treasury issuance?
reference: When the dollar strengthens markedly, the foreign sector gets squeezed because it buys dollar-based commodities and often carries dollar-denominated debts, so in aggregate it stops buying and even trims its large holdings of US financial assets, including Treasuries. Fed custody data (about 40% of foreign Treasury holdings, updated weekly) shows this pattern, and with the foreign sector on a Treasury buying strike, the US Treasury market has become volatile and illiquid, with the MOVE index at decade highs. The US Treasury Department's near-term advantage was that it didn't plan much net issuance through September 2022, thanks to high cash reserves and favorable tax revenue/expenditure timing in Q2 and Q3, but falling tax revenue from asset price destruction and economic deceleration means issuance would likely pick up by Q4 or the first half of the following year, when the Treasury would be more vulnerable to liquidity problems and missing foreign buyers. The Fed's two standing repo facilities announced in July 2021, a domestic SRF (daily overnight repos against Treasuries, agency debt, and agency MBS, up to $500 billion at a 25 basis point minimum bid rate) and a FIMA repo facility for foreign official institutions holding Treasuries in custody at the New York Fed (25 basis points, $60 billion per counterparty), address exactly this problem. They were seen as preparation for a QE taper amid doubt about whether private and foreign demand for Treasuries would be sufficient given planned US government issuance, and as a way to avoid a repeat of March 2020, when a global dollar shortage forced foreign entities to sell Treasuries for dollars, rendering the US Treasury market illiquid with spiking yields and forcing the Fed to buy $1 trillion of Treasuries in three weeks. By letting domestic and foreign holders pledge Treasuries for dollars at any time, the facilities increase the fungibility and liquidity of Treasuries with dollars.

I’ll be paying close attention to rent payment percentages and other signs this autumn. QE Taper Preparation: The Fed Standing Repo Facility At the end of July, the Fed announced two new standing repo facilities. These facilities let certain entities, domestic and foreign, loan Treasuries to the Fed in exchange for dollars: The Federal Open Market Committee on Wednesday announced the establishment of two standing repurchase agreement (repo) facilities—a domestic standing repo facility (SRF) and a repo facility for foreign and international monetary authorities (FIMA repo facility). These facilities will serve as backstops in money markets to support the effective implementation of monetary policy and smooth market functioning. Under the SRF, the Federal Reserve will conduct daily overnight repo operations against Treasury securities, agency debt securities, and agency mortgage-backed securities, with a maximum operation size of $500 billion. The minimum bid rate for repos under the facility will be set initially at 25 basis points, somewhat above the general level of overnight interest rates. Counterparties for this facility will include primary dealers and will be expanded over time to include additional depository institutions. Under the FIMA repo facility, the Federal Reserve will enter into overnight repurchase agreements as needed with foreign official institutions against their holdings of Treasury securities maintained in custody at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The rate for this facility will be set initially at 25 basis points with a per counterparty limit of $60 billion. By creating a temporary source of dollar liquidity for FIMA account holders, the facility can help address pressures in global dollar funding markets that could otherwise affect financial market conditions in the United States. This is interesting, because right now there is zero demand for repo activities from the Fed. To the contrary, there is nearly a trillion dollars in demand for the Fed’s reverse repo operations. So why implement this? It seems pretty clear that the Fed is preparing for a gradual taper in its rate of asset purchases. However, it’s unclear if there is enough private sector and foreign sector demand for Treasuries, at the rate of Treasury issuance that the US government plans over the next few years. Plus, the Fed doesn’t want a repeat of what happened in March 2020, where there was a global dollar shortage, the dollar spiked in value, and foreign entities had to sell Treasuries to get dollars. This resulted in the US Treasury market going illiquid with spiking yields, to which the Fed had to respond by buying $1 trillion worth of Treasuries in three weeks, with new money. So, this set of new repo facilities is interesting, and a number of Fed officials have been talking about implementing them for a couple years. They basically make permanent the types of operations that the Fed did from late 2019 through early 2020. Going forward, certain domestic and foreign holders of Treasuries have assurances that, any time they need to, they can use their Treasuries as collateral with the Fed to get dollars. This increases the fungibility/liquidity of Treasuries with dollars. Chart Source: Atlanta Fed We already had a negative real GDP print in Q1, so if this model ends up being roughly correct, it will mark two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth. The one pillar of the economy that continues to hold up decently is the labor market. However, this does tend to be a lagging indicator; we’re often firmly in a recession by the time it has noticeably rolled over, especially after revisions to the data are done later. Here’s the total nonfarm payroll numbers, represented as % off high: If I zoom in on the 1970s, which was the last time that we had inflation levels this high, we can see that payrolls often didn’t start falling until well into a recession: Here’s the employment to population ratio of 25-54 year olds in the past four decades or so: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Additionally, we need to look at real wages. Dollar Strength and Treasury Troubles The dollar has been rather strong in recent months, as the Fed tightens monetary policy more-so than some of its developed market peers. The dollar index, which is very heavily weighted towards the euro and the yen, has broken out to multi-decade highs: However, the sheer scale of that recent rally has more to do with euro and yen weakness than it has to do with dollar strength. For example, the US dollar vs the Canadian dollar has been strengthening a bit from a low base, but with nothing particularly remarkable going on: The US dollar vs the Brazilian real, the Chinese yuan, or the Australian dollar, is showing a bout of strength in 2022 but nothing really notable there either. The notable aspect of the move is mainly against the euro and yen. Europe is facing a crippling energy crisis that is worse than the rest of the developed world, and Japan is capping long-duration bond yields artificially low at 0.25%. This has given the USDEUR and the USDJPY currency pairs a huge chance to rally in USD’s favor. There are also of course some specific emerging or frontier market countries having currency problems, such as Sri Lanka, Argentina, Turkey, and so forth. To a lot of people, this probably sounds like a good thing for the United States. Our dollar is strengthening, which is great for us, right? Well, not really, as I’ve covered before. When the dollar strengthens notably, the foreign sector tends to get pretty squeezed, because they buy dollar-based commodities and in many cases have dollar-denominated debts. However, they also have tens of trillions of dollars worth of US financial assets, which they accumulated over decades from structural trade surpluses against the US. The US has a deeply negative net international investment position, which we dug into from decades of structural trade deficits with the rest of the world. When the dollar strengthens markedly, the foreign sector in aggregate tends to stop buying and even start trimming their dollar assets, which can render US financial markets illiquid. This chart shows the portion of US Treasuries that the foreign sector holds in custody at the US Federal Reserve. It represents around 40% of total foreign Treasury holdings, but unlike the full dataset that gets updated monthly with a two-month lag, this dataset is updated weekly. The MOVE index, which is a measure of US Treasury market volatility, has crept up to decade highs: Chart Source: Trading View One thing that the US Treasury Department currently has going for it is that they don’t intend to issue a lot of net Treasuries through September 2022. Their cash reserves are pretty high, and the timing of tax revenues and government expenditures is in their favor during Q2 and Q3 of this year. However, all of this destruction in asset prices and economic deceleration will likely start weighing on tax revenue, and by Q4 of this year or during the first half of next year, Treasury issuance will likely pick up. This will be when the Treasury is more vulnerable to liquidity problems and lack of foreign buyers, if these types of conditions are still present by that point. reference: The December 8, 2019 deep-dive presented The Cheesecake Factory as a well-managed small-cap restaurant stock with a hefty dividend and significant long-term potential, with a recent acquisition (Fox Restaurant Concepts) serving as a potential catalyst for improvement. In valuing it, the analysis downgraded management\'s 8% revenue growth target to a more conservative 6% because the company only grew revenue at a 3.7% annualized rate over the past five years and 4.0% annualized over the past ten years, making 8% roughly double its historical pace - even though post-acquisition drivers were credible, with The Cheesecake Factory brand expected to contribute about half the growth (3-4%, in line with history) and North Italia plus FRC contributing the other half at a faster rate from a smaller base. Combined with a current dividend yield of about 3.3% (versus the 2.5% the company assumed, and the S&P 500\'s ~1.8%), roughly 1.5% annual share count reduction, and debt paydown giving about 5.5% in total annual capital returns, the base case at the $43.22 price and $2.65 expected 2019 EPS (about a 16.3 P/E) implied roughly 10% expected long-term returns without valuation expansion. A more bullish case of 8% growth plus a re-rating to an 18 earnings multiple could deliver the company\'s targeted 13-14% annual returns, but that was treated as the optimistic rather than base case.

However, I’ll believe 8% when I see it. That’s double their 5-year and 10-year growth rates. That’s not bad, compared to the S&P 500 average yield of around 1.8% these days. Lastly, the company expects to reduce its share count by 1.5% per year, and to pay down acquisition debt over time even though its balance sheet remains in solid shape. Total capital returns from dividends, buybacks, and debt reduction are expected to average 5.5% per year. In addition, with a strong balance sheet, good management, and a proven business model, it’s not very risky, as long as it is part of a diversified portfolio. With a more bullish scenario of 8% growth and eventually selling the stock for a higher earnings multiple of 18, 13-14% long-term returns are indeed possible from today’s price point, but I would not use that as my base case. That’s the optimistic case. Margin improvement from North Italia‘s growth could also give a performance boost. The base case is pretty good, the downside risks are real but well-managed in my view, and the upside potential is very significant. Basically, this is an example of a stock that transitioned from a high-valuation growth stock into a more mature dividend-paying quality/value stock with a more modest growth rate. However, with the acquisition of FRC and the company’s plan to scale North Italia nationwide, the company has a realistic path to increase their growth rate again.

user_input: In the July 11, 2021 deep dive on Amazon and Marathon Digital, the analysis highlights the opportunity in publicly-traded North American bitcoin miners such as Marathon Digital Holdings in the context of the miner migration; how does the later bitcoin note, which reports on the Bitcoin Mining Council briefing, extend the case for Marathon Digital Holdings through its CEO's comments on utility colocation and load balancing?
reference: The July 11, 2021 report devoted its bitcoin section to the miner migration and to the resulting opportunity in publicly-traded North American bitcoin miners such as Marathon Digital Holdings (MARA), alongside macro coverage of rates, gold, the dollar, OPEC+, and China, and a separate look at Amazon (AMZN) breaking out of a one-year price consolidation. The later bitcoin note builds on that thesis by reporting on the Bitcoin Mining Council's quarterly sustainability update and livestreamed briefing, in which Marathon Digital Holdings CEO Fred Thiel argued that power companies will eventually become some of the largest bitcoin mining host facilities. He used a nuclear plant as an example: an always-on power source that is hard to adjust to fluctuating demand and that can benefit from on-site bitcoin miners acting as load balancers to profitably absorb excess supply. In the analyst Q&A, Thiel disclosed that his company, the largest bitcoin miner by market capitalization, had spoken with four of the top six power groups in North America, and that those groups now have dedicated teams studying bitcoin mining as a load balancer, are in discussions with miners and hosting providers, and have venture investments in the space. Hut 8 Mining CEO Jaime Leverton agreed, and DMG Blockchain Solutions CEO Sheldon Bennett said tests deploying mining containers to utilities as load balancers produced very positive results. Because on-site colocation eliminates transmission losses and duplicate security personnel while letting miners bargain for otherwise curtailed or wasted energy, it represents the most cost-effective and environmentally friendly form of mining, which is constructive and specific news for Marathon Digital Holdings and the North American miners flagged in the earlier report.

Bitcoin Note Bitcoin has consolidated after reaching new all-time highs. The long-term log chart remains very constructive: Chart Source: Blockchain.com On-chain indicators still look reasonably favorable for the next several months as well, indicating a relatively tight amount of liquid supply, as many coins are locked up in cold storage by longer-term holders who aren’t selling at current levels, and indeed are still dollar-cost averaging in. The wild card is that as futures become a larger part of the market, it contributes to speculation and rehypothecation and various short-term price spikes or dips. Ultimately it is spot-buying and spot-selling that drives the long-term price, while leveraged traders throw all sorts of spikes and dips into the price action along the way. There were three significant items of fundamental interest for bitcoin over the past couple weeks, in my view. 1) Bitcoin Mining Colocation News The Bitcoin Mining Council is the large trade association for bitcoin miners, and they issued their Q3 updates for the sustainability of the bitcoin mining ecosystem. They also livestreamed a briefing which included executives giving presentations and a section for analyst Q&A. Ever since I published my bitcoin energy article, I’ve been on the lookout for signs of utility colocation, referring to instances where bitcoin miners are located on the site of utility-scale energy production. Many utilities have always-on sources of power generation (nuclear, hydro, geo) and variable-on sources that are outside of their control (wind, solar), and they have to match this supply with fluctuating demand or “load” from their electrical grid. Any amount that they produce that there is no demand for gets curtailed, wasted. That happens a lot around the margins, and it’s not ideal for the environment, it’s not ideal for utility profits, and it’s not ideal for consumer electricity prices when energy is produced and yet wasted. Bitcoin miners are a unique electricity customer because they can go on-site of production, and they can deal with intermittent power as long as they have super-cheap electricity rates. If they go on-site with a power generator, the bitcoin miner can serve as a load balancer. Being on-site eliminates transmission losses and duplicate facility security personnel. During his presentation, the CEO of Marathon Digital Holdings (MARA), Fred Thiel, said that he thinks power companies will eventually be some of the largest bitcoin mining host facilities. He used the example of a nuclear power facility- an always-on source of power that is hard to turn up or down to match fluctuating demand, and that can benefit from on-site bitcoin miners as load balancers to profitably soak up any excess supply. In the analyst Q&A section, I asked if utilities are aware of this and looking into it, or if the topic is still mainly on the miner’s side (I know from private miners that there are some utility colocations, but was not sure of the scale since it’s just kind of starting to happen). Liquidity Check-Up US domestic liquidity and global liquidity conditions remain quite resilient despite the ongoing energy crisis. Back in December 2025, when bank reserve levels grew tight and domestic liquidity shortages were showing up, the Fed shifted from balance sheet reduction to gradual balance sheet expansion, to raise the aggregate level of reserves for banks on a structural basis. And specifically, the Fed determined that $20-$25 billion in monthly reserve creation was needed indefinitely, but purposely erred higher to $40 billion per month until tax day. This was to provide an extra liquidity buffer so that even when the April tax week liquidity suck occurs, banks would still have plenty of liquidity. And indeed, from Powell’s mid-December speech into mid-April, they averaged ::drumroll:: $41.5 billion in balance sheet growth per month over the span of four months. These were Fed chairman Powell’s remarks on the subject: As detailed in a statement released today by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, reserve management purchases will amount to $40 billion in the first month and may remain elevated for a few months to alleviate expected near-term pressures in money markets. Thereafter, we expect the size of reserve management purchases to decline, though the actual pace will depend on market conditions. […] So, you know, we announced that we’re resuming reserve management purchases. That is completely separate from monetary policy. It’s just we need to keep an ample supply of reserves out there. Why so big? The answer to that is, you know, if you look ahead, you will see that April 15th is coming up, and our framework is such that we want to have ample reserves even at times when reserves are at a low level temporarily. So that’s what happens on Tax Day. People pay a lot of money to the government, reserves drop sharply and temporarily. So this seasonal buildup that we’ll see in the next few months was going to happen anyway. It was going to happen because April 15th is April 15th. There’s also a secular ongoing growth of the balance sheet. We have to keep reserves, call it, constant as a—as it relates to the banking system or to the whole economy. And that alone calls for us to increase about $20 or $25 billion per month. -Jerome Powell, December 10th 2025 Press Conference Powell’s term as Fed chairman ends on May 15th, 2026. However, his term as a Fed governor goes until January 31, 2028 unless he elects to resign early (as outgoing chairmen often do) or is removed for cause. Kevin Warsh, who was previously on the Fed board, has been nominated by President Trump to be the next Fed chairman. He’s currently in the process of going through the Senate confirmation. Warsh has advocated for a smaller Fed balance sheet, but he’s unlikely to achieve that at scale, and if he does, it’ll mainly be in a liquidity-neutral way. I outlined the reasons and scenarios for that in my February 2026 public newsletter: Below-Baseline Scenarios President Trump has announced that his nominee for the next Fed chairman (a term that starts in May 2026) will be Kevin Warsh. The U.S. Senate would have to confirm it at that time to make it official. Warsh is on record saying he is in favor of a smaller Fed balance sheet, which is in contrast to the Fed’s existing forecasts. Therefore, it needs to be asked: could a shake-up in leadership at the Fed change their balance sheet composition? The answer is likely “not much” but with some caveats. -The chairman is powerful, but he’s only one of 12 votes on the Federal Open Market Committee, so he doesn’t unilaterally set policy. -The Fed and other federal agencies could further ease bank regulations, allowing them to hold more treasuries without negatively impacting their regulatory leverage ratios. That means the Fed can own fewer treasuries. -The Fed could take some steps to discourage excess reserve accumulation at banks, thereby distributing the reserves that are in the system a bit more evenly. This could let them shrink their balance sheet by perhaps a few hundred billion dollars. -The Treasury Department could increase its average debt duration and shrink its average cash account size (known as the Treasury General Account). A smaller cash account size would give more liquidity back to the banking system, enabling a smaller Fed balance sheet by perhaps a few hundred billion dollars. However, the government generally doesn’t want higher long-term interest rates, so they’re sensitive about how much supply of long-duration debt they issue. In theory, if all of those things were done, the Fed’s balance sheet could go down by somewhere around a trillion dollars. However, the chances of that happening are low. And importantly, all of those measures just move liquidity around. Banks buying more treasuries on fractional reserve is functionally similar to the Fed buying them with new reserves. And moving reserves around and reducing the Treasury General Account basically result in efficiency gains: doing more with less. At the end of the day, the Fed is going to optimize for 1) maintaining bank lending and broad money creation at a moderate pace, 2) ensuring the treasury security market remains liquid, and 3) ensuring that the repo market remains liquid and that any liquidity stresses that do pop up don’t remain acute for very long. -Lyn Alden, February 8th 2026 newsletter Current usage of the Fed’s standing repo facility remains muted, and the SOFR-IORB spread is fine as well, which together suggest that domestic liquidity conditions are fine at the moment. Bitcoin Supply Cycle As a reminder, or for investors new to the service, here’s an overview of Bitcoin price action. Bitcoin is a distributed open-source public ledger that has up to 21 million units (of which 18.5 million are already mined), which are divisible into fractions. No central authority can change this number; it requires a majority of decentralized network participants to agree to a change. So far, network participants only allowed for minor changes and security updates, because there is an in-built incentive not to change anything that would disrupt the scarcity of the tokens. One of the biggest updates was in 2017, which allowed for second-layer scaling solutions like the Lightning Network to connect with the base-layer blockchain. Some subnetworks have decided to make a bigger change, fork the Bitcoin protocol, and take their version in a new direction. These include Bitcoin Cash, Bitcoin Satoshi Vision, and other less well-known ones. So far, all of those forks failed to capture market capitalization from core Bitcoin itself, and lost value compared to Bitcoin. They are consistently unable to maintain the mining hash rate and large node network that Bitcoin maintains. Looking at the long-term logarithmic Bitcoin price chart, with instances of “halvings” annotated, we can see that Bitcoin is just doing what it has typically done at this stage of its supply cycle: A halving is a pre-programmed instance where the supply rate of new Bitcoin generated every 10 minutes gets cut in half, and occurs approximately every 4 years. Between halvings, there tends to be a period of price consolidation as the market reaches some degree of supply/demand equilibrium. Then, a pre-programmed halving occurs, new supply flow gets cut in half, the existing supply/demand balance gets disrupted, and a bull price run occurs as demand outpaces supply. This attracts more buyers and media attention (resulting in even higher demand vs reduced supply), momentum traders jump on board, and it encounters a huge blow-off top followed by a big correction. It then partially rebounds and eventually finds another consolidation range at a much higher level than the previous cycle. Then, another halving occurs and the fun starts all over… Many investors or financial media folks have been baffled by this year’s Bitcoin bull run, but doing homework on the protocol shows that, really, this bullishness was the higher-probability outcome all along after the halving event in May 2020, and lasting for about 18 months on average. I outlined this in detail in my public July 2020 article when Bitcoin was a little over $9,000. The sample size is small due to only having 12 years of price history, so there is never a guarantee of what it will do in any given cycle, but there are a variety of fundamental indicators we can watch to see how the current cycle is playing out compared to previous cycles. I think its properties are likely to lead to nation states buying it and mining it (and several smaller ones already have), but I prefer not to base decisions around the timing of when a particularly large nation state will buy it, and how much. Thus, I remain long-term bullish on bitcoin, and will monitor any purchase announcements by the U.S. government, but will consider them to be potential positive upside surprises. When the Bitcoin network had low fees, many of its critics said that the low fees would be a long-term problem, and that it’ll become insecure from lack of fees. This was despite the fact that overall fees were cyclically growing over time, and that the potential demand is nearly infinite while block space is fixed at four megabytes per ten minutes. Some of them breathlessly suggested all sorts of fixes for low fees, like to add a permanent tail emission to the network. And now that it went through several months of sustained high fees, there are people (sometimes the same critics, and sometimes other bitcoin proponents) complaining about high fees and saying that the network is damaged from all of these high fees. Many of them are breathlessly saying there should be immediate fixes to try to filter out more of these non-monetary use cases. The human urge to tinker is strong. As soon as a system doesn’t act exactly as people want, they immediately want to tinker with it. But some of the best things survive precisely because they are hard to tinker with, like the U.S. Constitution, and I would argue like the Bitcoin network. The Bitcoin network requires rather large supermajorities of opinion by node operators and miners to make major changes to its core functionality, which allows the network to remain consistent against the rapidly changing tide of human opinion, which tends to oscillate between extremes. In my view what both sides of this controversy fail to appreciate are the response functions. When fees were low, it incentivized people to find other uses for the block space, which led to higher fees. Now that fees are high, it is accelerating interest in layered solutions, and various companies have raised capital to build out more of those layers to address the high fees on the base layer and make more efficient use of block space. At ego death capital back during the bear market in 2022, we were expecting higher fees in the future even when fees were low at the time, which is why we invested in companies that are building out various scaling methods even at a time when they seemed unnecessary. The math is pretty straightforward; if Bitcoin as a network is going to continue to grow as it has been for 15 years now, meaningful base layer fees are going to develop, and so a variety of scaling methods are needed and will be demanded by the market. -Do I think that people should invest in meme tokens and NFTs on the Bitcoin network, which are currently responsible for causing higher fees on the network? No, I don’t. And I think the vast majority who do so will lose capital because they are buying into an expensive fad that is not scarce. -Do I think that miners and developers and node operators should rush to find ways to filter out these non-monetary use cases that are currently in demand? No, I don’t. And while they are welcome to try, I think that attempts to do so will continue to be unsuccessful. Filtering works well for spam that hardly anyone is willing to pay for, but doesn’t work well for spam that people do want to pay for. Instead, like any robust protocol that is resistant to rapid change and has value because of that fact, I think it will take time to develop an equilibrium. I view Bitcoin as a network to be well-designed as it is, meaning that it’s purposely simple and optimized for monetary transfers, but with the ability to put some non-monetary information into it, which goes through periods of fads as it matures. Samourai Wallet focuses on adding privacy back to bitcoins via a process known as a “coinjoin”. If you withdraw bitcoin from an exchange like Coinbase to your own self-custodial onchain wallet and spend that bitcoin at various merchants, then Coinbase (or any other exchange or custodian that you happened to withdraw from) can continue to track all of your spending details. In addition, those merchants that you pay for goods and services can check to see how much bitcoin you have in that address, and where it came from. It would be like if you withdraw physical cash from a bank, but the bank can see everything you spend the cash on going forward, and you have to write the amount that your savings account has on every dollar bill that you hand to merchants so that they can see that number and what bank it came from. That would be worse privacy than what we currently have with the current banking system. Coinjoins and similar privacy methods help to eliminate that fungibility issue with bitcoins and make them so that neither side can see how much bitcoin you have or where you are spending it. The vast majority of usage of coinjoin services like what Samourai offers is for legitimate privacy purposes. Various scaling solutions such as Lightning channels, the Liquid network, and Chaumian ecash wallets also provide good privacy for legitimate purposes. Bank Sector and Equal-Weight Market Analysis February 4, 2024 The macro section of this report focuses on liquidity conditions and the rate-of-change for various economic indicators. The digital asset section discusses bitcoin price action, mining news, and the unique intersection between macro and this industry. The investment analysis section provides an update on U.S. banks, and in particular the divergence between American Express and other banks. It also dives into the current dynamics between equal-weighted stock indices and market-weighted stock indices. As a housekeeping note, I’ll be doing a talk, discussion, and book signing at Princeton University on February 6th about Broken Money. The event will include a discussion with Carolyn Wilkins, the former deputy governor of the Bank of Canada. If you’re in the PA/NJ/NYC area near Princeton, consider coming to check it out. It’s open to the public but requires registration. Details are available here. Macro View Liquidity Indicators In the current era of fiscal dominance (which I would generally categorize as beginning in 2019), liquidity has been a driving force for many asset prices even more-so than it has been historically. Domestic liquidity has been flat-to-up since bottoming in late 2022 and early 2023. The Federal Reserve continues to run tight monetary policy, but the Treasury has offset that since late 2022 by running large deficits and shortening its average debt duration and helping to bring capital from reverse repos back into the financial system. As a result, the first three quarters of 2022 were particularly bad for liquidity, but the five quarters from late 2022 through 2023 have been decent for liquidity. This following chart shows the rate-of-change of domestic liquidity, where higher means better liquidity and down means worse liquidity. Sometimes the Fed and Treasury are moving in a similar direction, but more often than not they are moving in opposite directions and it comes down to a difference in magnitudes between them. The most recent major trend changes (Fed in early 2022 and Treasury in late 2022) are highlighted in green: That period during the first three quarters of 2022 was particularly brutal as both the Fed and Treasury were pointing downward for liquidity. Ever since the Treasury flipped the other way, it has been a more mixed situation with a mild upward bias. Meanwhile, the U.S. broad money supply was decreasing until spring 2023, but then began turning flat and more recently, upward: Looking globally, the dollar index matters quite a bit, and it has been moderately strengthening here in 2024. To summarize the past couple of years, it was rising in 2021 and 2022 until Q4 of 2022 coinciding with the bottom in liquidity, fell sharply in Q4 of 2022 as the Treasury’s operations became more positive for liquidity, and then has been flat throughout 2023 and into 2024. The global broad money supply denominated in dollars is a broad and straightforward global liquidity measure, and it has been consolidating sideways for two years generally but is well off its late-2022 lows. The base effects from exactly 12 months ago have reset the year-over-year percentage change (orange line) to zero, even as the absolute figure (blue line) remains roughly sideways: Overall, I expect flat-to-upward liquidity in 2024, and rising liquidity over the next few years, but I continue to monitor it every two weeks both quantitatively and policy-wise to look for potential changes to that outlook. U.S. Economy Over the past two years, the U.S. economy has been in sharp divergence mode. Some cyclical sectors have been sharply decelerating and then ultimately contracting, like manufacturing. Commercial real estate was severely damaged by the combination of work-from-home trends and higher interest rates. But industries directly or indirectly on the receiving side of the large fiscal deficits have been doing relatively good. A big challenge over the past several months has been to determine whether the cyclical aspects of the economy are still decelerating or if they are finding a floor and starting to stabilize. There are great analysts on both sides of that debate. Liquidity and PMIs are starting to stabilize and turn upward, while some other areas continue to point downward. Although I was in the recession camp during 2022, by early 2023 I’ve instead been straddling that debate somewhat by saying that there are no immediate signs of recession due to improving liquidity conditions, and to the extent that one materializes, I expect it to be a mild recession or “emerging market-like” recession due to the huge fiscal deficits that continue to stimulate parts of the economy. This coincided with the period where the Treasury began offsetting the Fed’s liquidity drain, and we entered a more neutral or positive liquidity regime. Overall, the trends in my view are pointing towards economic re-acceleration as a base case, but some of the downward areas can turn bad in a nonlinear way. Therefore, I don’t rule out the possibility of recession either, and still view us to be in this indeterminate state. PMIs and some of their leading sub-components are pointing upward from a low level: The Atlanta Fed’s current data points toward no recession here in Q1, although much of these inputs can be subject to revisions in hindsight: The cyclical side of the labor market (e.g. temporary workers and overtime hours) still looks weak. A drop of this magnitude is normally associated with a recession and there’s no significant sign of stabilization yet: Temporary workers were basically flat in January and technically ever-so-slightly up, which gave them the first uptick in two years. There were some months that were flat with a tiny downtick, so it’s all within the margin of error. Overall, the majority of indicators I track suggest some degree of upward re-acceleration, but it’s still fragile and subject to change, and not confirmed by all indicators. If it were to be confirmed by all indicators, it would likely already be in the middle of the uptrend by that point. Global Economy The copper-to-gold ratio is something I check regularly

user_input: Why did the US Treasury Department shorten its average debt maturity from 70 to 65 months during 2020 instead of locking in long-duration bonds, and how does that reliance on the US Treasury market's functioning relate to the Fed's likely policy response if Treasury liquidity deteriorates?
reference: During the pandemic year of 2020, the US Treasury Department abandoned its earlier plan to lengthen the average maturity of its debt issuance and instead cut the weighted average maturity from about 70 months to about 65 months, leaning heavily on short-term T-bill issuance. As its November 4, 2020 quarterly refunding statement explained, borrowing needs in the second half of FY2020 rose by an unforeseen and unprecedented $3.2 trillion, and roughly two-thirds of that, about $2.4 trillion, was met through increased bill issuance, effectively doubling bills outstanding. Although some analysts argued the US should have issued 50-year or 100-year bonds to lock in ultra-low rates, the more persuasive view is that yields were only that low because the Fed and other central banks were buying so many sovereign bonds; flooding the market with long-duration paper would have created a supply/demand problem. The fact that the Treasury reduced rather than extended maturities suggests it simply could not realistically do so while issuing trillions in debt. This matters for policy because the Treasury market sits at the core of the financial system. While the US Treasury and credit markets are not seized up, they have become shaky in terms of liquidity and yields. If the stock market falls, the Fed need not act for a while; if credit markets seize up, a Fed response is generally forced within weeks; but if the Treasury market seizes up, that represents totally broken market functioning at the core of the system and generally forces a Fed response within days. Beyond rate cuts, which markets began pricing in for 2023, the Fed has other tools it might deploy if Treasury liquidity does not improve, such as supplementary leverage ratio adjustments for commercial banks, which would let banks buy more Treasuries and help re-liquify that market.

Markets are starting to price in Fed rate cuts for 2023. Basically, markets now expect the Fed to keep tightening through 2022 but then to begin turning more dovish by next calendar year as economic conditions deteriorate. Given what’s happening with recession indicators, Treasury illiquidity, widening high yield spreads, and other factors, I do think this represents a reasonable base case. The Fed will probably perform significant rate hikes during the July and September FOMC meetings, but the further we go beyond that point, the harder it will be for the Fed to keep tightening policy at an aggressive pace. The Fed also has other tools that they might end up using by next year if liquidity in the Treasury market doesn’t improve, including supplementary leverage ratio adjustments for commercial banks, which would basically allow them to buy more Treasuries and help re-liquify that market. Germany’s structural trade deficit for decades has just evaporated down to nothing, since their energy bills are now so high. And notably, this has been a problem since late 2021, before the war. The war added additional uncertainty to the mix. Many people point out, correctly, that if Russia were to stop exporting gas to Europe, it would severely harm Russia as well as Europe. Russia is already severely hurting from import restrictions, so maintaining export cash flows is important to them. Russia and Europe in that sense are currently co-dependent on each other, Europe for energy imports and Russia for export cash flows, with both sides now eventually looking to build the infrastructure needed to sell or buy their natural gas respectively from other sources in the coming years. However, not all times are created equal. Suppose that Russia specifically shuts off natural gas to Germany and Poland for just the month of January, in the dead of winter. That alone wouldn’t impact Russian finances too much, but how would Germany and Poland fare with that happening to them during freezing temperatures? While natural gas prices remain so high, Europe’s economic competitiveness is declining, Russia is raking in record levels of export cash flows, and Russia maintains significant geopolitical leverage over the central/eastern portion of Europe, during a time when Europe is holding a lot of frozen Russian sovereign reserves due to Russia’s attack on Ukraine. user_input: How did Shanghai's zero-COVID lockdowns disrupt supply chains, and what was their status as lockdowns shifted toward Beijing?
reference: Shanghai was among the strictest areas under China's zero-COVID policy, with large portions of the city and dozens of other cities locked down over a three-week span even more thoroughly than in spring 2020. Subway traffic in Shanghai fell to basically zero, and the number of cargo ships waiting outside Shanghai's ports spiked to a record high, far surpassing the disruption of spring 2020, as confirmed by satellite ship tracking. Because Shanghai and other Chinese cities are massive manufacturing and logistics hubs, this breakdown in logistics and economic output carried negative implications for global supply chains and global economic growth in subsequent quarters, and it exacerbated supply-side inflation alongside the war in Ukraine. Subsequently, lockdowns appeared to have peaked in Shanghai and were easing somewhat, but the focus shifted to Beijing, where virus cases were found and anti-COVID measures were on the upswing. At the same time, Chinese policymakers signaled an end to the regulatory storm against tech companies and pointed toward fiscal and monetary easing, with the KWEB Chinese Internet ETF rising 7% on a day when most assets fell, though the ongoing lockdowns continued to create significant uncertainty for Chinese asset performance.

This year-to-date period has been one of the worst 4 months on record for a 60/40 stock/bond portfolio. We have to go back to 2008 to find a similar period. However, the 10-year yield piercing above 2.5% has been higher than my base case, even as an inflation bull and a bond bear. Due to how financialized the United States is, a drawdown in the stock market generally leads to less consumer spending (due to a reverse wealth effect), and consequently lower GDP growth and lower tax revenue. If bonds aren’t serving as a ballast for that, then the drawdown can be more impactful. The same is true for many other countries, but it is more often about their housing market rather than their stock market. As someone who has completely avoided long duration Treasury bonds for years, I’m actually somewhat sympathetic to them at this time on the long side. US Business Cycle Analysis Here is my updated heatmap of various economic indicators for the US economy over the past five years, measured in year-over-year percent change terms. Rather than describing the economy in narratives or qualitative terms, or cherry pick data to fit a particularly bullish or bearish view, it quantifies a broad section of data. The economic growth rate in year-over-year terms peaked in Q2 2021, while Q3 and Q4 had decelerating (but still positive) growth, along with persistently hot inflation. The first half of 2022 appears to be continuing the trend of decelerating growth and with still-hot inflation. The chart starts from the bottom and goes up over five years, and each column represents one of the economic indicators. For most of the chart, I use a green/yellow/red color spectrum. Green indicates solid growth, yellow indicates medium, and orange/red indicate slow growth or contraction, relative to the rest of the 5-year period for that indicator. In other words, green is good and red is bad. For inflation CPI, there is a separate blue/white/red color scale, because high or low inflation in a vacuum is not necessarily “good” or “bad” in the same way as the rest of the heat map. Red indicates higher price inflation, white indicates medium, and blue is lower price inflation, relative to the 5-year period. Economic slowdowns tend to be dis-inflationary while economic booms tend to be pro-inflationary, but there are also some business cycles that slow down with high inflation, and thus become “stagflationary”. So, inflation gets its own color scheme. Heat Map Indicators Referenced: Real Gross Domestic Product Industrial Production Advance Retail Sales, Excluding Food Services Total
