Macro View This continues to be an unusual macroeconomic environment. Demand-side inflation is beginning to subside in the US and elsewhere, with the removal of fiscal stimulus. However, supply-side inflation continues to be a significant problem, exacerbated by the war in Ukraine and China’s unusually strict lockdowns. Chinese Lockdowns China went through several weeks of doubling down on its zero-COVID policy, which has been quite a headscratcher for many analysts, myself included. The Omicron variant is extremely contagious but relatively mild, and yet they seem to be treating it like a zombie apocalypse disease from a horror movie. Large portions of Shanghai and dozens of other cities have been locked down over the past three weeks even more thoroughly than they locked down in spring of 2020. For example, overall subway traffic in Shanghai slowed to basically zero during these weeks, whereas there was still some minimal activity in spring 2020. Most notably, the number of cargo ships waiting outside of ports in Shanghai spiked to a record high, far surpassing the disruption that occurred two years ago in spring 2020. This has been confirmed with satellite ship tracking: Chart Source: Rodrigo Zeidan Documenting things in China is always difficult. The Chinese government is restrictive with data and speech, but then on the other hand, some western sources outside of the China sometimes try to sensationalize things to a greater degree than what is happening, and come off as xenophobic or unreliable. Filtering through sources to find what’s really happening is tricky. However, the available data clearly show that what’s happening is massive, and it’s confirmed in various ways by on-the-ground reporting. Approximately 40% of the Chinese population is estimated to be in strict lockdowns, with Shanghai being among the strictest. Jared Nelson, an American data compliance officer living in Shanghai has documented this situation in depth. People in his community were unable to leave apartments. Some volunteers for each building were allowed to exit and get supplies for the building but they had to wear a full-body hazmat-style suit to do so. Yaxue Cao pointed towards 100+ videos and images of rather extreme lockdown behavior throughout Shanghai. The government workers are often appearing as large groups of people all dressed in hazmat-style suits enforcing compliance on groups of people that are getting frustrated with their limited mobility and lack of resources. Patrick Madrid shared a video from a Chinese friend that showed tons of people screaming from their high-rise apartment windows. Similar videos have been shot and shared elsewhere in Shanghai. The issue is that food production, food delivery, medicine delivery systems are all strained. Many people have had trouble getting basic supplies while forced to remain in their apartments. Anthony Fu shared that he has been pretty lucky due to having some food stockpiles during his lockdown, but that the situation is harsh for his neighborhood. People have trouble getting food, and they get turned away from hospitals for many serious conditions. Qin Chen, who is locked down, shared a timeline of the lockdowns throughout Shanghai. Major media have reported on this as well. CNN reports of the difficulties getting food in the locked-down city of 25 million people, since the delivery system is not designed to handle 100% of food going through it. Reuters reports of the rising stress and difficulties that many residents are sharing on social media. The South China Morning Post had a very critical piece against the lockdowns, reporting that residents are frustrated with clunky lockdowns, lack of food and medicine, forced culling of their pets suspected to have the virus by health workers in hazmat suits, etc. In addition to having negative implications for Chinese asset prices and domestic politics, this breakdown in logistics and economic output has negative implications for global supply chains and global economic growth in the quarters ahead. Shanghai and other Chinese cities are massive manufacturing and logistics hubs, and all of that is now more disrupted in 2022 than in 2020. Inflation I’ve had an inflationary view for the past few years, which has played out even faster than I thought. This is due to both monetary inflation on the demand side and real resources constraints on the supply side. However, over the past several months I’ve been tracking a possible local top in year-over-year headline inflation occurring by the end of Q1 of this year. I described this back in December: From base effects in the CPI calculation, there’s a decent chance that we’ll see a local top in official CPI sometime in Q1 2022 within the 7-9% year-over-year range. As we look later into 2022 beyond that point, the future is less clear and depends on certain variables. -December 12, 2021 Two months ago, I re-iterated that year-over-year headline inflation would likely top by the end of Q1 or the early part of Q2. The caveat, however, was that if something caused energy prices to spike; in that scenario inflation could overshoot my base case. Here was my description, since it’s still mostly relevant: The producer price index is showing signs of having reached a local top in year-over-year terms. I think we’ll probably see the same for headline CPI by late Q1 or early Q2. The reason has to do with base effects. Monthly inflation has been rather steady for about a year now, so now high inflation prints are about to start lapping year-ago similarly-high inflation prints, and thus the year-over-year figures are likely to stop going up. Monthly inflation would need to break out to a higher level in order to get yearly inflation up at this point. However, if inflation remains relatively high (4-8%), even if it stops going higher on a year-over-year basis, that’s still a significant problem. Investor views about what inflation is going to do next tend to be very polarized. There is one camp that argues that all of this inflation is transitory, just caused by supply chain disruptions, and that it’ll go back to normal soon.

reference: The Inflation Reduction Act played two distinct roles. On the manufacturing side, it provided subsidies for building out semiconductor manufacturing facilities and other industries deemed strategically important, which helped drive a roughly $160 billion uptick in manufacturing construction spending during 2022 and 2023 above the roughly $80 billion/year baseline that represents the ongoing replacement cost of the existing manufacturing base; that surge is now showing signs of rolling over. On the pharmaceutical/biotech side, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 gave the U.S. federal government more authority to negotiate drug prices and included other measures aimed at reining in rising healthcare spending, with the Congressional Budget Office estimating the drug provisions would reduce the fiscal deficit by $237 billion over ten years. Because healthcare companies face regulatory risk rather than typical cyclical/recession risk, this made regulation their main concern, though the sector was viewed as already reasonably priced with the Act in mind, and a split Congress made larger changes unlikely within an investable time horizon.

It can still negatively affect foreign exporters, though, in the form of reduced volumes as overall economic growth decreases. Ethereum Note Ethereum 2.o staking has a rather significant centralization problem occurring, even faster than I would have guessed. There’s a network effect stacked on top of an economy of scale that is drawing a higher and higher percentage of staked ETH into one protocol. Alex Berge was one of the first to point this issue out in detail last year, and he did so before it became a huge measurable problem, from first principles analysis. It reached my attention at the time, but I wasn’t sure how quickly this issue would turn into a practical problem. Then, Dap wrote an article for SureSats about this a couple weeks ago, updating the issue and showing how quickly it’s indeed centralizing due to compounded network effects as Alex had anticipated. I read the article, checked a few points out, and wrote a tweet thread about it. A couple days later, Fortune Magazine picked up the story and wrote about the issue with a link to my thread and a few other threads on the subject. I’ll try to summarize it in a bit more detail here. Liquid Staking Derivatives 101 To run an Ethereum 2.0 validator, you need 32 ETH. If ETH is $3k per coin for example, that would be $96k to run a validator. Most people don’t have that amount. Only wealthy people can run Ethereum validators. So, third parties can stake ETH for normal customers in smaller amounts. Exchanges like Coinbase and Kraken, for example, can take a customer’s ETH with their permission and stake it along with other peoples’ ETH. They run many full validators, and their customers basically have an off-chain claim to a partial validator. The problem with this is that large centralized entities end up controlling a lot of the staked ETH in a custodial fashion, which means they have a lot of influence over which transactions are added to the blockchain. Smart contracts also popped up to do this, with liquid staking derivatives. The biggest one is called Lido. You can deposit your ETH coin into Lido’s smart contract, and receive a stETH coin in return, which represents your claim on that ETH. This is an extremely attractive solution from a profit point of view because it lets users earn double the interest on their ETH. Theoretically, staked ETH is supposed to have an opportunity cost compared to using it to earn yield in a DeFi protocol. Users give up DeFi yield, in order to stake their ETH and earn a yield from validation. However, with a liquid staking derivative stETH, a user can have their cake and eat it to. They can deposit their ETH into Lido, receive stETH as their claim on it, and earn the staking yield. Then they can take that stETH coin (which is equal in value to one ETH), and deposit it into a DeFi protocol to earn additional yield on that stETH. Basically, with this liquid staking protocol solution, users get liquidity similarly to unstaked ETH, while actually staking. And liquidity is a major network effect; a stETH token is a lot more desirable than the derivative coin of a much smaller staking provider, which begets more people staking with Lido and using stETH. Technically anyone can create a new liquid staking protocol, but in practice, it concentrates towards one. Lido has about 90% of the liquid staking market share despite the existence of multiple competitors. Source: Dune Analytics, @eliasimos More concerningly, Lido now has nearly 30% of all staked ETH and climbing. Additionally, processing transactions on a smart contract blockchain offers a lot more arbitrage opportunities than processing transactions on something simple like Bitcoin. Miners/stakers can run complex software analysis to find arbitrage opportunities in terms of how to order their transactions on smart contract blockchains, and this naturally comes with economies of scale. This is called miner extracted value or “MEV”. The combination of liquid staking providers with MEV represents a powerful set of network effects that are likely to quickly centralize the transaction processing of the system post-Merge, unless something is changed. Bitcoin miners don’t have this issue anywhere near the same degree. Mining has some economies of scale, but it starts to top out pretty quickly. In other words, it’s more cost effective to have 5% of the Bitcoin mining market than only 0.5% of the market due to various cost synergies and economies of scale, but there’s no significant benefit to a miner as they keep going higher than that, and so the ability to reach higher and higher is constrained. Liquid staking, however, has an actual self-reinforcing network effect rather than just an economy of scale from its MEV, and this can trend towards controlling the majority of the market unless big players deliberately go against their own economic interests and avoid using it. The risks of this are pretty apparent. The blockchain becomes more centralized, and a large number of staked ETH ends up in a single smart contract that, if it is exploited/hacked in some way, would result in billions of dollars worth of lost funds. Solana Note The Solana blockchain went offline again. I’ve lost track of how many times this has happened now. And as a proof-of-stake system, it required a manual restart by large validators coordinating together on Discord. It was completely offline for seven hours, followed by more hours of ongoing restoration. There is a case for semi-centralized blockchains like Solana. A federated database that a number of large entities can control and audit, is a bit more decentralized than a single database in one entity’s control, while still being quite efficient. However, the total addressable market of that sort of product remains unclear. Smart contracts are a competitive environment, with thin economic moats, and an emphasis on high speeds and low costs. Final Thoughts The Democrats’ Build Back Better bill was recently derailed for 2021 because it didn’t get support from Senator Joe Manchin, and it needs every Democrat vote to get through. They are going to attempt a revised bill in 2022 but it’s unclear if it will pass or not. My base case is that some smaller version of it will pass prior to the 2022 midterm election but I don’t have high conviction on that view. Things like the child tax credit extension in that bill would be relevant for nominal GDP and inflation forecasts. In recent news however, President Biden did extend the pause on student loan repayments through May 2022. All else being equal, that’s a minor stimulus around the margins for that period because it leaves more cash in borrowers’ hands. Overall, due to less monetary support and fiscal support for markets as I described in my prior report, I am not as bullish on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 in 2022 compared to the performance of these indices in 2020 and 2021. Here’s my chart from my prior premium report, showing the broad US stock market in red with the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet in blue, along with some annotations: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed, annotated by Lyn Alden In period since the global financial crisis, the broad US market has generally struggled when the Fed is not increasing its balance sheet and when fiscal stimulus is not actively occurring or anticipated to shortly occur (e.g. the rally in the purple circle regarding tax cuts). As the blue line flattens out in spring 2022, if the US doesn’t get another round of fiscal stimulus, then it wouldn’t be surprising to see the red line chop along for a period of time as well. That doesn’t mean that I necessarily think markets will crash. They might even grind up for a positive year. However, I don’t expect it to keep going up at this rapid of a rate, and instead expect more volatility in general. However, I’m not particularly bearish on the US economy itself for 2022; the labor market remains tight, credit growth is expanding mildly, and the Omicron variant seems to be highly transmissible but not very deadly. In other words, after 2020 and 2021 were years where the stock market did better than we might otherwise expect from the state of the economy, I suspect 2022 might be a year where the state of the economy does better than what the stock market will do. I’ll continue to monitor data on that idea. I continue to have a relatively defensive outlook, but I do like a lot of value stocks and global stocks, including healthcare, energy pipelines, homebuilders, and consumer staples. Scotiabank Update I most recently recommended the Bank of Nova Scotia or “Scotiabank” (BNS) in a November 22, 2020 report, and I think we’re due for an update here. An update with this one also helps us dig into what’s happening with financial stocks and value equities broadly. Since that November report, we’ve had a big uptick in Scotiabank stock, which brings up the reasonable question of whether it’s too hot now: However, when we zoom out, it’s still in a big sideways consolidation: Chart Source: F.A.S.T. Graphs That chart is for the Canadian dollar version, but whether in US dollars or Canadian dollars, it’s pretty similar. The stock is trading at less than 11x analyst-consensus 2021 earnings, with a 4.5% dividend. I wouldn’t call that overheated yet, when talking about a long-term dividend stock holding. The stock remains mildly below-average in terms of valuation, despite the recent euphoria in risk assets more broadly. The dividend yield is above-average, the cyclically-adjusted price/earnings ratio is below average, and the price/book is below average: And this chart shows Scotiabank’s dividend yield minus Canada’s 10-year government bond yield: Decades ago, government bonds had a much higher yield. Scotiabank had a lower yield, in exchange for more growth. Now, you get almost 3% more yield by being willing to hold Scotiabank, and historically it grows the dividend in most years as well. So, when everyone is talking about an overvalued market, it really only refers to growth stocks in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. In contrast, there are plenty of boring companies trading at below-average valuations around the world, but they are often things like banks and energy pipelines that underperformed over the past decade and few people want to touch. Fundamentally, Scotiabank is doing pretty good. Their loan losses are well-provisioned, and they continue to increase their rate of mobile app usage among customers, adapting well to modern banking trends. They have diverse retail and business banking relationships, and are active among multiples lines of business. Importantly, unlike Europe and Japan, Canada and the Latin American markets that Scotiabank operates in have positive yield curves. More Broadly: Value vs Growth This chart shows the MSCI ACWI value index vs the MSCI ACWI growth index. Whenever it goes up, it means value stocks are globally outperforming growth stocks, and whenever it goes down, it means growth stocks are outperforming: Looking back historically longer-term, periods of higher inflation correspond to value stocks generally outperforming growth stocks. This was true in the 1940s, the 1970s, and the 2000s. On the value side, commodity producers benefit from higher prices and banks benefit from positive yield curves. On the growth side, the growth/tech companies do fine fundamentally, but their valuations get pressured from higher inflation and higher long-end interest rates. As an example of the type of growth stocks that are on the other side of that growth-to-value rotation, we can see examples like Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) that rolled over but are still very pricey by historical standards: Chart Source: F.A.S.T. Graphs Basically, companies like Cadence are great in terms of underlying fundamentals, but became quite overheated in terms of valuation in 2020. Cadence trades at a forward estimated price/earnings/growth ratio (“PEG ratio”) of 4x. And despite being a mature company, it still doesn’t pay a dividend. While there are select growth stocks I own and would buy on corrections, I continue to prefer a value tilt at this time. There are plenty of good companies in the healthcare sector, financial sector, and energy sector that remain at below-average valuations despite in many cases having improved their underlying quality in a difficult disinflationary environment over the past several years. Scotiabank Risks Scotiabank has a variety of risks, in line with the rest of the global banking sector. Credit Risk The global banking system still faces considerable uncertainty. As governments taper stimulus, banks could face more headwinds. However, I think that there is a feedback function here; any slowness of growth and return of disinflation and solvency problems, has a good chance of stirring up another round of fiscal support. At this stage of the long-term debt cycle with rising populism, policymakers have a tight response time towards economic issues. Scotiabank has exposure to Canada’s expensive housing market, but less-so than some of their rival banks which is why it is my preferred Canadian bank. Instead, Scotiabank has diversified into Latin America via Mexico, Chile, Peru, and Columbia. That’s a combination that I like quite a bit because it gives investors curated emerging market exposure through a developed market bank. Interest Rate Risk One of the biggest risks for banks around the world is interest rate risk. Unlike credit risk which hits hard and fast, interest rate risk slowly bleeds the banks of profitability over time. Banks don’t do well in zero-rate or negative-rate environments, and tend to prefer steeper yield curves. European and Japanese banks have been absolutely crushed by low rate policy for decades now. Canada and the United States offer better prospects for this than their European and Japanese peers. Scotiabank further distributes their risk by having exposure to emerging markets that generally have higher inflation and higher rates, in exchange for more volatility and credit risk. At this time, I like gold as a hedge for interest rate risk. The gold price is strongly inversely correlated to real yields. Gold does better if real rates stay low. Banks do better if nominal yields go up and the yield curve has a positive slope. If inflation runs hot and the yield curve remains steep but below the inflation rate (my base case for the time being), then both gold and banks can do well. Currency Risk Scotiabank operates in multiple countries and has broad currency exposure. reference: Kevin Warsh was named President Trump\u2019s nominee to replace Jerome Powell as Fed chairman when Powell\u2019s term as chair ends in May. Warsh, a former Fed board governor, has historically been more hawkish than average, favoring higher interest rates and a smaller Fed balance sheet, and many market participants view his selection as the primary catalyst for the sharp sell-off in precious metals and bitcoin in the days after the news \u2014 bitcoin briefly reclaimed $96k then fell back into the $80ks and even sub-$80k in illiquid weekend trading, with leveraged traders being liquidated adding to the downside volatility. However, Warsh\u2019s recent statements suggest he wants to cut rates, pointing to AI-driven productivity growth as a deflationary force, and Trump has been vocal about wanting lower rates. On the balance sheet, the odds of meaningful shrinkage are low: banks are near the low end of their ample reserve range, which is why the Fed already shifted to balance sheet expansion. The structural options (disincentives for excess reserves, bank deregulation to hold more treasuries, encouraging the Treasury to term out debt and shrink its General Account) are each worth only a couple hundred billion in minimum reserve size, are unlikely to all happen, and are themselves pro-liquidity substitutions. The takeaway is that a Warsh-led Fed is unlikely to cause treasury dysfunction, repo illiquidity, or a material slowdown in bank lending, and bitcoin is still expected to have a reasonably strong 2026-2027 given favorable liquidity conditions and washed-out sentiment.

The Boom in AI Agents February 1, 2026 The macro section of this report looks at liquidity conditions, US GDP growth, and the new Fed chairman nominee. The digital assets section takes a look at bitcoin and other crypto price action, which has been weak lately. The investment analysis section focuses on the latest round of AI news, sifting out substance from the hype. Macro View New (Expected) Fed Chair President Trump announced that his nominee for the next chairman of the Federal Reserve will be Kevin Warsh. Jerome Powell’s term as chairman ends in May of this year, although he will still be a Fed board governor until 2028, unless he resigns from that or is otherwise removed for cause. Kevin Warsh was formerly a Fed board governor, and has historically taken a more hawkish stance on monetary policy than average. He has generally favored higher interest rates and a smaller Fed balance sheet. Many market participants consider his selection to be the primary catalyst for the sharp sell-off in precious metals and bitcoin that occurred in the days following the news. However, Warsh’s recent statements have indicated a desire to cut interest rates. He has pointed to AI-driven productivity growth for providing enough of a deflationary force to ease up on monetary policy while keeping broad price inflation in check. President Trump has been vocal about his desire for lower rates, so it strains credulity to think there haven’t been discussions between Trump and his candidates about rates with an understanding that his next Fed chairman would lean dovish in the intermediate term. I would place low odds that Warsh would be able to meaningfully shrink the balance sheet. With current policies in place, banks are near the low end of their ample reserve range, which is why the Fed has shifted toward balance sheet growth. Technically, there are some steps the Fed can take to reduce the balance sheet without impacting liquidity too much. However, they’re pretty structural and some of them involve coordination with other federal groups. They can add some disincentives to banks for holding excess reserves, so that the reserves that are in the system are more spread out. They can encourage more bank deregulation to let banks hold more treasury securities without negatively impacting their various capital requirements. They can encourage the Treasury Department to term out their debt more and reduce the average size of their Treasury General Account with the Fed. Each of those items could save a couple hundred billion dollars in minimum reserve size. While one of these items may happen (and the Fed has already worked with other groups to lighten SLR bank regulations around holding treasury securities), it’s unlikely for multiple of them to happen. And they are all pro-liquidity changes that basically replace a portion of reserves with other types of liquidity (e.g. more bank fractional reserve liquidity, or less sucking-out of liquidity by the Treasury). The main takeaway is that a Warsh-led Fed is not going to take actions that result in treasury security dysfunction, repo illiquidity, or a material slowdown in bank lending and deposit growth. Domestic Liquidity Domestic liquidity conditions in the US are on the uptrend ever since the Fed shifted from balance sheet reduction to balance sheet expansion. The liquidity shortages that were present in the repo market from September through December have been mostly absent in January. However, the Treasury General Account has been rising to above-normal levels in the past two weeks, which sucks liquidity out of the financial system. Therefore, overall liquidity levels are chopping sideways at the moment, with the Treasury and Fed pulling in two different directions: I expect liquidity conditions to stabilize and then gradually trend upward through April. At that point, we’ll see what the new guidance from Warsh is (assuming he indeed gets confirmed as the new Fed chairman). Global Liquidity Approximately a week ago, the dollar index tumbled to the lowest level it has been since late 2021. Since the dollar is the unit of account for the majority of cross-border debts, a weaker dollar tends to be good for global liquidity, all else being equal. However, it strengthened a bit on the news of Warsh being nominated. There’s nothing on the horizon that looks set to greatly boost or diminish global liquidity, and so my base case is for global liquidity to gradually grind upward in the coming year. I expect the dollar to continue to devalue a bit versus the Chinese yuan, but have no particular view on its direction relative to the euro. US Economy In my prior report, I highlighted that economic numbers are coming in pretty hot, but that some tariff-timing impacts are artificially boosting them, which is the opposite of the drag that tariff-timing impacts had in Q1 2025: In particular, the Atlanta Fed is showing a 5% annualized real GDP growth rate for Q4 2025, which is completed but not yet reported: However, there’s a big caveat to that. They have over $900 million in cash equivalents, they have total net debt equal to about one year’s worth of net income, and they operate with a solid balance sheet broadly. One of Copa’s smart strategies is that all 106 airplanes in their fleet are the same type: Boeing 737. They have some different versions/ages of the 737 family, but every single aircraft is a 737. The Boeing 737 is the most common commercial aircraft globally. It’s ideal for short-to-medium range trips, which are the types of trips that Copa operates. Other larger types of aircraft are generally used for cross-ocean trips, which Copa doesn’t do. And they don’t use a mix of Boeing and Airbus. By specializing in short-to-medium trips with Boeing 737s, they are able to unify their maintenance and pilot training all under one type and keep costs lower than competitors. Although it’s funny to apply a Steve Jobs quote to an airline, it’s relevant here: Even though I used to work in the aviation simulation industry (including working a lot with Boeing 737 avionics), I have historically not been a fan of investing in airline stocks. When I’m bullish on the industry, I generally buy airports or travel agencies (e.g. OMAB and BKNG) which have stronger economic moats and less cyclicality. And one tragic accident or other negative headline can severely disrupt a small airline. So, to the extent that I’m interested in Copa, it would only be with a small position. user_input: how Coinbase show up two times in these reports - like with Grayscale trust holdin coins, and also privacy stuff when you take bitcoin off exchange?
reference: Coinbase appears in two different roles. First, Grayscale is described as a self-contained entity whose coins are custodied at Coinbase’s institutional custody platform, which still carries counterparty risk since holding bitcoin through any third party does. This mattered because Genesis and its parent DCG got into trouble, raising questions about the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust (GBTC), which traded at a deep discount to NAV with possible outcomes including a sale of the Grayscale business, an ETF conversion, or a liquidation. Second, Coinbase is used as the example exchange in the privacy discussion: if you withdraw bitcoin from an exchange like Coinbase to your own self-custodial onchain wallet and then spend it at merchants, Coinbase (or whichever custodian you withdrew from) can keep tracking your spending details, and merchants can see how much bitcoin is in that address and where it came from. That is why coinjoin services such as Samourai Wallet, plus Lightning channels, Liquid, and Chaumian ecash, exist to restore fungibility and privacy — though the DOJ seized Samourai’s assets and arrested its co-founders, and the FBI warned people to use only KYC-collecting crypto services.

Grayscale on Watch Genesis is a huge trading desk and lender in the broad crypto industry, and has been in operation since 2013. It’s part of Digital Currency Group “DCG” which as a parent company also owns the Grayscale set of trusts, the Coindesk media publication, and has portfolio exposure to countless crypto and crypto-adjacent entities. Genesis has faced massive losses this year, especially with the Luna/Celsius/3AC blow-up this past spring, and continuing into FTX exposure more recently. As a result, they had to pause withdrawals on their lending products, which impacted various other entities including Gemini, one of the largest crypto exchanges. The parent company DCG loaned money to Genesis, and so now DCG itself is in trouble, and is trying to raise emergency capital in a tough market. Naturally, this brought up some questions about the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust (GBTC). Grayscale is a self-contained entity, with its coins custodied at Coinbase’s institutional custody platform. Whenever you hold bitcoin through a third party, though, it always comes with some counterparty risks. It’s possible that DCG will sell its Grayscale business to another asset manager. Grayscale provides large cash flows from relatively high fees, and can be sold for an upfront infusion of cash. Alternatively, it’s possible that the Grayscale trusts could be liquidated. If the trusts are liquidated, it would result in selling a lot of bitcoin and other cryptos, which could hurt the price, but it would also close the gap to NAV as the shareholders are cashed out. In that event, it would probably do well to be long GBTC and short BTC futures, although it’s not a trade I intend to perform, since I view the potential liquidation as being outside of my base case. It’s pretty unusual for a closed-end fund or trust to persistently trade more than 20% below net asset value, and yet GBTC’s discount is more than twice that. Other than an eventual conversion to an ETF, or a liquidation of the trust, or a decision by Grayscale to do a buyback or allow redemptions, there aren’t any catalysts that would force it to trade at NAV. A number of entities, ranging from Three Arrows Capital to BlockFi, have been forced sellers of GBTC, which seems to have put a lot of downward pressure on its price. I view GBTC as a deep value play for a portfolio, but I would continue to be cautious with position sizing. Overall, GBTC has been pretty disappointing relative to holding bitcoin directly, but with the SEC not allowing a spot bitcoin ETF, there have been limited alternatives. But then, oops, in response to disinflation the government and central bank print and distribute trillions of dollars and generate inflation, and that disinflationary thesis goes out the window. In other words, they failed to appreciate the incentives and power behind the likely response function to disinflation. When the Bitcoin network had low fees, many of its critics said that the low fees would be a long-term problem, and that it’ll become insecure from lack of fees. This was despite the fact that overall fees were cyclically growing over time, and that the potential demand is nearly infinite while block space is fixed at four megabytes per ten minutes. Some of them breathlessly suggested all sorts of fixes for low fees, like to add a permanent tail emission to the network. And now that it went through several months of sustained high fees, there are people (sometimes the same critics, and sometimes other bitcoin proponents) complaining about high fees and saying that the network is damaged from all of these high fees. Many of them are breathlessly saying there should be immediate fixes to try to filter out more of these non-monetary use cases. The human urge to tinker is strong. As soon as a system doesn’t act exactly as people want, they immediately want to tinker with it. But some of the best things survive precisely because they are hard to tinker with, like the U.S. Constitution, and I would argue like the Bitcoin network. The Bitcoin network requires rather large supermajorities of opinion by node operators and miners to make major changes to its core functionality, which allows the network to remain consistent against the rapidly changing tide of human opinion, which tends to oscillate between extremes. In my view what both sides of this controversy fail to appreciate are the response functions. When fees were low, it incentivized people to find other uses for the block space, which led to higher fees. Now that fees are high, it is accelerating interest in layered solutions, and various companies have raised capital to build out more of those layers to address the high fees on the base layer and make more efficient use of block space. At ego death capital back during the bear market in 2022, we were expecting higher fees in the future even when fees were low at the time, which is why we invested in companies that are building out various scaling methods even at a time when they seemed unnecessary. The math is pretty straightforward; if Bitcoin as a network is going to continue to grow as it has been for 15 years now, meaningful base layer fees are going to develop, and so a variety of scaling methods are needed and will be demanded by the market. -Do I think that people should invest in meme tokens and NFTs on the Bitcoin network, which are currently responsible for causing higher fees on the network? No, I don’t. And I think the vast majority who do so will lose capital because they are buying into an expensive fad that is not scarce. -Do I think that miners and developers and node operators should rush to find ways to filter out these non-monetary use cases that are currently in demand? No, I don’t. And while they are welcome to try, I think that attempts to do so will continue to be unsuccessful. Filtering works well for spam that hardly anyone is willing to pay for, but doesn’t work well for spam that people do want to pay for. Instead, like any robust protocol that is resistant to rapid change and has value because of that fact, I think it will take time to develop an equilibrium. I view Bitcoin as a network to be well-designed as it is, meaning that it’s purposely simple and optimized for monetary transfers, but with the ability to put some non-monetary information into it, which goes through periods of fads as it matures. The U.S. Government’s Privacy Crackdown On April 24th, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that they seized assets of Samourai Wallet and arrested the co-founders for money laundering and unlicensed money transmission. They are extraditing one of the defendants from Europe. And then on April 25th, the FBI put out a warning saying that people should avoid non-KYC crypto services and only use crypto services that do indeed collect all their users’ identity information. Samourai Wallet focuses on adding privacy back to bitcoins via a process known as a “coinjoin”. If you withdraw bitcoin from an exchange like Coinbase to your own self-custodial onchain wallet and spend that bitcoin at various merchants, then Coinbase (or any other exchange or custodian that you happened to withdraw from) can continue to track all of your spending details. In addition, those merchants that you pay for goods and services can check to see how much bitcoin you have in that address, and where it came from. It would be like if you withdraw physical cash from a bank, but the bank can see everything you spend the cash on going forward, and you have to write the amount that your savings account has on every dollar bill that you hand to merchants so that they can see that number and what bank it came from. That would be worse privacy than what we currently have with the current banking system. Coinjoins and similar privacy methods help to eliminate that fungibility issue with bitcoins and make them so that neither side can see how much bitcoin you have or where you are spending it. The vast majority of usage of coinjoin services like what Samourai offers is for legitimate privacy purposes. Various scaling solutions such as Lightning channels, the Liquid network, and Chaumian ecash wallets also provide good privacy for legitimate purposes.
